name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
summary: Captured by Fulani slave raiders in March 1821 at about age 12 and sold to Portuguese slavers, Ajayi was freed when a British Royal Navy ship intercepted the vessel and was resettled in Freetown, Sierra Leone. Taken into the care of the Church Missionary Society, he learned to read with remarkable speed - reading the Bible with ease within months - and converted to Christianity. He was baptized on 11 December 1825 by the missionary John Raban, taking the name Samuel Crowther after a CMS pioneer. He became the first student of Fourah Bay College (1827), married fellow freed slave Susan Asano, was ordained in 1843, and in 1864 was consecrated the first African Anglican bishop. He translated the Bible into Yoruba and, in 1848 at Abeokuta, was reunited with and baptized his long-lost mother Hannah.
sources: Samuel Ajayi Crowther — National Portrait Gallery, London (label text, 2025)

name: Olaudah Equiano
summary: Kidnapped as a boy from an Igbo village (in present-day Nigeria), Equiano survived the Middle Passage, bought his own freedom in 1766, and was baptized into the Church of England in 1759. His autobiography, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (1789), describes a genuine Christian conversion interwoven with visions and a deepening faith, and became one of the most influential texts of the British abolition movement.
sources: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano — self-published, London, 1789

name: William Wade Harris
summary: A Grebo from eastern Liberia raised between Methodist Christianity and traditional religion, Harris was a political prisoner in Monrovia when he reported a vision of the angel Gabriel commanding him to preach. Beginning in 1913 he walked barefoot through Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast baptizing an estimated 100,000-200,000 converts in 18 months. Though deported by French authorities in 1915, his mass movement laid the groundwork for the Harrist churches and the growth of Christianity in Ivory Coast.
sources: Gordon M. Haliburton — The Prophet Harris, Longman, 1971

name: Jacobus Elisa Johannes Capitein
summary: Born around 1717 near Elmina on the Gold Coast, he was captured at age seven or eight and sold to a Dutch sea captain, who gifted him to the trader Jacobus van Goch. Van Goch took him to the Netherlands in 1728 and raised him as an adopted son in The Hague, where the boy attended the catechism class of the local Dutch Reformed church and was baptized into the Protestant faith in July 1735. Expressing a desire to return to Africa as a missionary, he studied theology at Leiden University from 1737 and on 10 March 1742 defended a Latin dissertation arguing that slavery was not incompatible with Christian freedom. Ordained in the Dutch Reformed Church, he returned to Elmina Castle as chaplain and schoolmaster, producing the first Fante grammar and translating the Ten Commandments and catechism into Fante before his death in 1747.

name: Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga)
summary: Born Mvemba a Nzinga, son of the Kongo king Nzinga a Nkuwu, he encountered the gospel when Portuguese Franciscan and Dominican priests arrived with Diogo Cao's expedition, aided by young Kongolese nobles who had been educated and baptized in Portugal. In 1491 he was baptized together with his father, taking the Christian name Afonso. After his father's death he defeated a rival half-brother in battle and became manikongo (c. 1506-1509), establishing Catholicism as the kingdom's religion: churches and chapels rose in every province, schools trained a Kongolese clergy, and his son Henrique became the first African Catholic bishop. From his capital at Mbanza Kongo he wrote a remarkable series of letters to the kings of Portugal (1509-1541), including famous protests against the slave trade, earning him the title 'Apostle of Kongo.'

name: John Chilembwe
summary: Converted through the radical Baptist missionary Joseph Booth, Chilembwe studied theology in the United States (supported by the National Baptist Convention) and was ordained in 1899. Returning to Nyasaland in 1901, he founded the Providence Industrial Mission — the first African-initiated church in the region — and built schools and churches. Outraged by colonial labor abuses, he led the 1915 Chilembwe uprising and was killed by colonial forces; Malawi honors him as a national hero.
sources: George Shepperson & Thomas Price — Independent African: John Chilembwe and the Origins, Setting and Significance of the Nyasaland Native Rising of 1915 — Edinburgh University Press, 1958

name: Apolo Kivebulaya
summary: Born Waswa Munubi and first apprenticed to a witch doctor, then drawn to Islam at the Kabaka's court, Apolo encountered the CMS missionary Alexander Mackay and was baptized in 1895, taking the name of the biblical Apollos. Sent as a catechist to Toro and later the Ituri forest, he survived imprisonment and beating, became known as the 'apostle to the pygmies' (Mbuti), translated Scripture, and was made Canon of Namirembe Cathedral. He is commemorated in the Church of England calendar on 30 May.
sources: Emma Wild-Wood — The Mission of Apolo Kivebulaya — James Currey, 2020

name: Charles Lwanga (Kaloli Lwanga)
summary: A page in the court of Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda, Lwanga converted to Catholicism through the White Fathers and was baptized on 15 November 1885. As master of the royal pages he instructed and protected the younger Christian pages from the king's demands. When persecution broke out in 1886 he refused to renounce his faith and was burned alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886, dying while praying for his executioners; he was canonized by Pope Paul VI in 1964 as patron of African youth.

name: Ntsikana
summary: A Xhosa councillor's son raised in traditional life — initiation, polygamous marriage, praise-singing — Ntsikana encountered London Missionary Society preaching and then, around 1815, reported a life-changing vision of God. Converted, he divorced one wife, composed the first hymns in isiXhosa (including the famous 'Great Hymn', Ulo Thixo omkhulu), and preached a Christianity expressed in Xhosa categories of hunting and pastoral life, founding an indigenous Xhosa Christian movement.

name: Tiyo Soga
summary: Born to a Xhosa councillor, Soga's Christian mother secured his upbringing at the Thyume mission; he made a formal profession of faith and was baptized in Glasgow, Scotland in May 1848. Ordained in Scotland in 1856 — the first Black South African ordained to Christian ministry — he returned to the Eastern Cape, translated the Bible and Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress into isiXhosa, and wrote hymns still sung today, embodying a faith both Christian and African.
sources: Donovan Williams — Umfundisi: A Biography of Tiyo Soga, 1829-1871 — Lovedale Press, 1978

name: Magema Magwaza Fuze
summary: Born in the mid-1840s near Pietermaritzburg, Magema was sent at about age 12 (1856) by his father to Ekukhanyeni, the mission station of Anglican Bishop John William Colenso, where he learned to read and write. There he converted to Christianity and was baptized into the Anglican Church. Trained as a printer and compositor on Colenso's press, he printed Bibles and mission literature, later opening his own print shop in Pietermaritzburg and writing for isiZulu newspapers. In 1896-1898 he served as secretary to the exiled Zulu king Dinuzulu on St Helena, and in 1922 he published Abantu Abamnyama Lapa Bavela Ngakona - the first book-length history in isiZulu by a native speaker - as a kholwa (Christian convert) intellectual.

name: Bernard Mizeki (Mamiyeri Mitseka Gwambe)
summary: A migrant laborer from Inhambane, Mozambique, working in Cape Town's slums, Mizeki attended Anglican night school, converted, and was baptized on 9 March 1886. Recruited by Bishop Knight-Bruce as a catechist for Mashonaland, he mastered Shona, translated much of the Bible and Prayer Book into Chishona, and built a mission at Nhowe. When warned to flee the 1896 uprising, he refused to abandon his converts and was speared to death on 18 June 1896; his shrine is a major pilgrimage site.
sources: Jean Farrant — Mashonaland Martyr: Bernard Mizeki and the Pioneer Church — 1966

name: Sechele I (Kgosi Sechele a Motswasele)
summary: Chief of the Bakwena, Sechele met David Livingstone in 1847, learned to read with extraordinary speed, and was baptized in 1848 after giving up polygamy and his role as rainmaker. Though Livingstone later denounced him over moral lapses, Sechele answered, 'I shall never give up Jesus. You and I will stand before him together.' He became a missionary to his own and neighboring peoples, and under his rule his chiefdom became a refuge where Christianity spread widely.
sources: Neil Parsons — King Khama, Emperor Joe and the Great White Queen — University of Chicago Press, 1998

name: Onesimos Nesib (born Hika)
summary: Born Hika (meaning 'translator') among the Oromo, Onesimos was captured by slave traders as a boy and ransomed by Swedish missionaries at Massawa. Educated in Eritrea and Sweden, he was baptized at Easter 1872, took the biblical name Onesimus, and devoted his life to translating the entire Bible into Afaan Oromo (completed 1899), laying the foundation of Oromo literacy and of the Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus. He is commemorated as a saint in the Lutheran calendar on 21 June.
sources: Gustav Arén — Evangelical Pioneers in Ethiopia — EFS Förlaget, 1978

name: Aster Ganno
summary: An Oromo woman freed from slavery by the Swedish Evangelical Mission, Aster Ganno converted to Christianity and became the indispensable co-worker of Onesimos Nesib: a gifted native speaker, she dictated idiomatic Oromo while he rendered Scripture, completing the Oromo New Testament translation. The Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus honors her alongside Onesimos through the Aster Ganno Literary Society, and both are listed among the saints of the Lutheran Church.
sources: Mekuria Bulcha — 'Onesimos Nasib's Pioneering Contributions to Oromo Writing' — Nordic Journal of African Studies 4(1), 1995

name: Rafaravavy Rasalama
summary: One of the first pupils of the London Missionary Society village schools in Madagascar, Rasalama was among the first Malagasy baptized (May 1831) and to receive communion. When Queen Ranavalona I outlawed Christianity in 1835 she went into hiding; discovered in a cave in July 1837, she was enslaved and then condemned to death for refusing to work on Sundays and reasserting her faith. Speared at Ambohipotsy on 14 August 1837 while singing hymns, she is remembered as Madagascar's first Christian martyr.

name: Francis Piol Bol Bok
summary: Abducted at age seven in May 1986 during an Arab militia raid on his Dinka village market, Francis was enslaved for ten years in Kordofan, beaten, forced to tend livestock, and coerced into Islam. Through the captivity he prayed daily to God - 'I talk to God every day and every night and he's with me.' He escaped at seventeen in 1996, fled to Cairo where he found refuge in a church, and in 1999 was resettled in the United States as a refugee. There he embraced the Christian faith, gave his first public testimony at the Southern Baptist Church in Roxbury, Massachusetts, and in 2000 became the first escaped slave to testify before the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee. His memoir Escape from Slavery (2003) and his work with the American Anti-Slavery Group brought modern Sudanese slavery to world attention.
sources: Francis Bok with Edward Tivnan — Escape from Slavery: The True Story of My Ten Years in Captivity and My Journey to Freedom in America — St. Martin's Press, 2003

name: Yassir Eric
summary: Born into one of independent Sudan's leading Muslim families - his great-grandfather joined the 1881 Mahdist revolt and his father governed Darfur - Yassir was sent at eight to a desert madrasa to memorize the Quran, and as a teenager took part in the brutal ambush of a Dinka Christian schoolmate, Zakariya. The first crack came when his uncle Khaled, an intelligence officer, announced he had become a Christian after hearing a sermon on the apostle Paul in a Khartoum church; the decisive moment came when two Egyptian Copts prayed over Yassir's comatose young cousin, who miraculously recovered. At dawn prayers the next morning Yassir prayed to Jesus for the first time; after two months of secretly reading the Bible he confessed 'I am a Christian' in February 1991. Disowned - his family held a funeral with an empty coffin - baptized in the Nile, and jailed 49 days in solitary for preaching, he eventually reached Germany, where he became a presiding Anglican bishop ministering to former Muslims. In 2008 he met Zakariya again, alive and a pastor, who showed him a Bible with Yassir's name first on his prayer list.

name: Helen Berhane
summary: In her own testimony, Helen 'came to know Jesus' at the age of eight, while her mother, father and sister were imprisoned for political reasons; she found that when she sang, 'the sadness disappeared.' By fourteen she was writing her own worship music, and by eighteen she was preaching in the streets of Asmara as a member of the Rhema (Rema) Pentecostal church. After Eritrea's 2002 crackdown on unregistered churches, she was arrested in May 2004 for releasing a Christian gospel CD and spent 32 months in a metal shipping container at Mai Serwa military camp, tortured and repeatedly pressured to sign a denial of Christ - she refused, singing hymns to encourage fellow prisoners. Released in October 2006 near death, she fled to Sudan and then Denmark, and published her memoir Song of the Nightingale in 2009.
sources: Helen Berhane with Emma Newrick — Song of the Nightingale — Authentic Media, 2009

name: Rooble (name changed for security)
summary: A Somali man documented by Open Doors (identity withheld for safety), Rooble spent four years wrestling with questions of faith before concluding 'Jesus was the truth and the way to salvation.' His conversion cost him his family, inheritance and livelihood; he was imprisoned several times for sharing the gospel and his brother was killed. He still lives secretly among Somali Muslims in the Horn of Africa, sustained by Scripture, and attends underground discipleship gatherings. Note: name is a pseudonym assigned by the reporting organization.

name: Sadhu Sundar Singh
summary: Born into a wealthy Sikh family in Punjab, Sundar Singh rebelled against religion after his mother's death and even burned a New Testament. One night in December 1904, while planning suicide, he prayed for God to reveal Himself and saw a vision of the risen Christ. He was baptized in 1905, cut his hair as a break with Sikh identity, was cast out by his family, and became a barefoot sadhu-evangelist who preached across India and Tibet in saffron robes.

name: Ko Thah-byu (Tha Byu)
summary: A former robber and murderer sold into slavery to a Christian Burmese, Ko Thah-byu was converted through Adoniram Judson and baptized in 1828, becoming the first Karen Christian. He accompanied missionary George Boardman to Tavoy and walked the Karen hills for weeks at a time preaching in his own language. Within twelve years some 1,270 Karen had been baptized, and he is remembered as the 'Karen Apostle.'

name: Khuma
summary: One of two young men tutored by pioneer missionaries Lorrain and Savidge, Khuma was baptized by Rev. D.E. Jones on 25 July 1899, among the first Mizo Christians. Unlike his companion Khara, who reverted to the old faith, Khuma became a tireless itinerant preacher, traveling alone into remote hills despite persecution by chiefs. He died in 1917, and the Mizo churches raised a monument to him as 'our first Lushai Christian.'

name: Pandita Ramabai
summary: A celebrated Sanskrit scholar widowed young, Ramabai traveled to England in the early 1880s and converted to Christianity, finding in the Bible a hope for women that the Hindu Shastras denied. She returned to India and founded Sharada Sadan and the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon, sheltering thousands of destitute widows and orphans. She endured fierce criticism for her conversion and later translated the Bible into simple Marathi for rural readers.

name: Liang Fa
summary: A woodblock printer hired to carve printing blocks for Robert Morrison's Chinese New Testament, Liang Fa was baptized by William Milne in 1816, among the first Chinese Protestant converts. Beaten and arrested for distributing Christian tracts, he persisted, was ordained by Morrison in 1827 as the first Chinese Protestant pastor, and printed tens of thousands of tracts, including 'Good Words to Admonish the Age,' which later influenced Hong Xiuquan.

name: Watchman Nee (Ni Tuosheng)
summary: Born to Methodist parents in Fuzhou but unconverted, 17-year-old Nee attended evangelist Dora Yu's revival meetings in April 1920 after his mother's apology convicted him. Alone in his room on 28 April 1920, he wept over his sins, saw Christ's outstretched hands on the cross, and surrendered his life, abandoning university plans for ministry. He went on to plant hundreds of indigenous 'local churches' across China and was imprisoned for his faith from 1952 until his death in 1972.

name: Wang Mingdao
summary: Born in Beijing's foreign legation quarter in 1900 during the Boxer siege, Wang grew up in a poor Christian family and attended a London Missionary Society school, where he was converted to Christianity at fourteen. In 1920 he 'unconditionally submitted to God,' changing his name from Yongsheng to Mingdao ('Testify to the Way'), and insisted on baptism by immersion - a stand that cost him his teaching post at a Presbyterian mission school. He founded the independent Christian Tabernacle in Beijing, refusing to join first the Japanese-controlled federation and later the Communist state-controlled church. Arrested with his wife in August 1955, he spent twenty-three years in prison and labor camps, was released in 1980, and became known as the 'Dean of the House Churches' until his death in 1991.

name: Joseph Hardy Neesima (Niijima Jo)
summary: Son of a samurai retainer in Edo, Niijima hungered to learn English and read the Bible, which was forbidden under Japan's isolation laws. In 1864 he stowed away on an American ship at Hakodate at risk of execution, was taken in by Boston merchant Alpheus Hardy, and was baptized in the United States. He returned to Japan and founded Doshisha English School in Kyoto in 1875, becoming a father of Japanese Protestant Christianity.

name: Uchimura Kanzo
summary: A samurai's son studying at Sapporo Agricultural College, Uchimura was swept up in the Christian atmosphere left by American teacher William S. Clark and was baptized by a Methodist missionary in June 1878 at age 16. Dissatisfied with the mission church, he helped found an independent Japanese church and later the Non-Church (Mukyokai) movement. He lost a government teaching post in 1891 for refusing to bow to the Imperial Rescript, yet became one of Japan's most influential Christian thinkers.

name: Alimujiang Yimiti (Alimjan Yimit)
summary: A Uyghur Muslim who converted to Christianity in 1995, Alimujiang became a house-church pastor ministering to Uyghurs in Kashgar, Xinjiang. He was detained in January 2008 and sentenced to 15 years in prison on charges of 'leaking state secrets' after a private phone conversation with an American Christian friend; the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention ruled he was held solely for his faith. He was released in March 2023 after serving the full sentence. No published account documents how or through whom Alimujiang came to faith; sources record only that he converted from Islam to Christianity in 1995.

name: Kautap
summary: A chief among the Sawi, a headhunting people of Papua (then Irian Jaya) who prized treachery, Kautap was a central figure in missionary Don Richardson's 'Peace Child' story. When Richardson showed the Sawi that God's peace child, Jesus, fulfilled their own peacemaking ritual of giving a child to enemies, Kautap and many Sawi turned to Christ. More than half the tribe eventually professed faith, and Richardson translated the New Testament into Sawi.
sources: Peace Child — Don Richardson, Regal Books, 1974

name: Nabeel Qureshi
summary: Raised in a devout Pakistani Ahmadi Muslim family in the United States, Qureshi was a passionate defender of Islam who debated his Christian friend David Wood for years. Through dreams, close study of the New Testament's reliability, and the cost of following Jesus, he converted to Christianity, a decision that cost him his family's favor. He became a well-known apologist and author of 'Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus' before his death from cancer in 2017.
sources: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus — Nabeel Qureshi, Zondervan, 2014

name: Ganga Prasad Pradhan
summary: Born on 4 July 1851 in Kathmandu to a wealthy Newar family, Ganga Prasad was taken at age ten to Darjeeling to join his older brother at the school of Scottish missionary William MacFarlane, where he was educated and converted to Christianity. Enlisted by the Church of Scotland mission as a translator, he labored with missionaries Turnbull and Kilgour on the Nepali Scriptures; appointed the British and Foreign Bible Society's official Nepali translator in 1894, he completed the New Testament in 1902 and the full Bible in 1914 - the first complete Nepali Bible. He became the first ordained Nepali pastor, edited the monthly Gorkhey Khabar Kagat from 1901, and pioneered Nepali Christian literature. In 1914 he returned to Kathmandu with some forty followers to establish a Christian presence, but the Rana rulers expelled them with the words, 'There is no room for Christians in Nepal'; he died in exile in India in 1932.

name: Seo Sang-ryun
summary: A Korean merchant trading in Manchuria, Seo encountered Scottish Presbyterian missionary John Ross and was baptized in 1879, among the first Korean Protestants. He worked alongside Ross translating the New Testament into Korean, and carried the gospel back across the border into Korea. His conversion seeded the Korean church years before missionaries were permitted to reside in Korea itself.

name: Bakht Singh
summary: Born in 1903 in Joiya, Punjab, to devout Sikh parents, Bakht Singh studied at a Christian missionary school and went to England in 1926 for agricultural engineering, promising his parents he would not convert - but there he drifted into drinking and smoking and cut his hair, breaking the Sikh article of faith. In 1929 he moved to Winnipeg, Canada, for further study, where devout Christians John and Edith Hayward took him into their home, read the Bible at every supper, and gave him a Bible of his own. He began attending church and reading Scripture, and 'after seeking for some time, he became Christian,' being baptized on 4 February 1932 in Vancouver. Returning to India in 1933, he was disowned by his family and slept on Bombay's streets - 'the street was my home and the lamp post was my light' - before becoming an itinerant evangelist who founded the indigenous Hebron assemblies, planting thousands of churches across South Asia.

name: John Sung (Song Shangjie)
summary: Born Song Shangjie in 1901 in Hinghwa, Fujian, to a Methodist pastor, John Sung was a brilliant student sent to America in 1920, earning a chemistry PhD from Ohio State in 1926 before entering New York's Union Theological Seminary, where liberal teaching left his faith 'like a storm-tossed ship.' In December 1926 he began attending evangelistic meetings at Calvary Baptist Church, where fifteen-year-old evangelist Uldine Utley preached; after weeks of spiritual struggle, on 10 February 1927 he repented deeply, crying 'This was my spiritual birthday!' as he believed his sins forgiven, and took the new name John. Seminary authorities judged him unbalanced and committed him to an asylum for 193 days, where he read the entire Bible through forty times. Released late in 1927, he sailed for China - throwing his academic diplomas overboard - and spent fifteen years as an itinerant evangelist whose revival preaching drew hundreds of thousands across China and Southeast Asia before his death in 1944.

name: Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan)
summary: Born in 1866 to poor farmers in Cuiheng, Guangdong, Sun was sent at thirteen to Hawaii, where Christian schooling at Iolani College turned him against traditional religious practice - he even smashed a village idol, and was sent home in disgrace. In Hong Kong he studied at the Diocesan school and Queen's College, where he met the American Congregational missionary Charles R. Hager, who baptized him on 4 May 1884, to his elder brother's disdain. He attended To Tsai Church while studying medicine, described revolution as akin to the church's salvation mission, and said his hope was 'to make the Bible and Christian education... the means of conveying to our countrymen' just laws. He went on to lead the 1911 revolution that toppled the Qing dynasty and became the first president of the Republic of China, dying in 1925.
sources: Note: historians debate the depth of Sun's personal faith; his baptism (4 May 1884) and public Christian profession are documented.

name: Nehemiah Goreh
summary: A learned Maharashtrian Brahmin, Goreh was converted in 1848 through contact with Anglican missionaries and study of the Scriptures. His baptism as a high-caste Hindu caused a sensation in western India. He became an Anglican clergyman and a thoughtful apologist, writing on Christianity's fulfillment of India's spiritual longing.

name: St. Patrick
summary: Born in Roman Britain and kidnapped by Irish raiders at 16, Patrick spent six years enslaved as a shepherd in Ireland, where he turned to God in constant prayer. After escaping, he trained for ministry and returned to Ireland as a bishop, preaching the Gospel, baptizing thousands, and confronting druidic power; his own Confessio is a firsthand record of his conversion.
sources: Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus — St. Patrick, 5th century

name: Lydia of Philippi
summary: A merchant of purple cloth from Thyatira living in Philippi, Macedonia. As Paul preached by the riverside, 'the Lord opened her heart to respond' (Acts 16:14); she and her household were baptized, and she hosted in her home what became the first recorded church on European soil.

name: Tiridates III of Armenia
summary: Tiridates III was the pagan king of Armenia who had Gregory the Illuminator imprisoned for nearly fifteen years in the dungeon of Khor Virap and ordered the martyrdom of the Christian virgins Hripsime, Gayane, and their companions. After their deaths he was struck by a severe illness — tradition says he was reduced to the state of a wild boar — and, on his sister Khosrovidoukht's counsel, he released Gregory, whose prayers brought his healing. Persuaded by the power of the cure, Tiridates was converted and baptized with his family around 301, and he proclaimed Christianity the state religion, making Armenia the first Christian nation. He appointed Gregory as Catholicos and spent the rest of his life spreading the faith, as recorded in Agathangelos' History of the Armenians.
sources: History of the Armenians — Agathangelos, 5th century

name: Mirian III of Iberia
summary: Pagan king of Iberia (eastern Georgia) converted through the witness of St. Nino, a Cappadocian missionary woman; tradition records that he was struck blind while hunting and regained his sight after praying to Nino's God. He declared Christianity the state religion of Iberia (c. 327–337), as recorded in the Georgian chronicles.
sources: The Life of St. Nino — Georgian hagiography

name: Æthelberht of Kent
summary: Pagan king of Kent whose Frankish Christian wife Bertha prepared the way for the Gospel. He received Augustine's mission in 597, listened to the preaching in the open air, and was baptized — the first Anglo-Saxon king to convert. Bede records that thousands of his people followed him into the faith.
sources: Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Books I–II — Bede, 731

name: Clovis I
summary: Pagan king of the Franks who, facing defeat at the Battle of Tolbiac, vowed to follow Christ if granted victory. Baptized at Reims by St. Remigius along with some 3,000 of his warriors — an event recorded by Gregory of Tours — his conversion aligned the Frankish kingdom with Nicene Christianity and shaped Christian Europe.
sources: Historia Francorum, Book II — Gregory of Tours, 6th century

name: Boris I of Bulgaria
summary: Khan Boris of Bulgaria was baptized as the Christian Michael around 864, in the wake of a military and diplomatic settlement with the Byzantine Empire. The popular legend that a painting of the Last Judgment frightened him into conversion is described by the scholar Francis Dvornik as certainly apocryphal, and stories of a Christian sister's influence remain uncertain. After his baptism he suppressed a pagan revolt of his nobles, secured the independence of the Bulgarian Church, and welcomed the disciples of Cyril and Methodius, fostering Slavonic literacy and worship. His reign laid the foundations for Bulgaria's Christian identity.
sources: documented in 9th-century Byzantine chronicles and Bulgarian church histories
Khan Boris and the Conversion of Bulgaria — R. E. Sullivan, Studies in Medieval and Renaissance History 3 (1966)

name: Mieszko I of Poland
summary: First historical ruler of Poland, baptized in 966 — the 'Baptism of Poland' — following his marriage to the Christian Bohemian princess Doubravka. His conversion brought Poland into Latin Christendom, recorded by Thietmar of Merseburg and the early Polish chroniclers.
sources: Chronicon — Thietmar of Merseburg, early 11th century
documented in early Polish chronicles (e.g., Gallus Anonymus)

name: Vladimir the Great
summary: Pagan prince of Kiev who, after sending envoys to compare the faiths of neighboring peoples, was baptized at Chersonesus in 988 and ordered the mass baptism of Kiev's people in the Dnieper — the 'Baptism of Rus''. The Primary Chronicle records his transformation from a violent ruler to a Christian prince.

name: Stephen I of Hungary
summary: Son of Grand Prince Géza, baptized with his father around 985 and crowned the first Christian king of Hungary in 1000/1001. He founded bishoprics, built churches, and legislated Christian life for his people; his conversion is documented in Hartvic's Life of St. Stephen. The sources record his baptism alongside his father around 985 but do not preserve any personal account of his conversion.
sources: Life of St. Stephen — Bishop Hartvic, early 12th century

name: Blaise Pascal
summary: Brilliant mathematician and religious skeptic who experienced a decisive 'night of fire' on 23 November 1654 — an overwhelming encounter with 'the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not of philosophers and scholars.' He sewed his written Memorial into his coat and devoted his remaining years to the Christian faith, producing the Pensées.

name: John Wesley
summary: Anglican clergyman and Oxford scholar who, after a failed mission to Georgia, attended a Moravian meeting on Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738, where he felt his 'heart strangely warmed' as he trusted in Christ alone for salvation. His Journal records the moment, and he went on to lead the Methodist revival across Britain.
sources: The Journal of John Wesley, 24 May 1738

name: Christmas Evans
summary: Born on Christmas Day 1766 to a poor shoemaker, Christmas Evans grew up an illiterate farm laborer after his father's death. Around age 17 he came into the service of the Presbyterian minister and schoolmaster David Davies, heard him preach the gospel, and was discipled by candlelight in an old barn; within about a month he professed Christ and began learning to read the Bible. He joined the Baptists and was baptized in the River Duar in 1788, and after ordination, during a preaching journey, he experienced a deeper conversion that gave his preaching its famous power. He went on to build up Baptist churches across Anglesey and North Wales, becoming one of Wales's greatest preachers.
sources: Dictionary of National Biography entry 'Evans, Christmas' (1885–1900)

name: Hans Nielsen Hauge
summary: A farmer's son raised in a devout home who, while plowing on 5 April 1796, received a powerful assurance of salvation and a call to preach 'the living faith.' He traveled Norway mostly on foot, wrote 33 books, and was imprisoned repeatedly for unauthorized preaching, founding the Haugean revival that reshaped Norwegian religious life.

name: Paavo Ruotsalainen
summary: A Finnish farmer tormented over his soul who walked 200 km in the winter of 1799 to meet the lay preacher Jakob Högman, who told him: 'One thing you lack, and with it everything: the inner feeling of Christ.' The encounter grounded his faith, and he became the leader of Finland's Awakening (Herännäisyys) revival, traveling an estimated 40,000 km on foot.

name: Lars Levi Laestadius
summary: A Swedish state-church pastor of partial Sami descent who, after 19 years of formal ministry, met the Sami laywoman Milla Clementsdotter in 1844. Her testimony of living faith brought him to a 'born-again' experience of grace; his transformed preaching ignited the Laestadian revival that swept Sami communities across Sweden, Norway, and Finland, also confronting the ravages of alcoholism.

name: Rodney 'Gipsy' Smith
summary: Rodney 'Gipsy' Smith was born in a Romani tent in Epping Forest to an illiterate basket-selling family. His father's witness and prayers, hearing the singer Ira Sankey, and a visit to John Bunyan's home prepared him; at Bunyan's statue he vowed to live for God. On 17 November 1876, at the Primitive Methodist Chapel on Fitzroy Street, Cambridge, he answered preacher George Warner's invitation and trusted Christ. He immediately told his father, obtained a Bible and dictionaries, taught himself to read and write, and began preaching — going on to a seventy-year evangelistic ministry across Britain and America.
sources: Gipsy Smith: His Life and Work — Fleming H. Revell, 1902 (autobiography)

name: Edith Stein
summary: A brilliant phenomenologist and assistant to Edmund Husserl, raised in an observant Jewish family but agnostic by her teens. One night in 1921 she read the autobiography of Teresa of Ávila in a single sitting and concluded, 'This is the truth.' Baptized on 1 January 1922, she became the Carmelite nun Teresa Benedicta of the Cross and was martyred at Auschwitz in 1942.

name: C. S. Lewis
summary: Belfast-born Oxford scholar and committed atheist who, through long debates with J. R. R. Tolkien and Hugo Dyson and his own wide reading, came to theism in 1929 and knelt in prayer as a Christian in September 1931. He chronicled the journey in Surprised by Joy and became one of the twentieth century's great Christian apologists.
sources: Surprised by Joy — C. S. Lewis, 1955

name: André Frossard
summary: Son of a founder of the French Communist Party and a self-described 'perfect atheist.' At 20, while waiting for a friend outside a Paris adoration chapel in July 1935, he stepped inside and was overwhelmed by the sudden certainty that God exists — 'I entered an atheist, I left a believer.' He wrote the bestselling memoir Dieu existe, je l'ai rencontré (God Exists: I Have Met Him).
sources: God Exists: I Have Met Him — André Frossard, Herder and Herder, 1969 (English 1970)

name: Bruno Cornacchiola
summary: A Rome tram worker, militant Seventh-day Adventist and former communist sympathizer who plotted to assassinate Pope Pius XII. On 12 April 1947 at Tre Fontane, he and his three children witnessed an apparition of the Virgin Mary calling him back: 'You persecute me. Now enough. Return to the holy fold.' He converted to Catholicism, surrendered his dagger to the Pope, and spent his life preaching.

name: Brother Andrew (Anne van der Bijl)
summary: Anne van der Bijl, a Dutch commando wounded in the East Indies, returned home wounded and aimless. During his long convalescence he read the Bible and was converted to Christ, committing himself to mission work. Revelation 3:2 later shaped his call to 'strengthen what remains' of the churches under communism. In 1955 he drove his Volkswagen Beetle into Poland loaded with Bibles, beginning decades of smuggling Scriptures to believers behind the Iron Curtain — the story told in God's Smuggler.
sources: God's Smuggler — Brother Andrew with John & Elizabeth Sherrill, 1967

name: Richard Wurmbrand
summary: Richard Wurmbrand was a Romanian Jew, a committed Marxist, and an atheist. In 1937, while convalescing from tuberculosis in the mountain village of Noua, he and his wife Sabina befriended Christian Wölfkes, a Lutheran carpenter who had been praying to lead a Jew to Christ. Wölfkes gave Wurmbrand a Bible, which Wurmbrand described as written 'in flames of love fired by his prayers.' Richard and Sabina converted in 1938, were baptized, and began ministry among Jews and others; he went on to pastor under communism, enduring fourteen years of imprisonment and torture, as recorded in Tortured for Christ.

name: Haralan Popov
summary: Haralan Popov describes himself in his autobiography as an egotistical young atheist. In November 1925, after moving to Ruse, his friend Christo invited him to a Baptist church, where Bulgarian hymns and an educated pastor challenged his belief that religion was only for the ignorant. The testimony of educated Christian women, and later the personal witness of a believer named Petroff reading Scripture with him, convinced him that God existed; after earnest seeking he experienced what he called a life-changing salvation in Jesus Christ. He moved in with Petroff for Bible instruction, trained for ministry, and pastored and evangelized across Bulgaria before enduring thirteen years of communist imprisonment.
sources: Tortured for His Faith — Haralan Popov, 1970

name: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
summary: Baptized as a child, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn became a committed Marxist and atheist as Soviet ideology took hold. During eight years in the Gulag (1945–1953) and the cancer treatment and exile that followed, suffering stripped away his ideology: he was moved by the faith of Christian prisoners, including the Jewish convert Boris Kornfeld, and turned back to Christianity. In The Gulag Archipelago he describes how his experience taught him that 'the line separating good and evil passes through every human heart.' He became a philosophically minded Russian Orthodox Christian, and his writing — including One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich — exposed the Soviet system; he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970.
sources: documented in biographies, e.g., Solzhenitsyn: A Soul in Exile — Joseph Pearce, 1999

name: Ivan 'Vanya' Moiseyev
summary: Ivan 'Vanya' Moiseyev was raised in a Christian family in Moldova. After finishing school in 1968 he came to Christ at the Evangelical Christian Baptist church in Slobodeyska, was baptized and joined the church in 1970, and developed a strong desire to witness. Drafted into the Soviet Army in November 1970, he prayed openly and preached to fellow soldiers despite intimidation and torture, and was martyred in July 1972 at age 20. His letters and his family's testimony, published as Vanya, inspired millions of believers worldwide.

name: Igor Stakhovskiy
summary: Igor Stakhovskiy was part of the wave of new believers who converted in Ukraine around the fall of the Soviet Union. After finishing his military service in Moscow in 1991, he visited a Baptist church with his mother; there a friend presented the gospel to him and told him it was the hour of his salvation. 'From that moment, there was no question about it,' he later said; he was baptized into the church and gradually learned about God. He became a pastor of a small evangelical church in Kyiv, serving his family and community — profiled by Christianity Today.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION — full conversion details rest on a single profile

name: Alister McGrath
summary: A Belfast-born atheist and Marxist sympathizer who went up to Oxford to study the natural sciences. Through reading and debate he concluded that Christianity was intellectually compelling, and converted as a student in November 1971. He became one of the world's leading theologians and apologists, chronicling his journey in works such as The Twilight of Atheism.
sources: The Twilight of Atheism — Alister McGrath, 2004
documented in his published testimony and biographical interviews

name: Urim Bogaj
summary: Urim Bogaj grew up in a Muslim family in Malisheve, Kosovo, that hated Christians. After the 1999 Kosovo war, his aunt converted to Christianity, and Bogaj himself eventually came to faith. He went on to plant a church in Malisheve — the first church the majority-Muslim town had seen in 700 years, as reported by CBN News in 2018.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION — full conversion details rest on news reporting

name: Dayuma
summary: Dayuma fled her Waorani people's revenge killings as a young girl and lived and worked outside the tribe. She befriended missionary Rachel Saint, helped her learn the Wao Terero language, and through the Bible — which she called 'God's Carving' — came to faith in Christ before returning to her people in 1958. As the first Waorani Christian, she was decisive in the peaceful contact that followed: teaching, translating, and helping lead her people away from revenge violence toward reconciliation, alongside Elisabeth Elliot and Rachel Saint.
sources: Through Gates of Splendor — Elisabeth Elliot (1957)

name: Mincaye Enquedi
summary: Mincaye was one of the Waorani men who speared five Operation Auca missionaries in January 1956. After Elisabeth Elliot and Rachel Saint came to live among the Waorani and taught the Bible, Mincaye converted to Christianity. He later became a church elder and preacher among his people, a transformation documented in the film Beyond the Gates of Splendor.

name: Kimo
summary: Kimo was one of the Waorani men involved in the 1956 killing of the Operation Auca missionaries. Baptist Press reporting on the Beyond the Gates of Splendor documentary states that both Mincaye and Kimo, two of the killers, later became Christians. Beyond that confirmation, little individual detail about Kimo is available in published sources. Published sources confirm that Kimo became a Christian after the events of 1956, but they do not preserve the personal circumstances or timing of his conversion.

name: Rómulo Sauñe Quicaña
summary: Rómulo Sauñe was an Ayacucho Quechua evangelist and Bible translator who helped bring Scripture to his people in their own language. He pastored and led during the years of Shining Path violence in the Andes. On September 15, 1992, he was martyred for his faith along with members of his family. Published sources document his faith, ministry, and martyrdom in detail; the precise moment of his conversion is not documented. The surviving published sources document his faith and ministry but do not preserve the circumstances of his conversion.
sources: One Bright Shining Path / Ayacucho for Christ — Terry Whalin
The Path and the Peacemakers — David Miller (2001)

name: Manuel Zúñiga Camacho
summary: Manuel Zúñiga Camacho was an Aymara man living near Lake Titicaca who received a Bible from Eduardo Forga. He made contact with Seventh-day Adventists, studied the Scriptures, and adopted Adventist convictions. He went on to establish a school serving Aymara communities, one of the earliest documented indigenous Adventist conversions in the Andes. (Denominational note: his conversion was to Seventh-day Adventism.)

name: Tomás Guzaro
summary: Tomás Guzaro's memoir Escaping the Fire traces his spiritual pilgrimage through all three of Guatemala's main religions: raised as the son of a Maya priest, he later became a leader in the Catholic Church, and eventually converted to Protestant Christianity. He became an evangelical pastor among the Ixil Maya during Guatemala's civil war, when guerrilla occupation brought limited religious freedom and murdered church leaders. In the war's darkest phase he reported a harrowing vision that induced him to lead more than two hundred Mayas out of guerrilla-controlled territory to safety.
sources: Escaping the Fire: How an Ixil Mayan Pastor Led His People Out of a Holocaust During the Guatemalan Civil War — Tomás Guzaro and Terri Jacob McComb (University of Texas Press, 2010)

name: Israel Narvaez
summary: Israel Narvaez was the president of the Mau Maus gang in New York. He and his best friend Nicky Cruz became born-again Christians in July 1958 after hearing evangelist David Wilkerson preach. Narvaez later became disillusioned and rejoined the gang, becoming its leader again; in February 1959 he took part in the shooting of Anthony Lavonchino. He later returned to the Christian faith, as chronicled in his autobiography Second Chance.

name: Luis Palau
summary: Luis Palau converted to Christianity at a summer camp in Argentina when he was about twelve, after a counselor led him to Christ. He went on to become one of the most widely heard evangelists of the twentieth century, preaching to hundreds of millions across Latin America and the world. His conversion story is recounted in his autobiography Palau: A Life on Fire.
sources: Palau: A Life on Fire — Luis Palau with Paul J. Pastor (2019)

name: Carlos Annacondia
summary: Carlos Annacondia was a successful Argentine businessman who felt spiritually empty despite his prosperity. In 1979 he and his wife responded to an evangelistic invitation and committed their lives to Christ. Two years later he left business to become an itinerant preacher, and his evangelistic campaigns drew enormous crowds across Latin America.
sources: Listen to Me, Satan! — Carlos Annacondia

name: Marcelino Cruz
summary: Marcelino Cruz was a Chamula Tzotzil in Chiapas who converted to Presbyterianism in the early 1990s. Disillusioned with the Chamulan blend of Catholicism after local shamans failed to cure his sick father, he embraced the evangelical faith and became pastor of the Prince of Peace church. In 1993 he was among 534 Chamulan Protestants expelled from their community for refusing to abandon the faith, yet the congregation went on to build five churches and open its own school.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION — full conversion details rest on a single news report

name: Tomás Pérez Méndez
summary: Tomás Pérez Méndez, 60, was a Tzotzil Maya man imprisoned in connection with the Acteal massacre case in Chiapas. He told the Mexican newspaper El Universal, 'In prison, the majority of us converted to the Presbyterian faith.' He said he bore no anger or resentment toward those who accused him and planned to preach upon release. His testimony documents a genuine prison conversion among the Tzotzil. Sources attest that he encountered Christ during a prison sentence, but the published record preserves no further detail of how he heard the gospel or the circumstances of his conversion.

name: Thiago
summary: Thiago was a locally renowned Mixtec musician and his community's cantor — the elected representative who performs Catholic rites in villages without a resident priest. After the leader of his music group committed his life to Christ upon hearing the gospel from IMB missionary Jake Glover, Thiago also committed his life to Christ. His conversion carried real cost: he was jailed in his village's one-room police cell for his new faith. (Only his first name is published.)

name: Jean Junior Cineas
summary: Jean Junior Cineas grew up as the son of a Vodou priest in Haiti and was expected to follow his father's path. At age 16 he heard the gospel from an IMB missionary and received his family's permission to become a Christian. He endured ongoing family opposition and went on to become an evangelist leading other Haitians to Christ.

name: Rote Kuka ("Red Grandmother")
summary: Rote Kuka was a Miskito woman documented in Moravian mission literature from the 1890s as being interested in becoming a Christian. She attended church regularly and became devoted to the mission community. Her story survives only through colonial-era missionary accounts, which should be read critically, but she is one of the few named Miskito converts of that era. (Note: the source material uses colonial-era language about dress and 'civilizing' that is not repeated here.) The only surviving source on Rote Kuka is an 1895 Moravian missionary pamphlet describing her interest in Christianity and church attendance, which records no conversion event, baptism, or profession of faith.
sources: Moravian mission history of the Mosquito Coast (via secondary academic sources)

name: Jose Rolando Arevalo
summary: Jose Rolando Arevalo, 24, joined the Barrio 18 gang at age 14 after his brother was assassinated by a rival gang. Like many former gang members, he embraced evangelical Christianity when a pastor approached him in prison and talked with him about his life and about God; he says his heart was touched. After his release he left the gang and began attending a Baptist church in the La Dina neighborhood of San Salvador.

name: Peter
summary: Peter grew up in Rio de Janeiro, became hooked on drugs as a teenager, and fell into dealing, theft, and repeated jail time. After one release his father greeted him with the words 'My prodigal son, I love you,' and on his knees beside his weeping mother he repented and began a new life with Jesus. He later became a pastor and director of an English-language course, sharing his faith across the city. (Only his first name is published.)

name: Clarense Dionisio Romig Christian
summary: Clarense Christian, born 1929 in San Pedro de Macorís, first encountered the Seventh-day Adventist church at 14 when a neighbor invited him to Sabbath School. After attending evangelistic meetings in 1946 — and living through the great earthquake of August 4, 1946, while reading Matthew 24 — he committed himself to God and was baptized on September 27, 1947. He went on to a lifetime of Adventist ministry and research. (Denominational note: his conversion was to Seventh-day Adventism.)

name: Cleve "Lieutenant Stitchie" Laing
summary: Cleve Laing, known as Lieutenant Stitchie, was the first dancehall reggae artist signed to a major label (Atlantic Records, 1988). After a serious car crash in August 1997 on his way to Reggae Sumfest, he was given a Gideon Bible, read it in his hotel room, prayed the salvation prayer, and became a Christian. He abandoned secular dancehall and pioneered gospel reggae, winning Caribbean gospel music awards and entering the Gospel Hall of Fame in 2016.

name: Brinulfo González
summary: Brinulfo González, a Wayuu man, dreamed one night that three men with arrows were chasing him; he saw a church, ran to it, and the men turned back. When he told his grandmother, an evangelical, she said the men were devils and urged him to convert to Christ — 'so I converted to Christ,' he testified. His account is preserved in a Universidad Nacional de Colombia anthropological study of Wayuu evangelical conversion.

name: Darío Silva Silva
summary: Darío Silva Silva was a prominent Colombian journalist and director of the Noticiero Noticolor newscast whose business was collapsing for lack of funding. A cousin introduced him to Esther Lucía, who shared the Word of God with him; he converted to Christianity and later married her. He left journalism for ministry and founded the Casa sobre la Roca church in Bogotá, which marked 39 years in 2025. He died on September 7, 2026.

name: Adelina Zúñiga
summary: Adelina Zúñiga is an Afro-Colombian woman who fled conflict with her family and resettled in Sincelejo, where she became pastor of the tiny Pentecostal church Remanso de Paz. Through the church she found community, confidence, and a leadership role she had never held before, and she now leads other displaced women. Her husband, Jasper Rodriguez, converted eight years after she did. The report documents her faith and ministry; the moment of her own conversion is not detailed. The cited report documents Adelina Zúñiga's faith and ministry but gives no account of how or when she herself converted.

name: St. Mary of Egypt
summary: Born in Egypt around 344, Mary ran away to Alexandria at twelve and lived there as a prostitute for seventeen years. Traveling to Jerusalem with pilgrims for the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, she was repeatedly repelled by an unseen force when she tried to enter the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Weeping in remorse before an icon of the Theotokos, she prayed for forgiveness and promised to renounce the world; she was then able to enter and venerate the True Cross. Hearing a voice say, 'If you cross the Jordan, you will find glorious rest,' she crossed the river and lived as a hermit in the desert for forty-seven years. Her life, recorded by St. Sophronius of Jerusalem, became a classic model of repentance in the Eastern Church.
sources: St. Sophronius of Jerusalem, 'The Life of Our Venerable Mother Mary of Egypt' (7th century)

name: St. Pachomius the Great
summary: Born in 292 in Thebes, Upper Egypt, to pagan parents, Pachomius was forcibly conscripted into the Roman army around 313. While the recruits were being transported down the Nile, local Christians overwhelmed them with kindness — bringing food and comfort to the suffering men — and Pachomius resolved to become a Christian. After his release he was baptized at Chenoboskion, became a disciple of the hermit Palamon, and then founded the first cenobitic (communal) monastery at Tabennisi. Before his death in 346 he governed eight or nine monasteries of men and two of women, making him the founder of communal monasticism.
sources: Dictionary of Christian Biography and Literature — 'Pachomius, St'

name: St. Cyprian of Carthage
summary: Born around 200 in Carthage to a wealthy pagan family, Thascius Cyprianus was a celebrated teacher of rhetoric who debated Christians with confidence — until the aged presbyter Caecilianus won him over to the faith. Converted around 246, he sold much of his property for the poor and took the name Caecilius in honor of the priest who had led him to Christ. In his 'Ad Donatum' he described how baptism washed away the stain of his former life and restored him as a new man. Within two years he was elected bishop of Carthage, and in 258 he was beheaded under Valerian, becoming the first African bishop to win the martyr's crown.
sources: Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience catechesis on St. Cyprian (6 June 2007)

name: St. Augustine of Hippo
summary: Born in 354 AD in Thagaste (Roman North Africa) to a Berber Christian mother, Monica, and a pagan father, Augustine lived a restless youth of ambition and sin, eventually joining the Manichean sect. His intellectual and spiritual crisis in Milan led to his conversion to Christianity in 386, recorded in his 'Confessions'. He became Bishop of Hippo and one of the most influential theologians in Christian history.

name: St. Gregory Thaumaturgus
summary: Born around 213 to noble pagan parents in Neocaesarea, Pontus, Theodorus was studying civil law when, escorting his sister to Caesarea in Palestine around 233, he met the celebrated Christian scholar Origen. Curiosity led him to hear Origen teach; he forgot all about Beirut and Roman law and, over five years of study, was gradually won over to Christianity, taking the name Gregory. Returning home, he was consecrated bishop of Neocaesarea around 240 and evangelized the city with such success that tradition says only seventeen pagans remained at his death. His 'Panegyric on Origen' preserves his own account of the conversion.
sources: Gregory Thaumaturgus, 'Panegyric on Origen' — primary account of his conversion

name: Abu Atallah
summary: Born and raised in a Muslim family in Egypt, Abu Atallah joined the Muslim Brotherhood in high school to be near a friend, but left after witnessing the movement's aggression — including a Brotherhood member assaulting a Coptic Christian student. Dragged by an atheist friend to a Christian meeting, he was struck by believers who prayed to God spontaneously, as to a friend and Father. Finding an Arabic Bible in his brother's drawer, he read it and saw that 'God is love' (1 John) stood in stark contrast to the Allah of law and submission he had known. After a two-year period of study, prayer, and meeting with Christians, he was baptized on Christmas Day 1977, taking the Christian name Stephen. He later moved to the United States, answered a call to ministry at the 1979 Urbana conference, and founded the Arab American Friendship Center in Dearborn, Michigan, ministering across 56 countries.
sources: Abu Atallah, 'From Cairo to Christ: How One Muslim's Faith Journey Shows the Way for Others' — InterVarsity Press, 2017

name: Mehdi Dibaj
summary: Born into a Muslim family in Iran in the mid-1930s, Mehdi Dibaj was about fourteen when, while visiting a relative at the Christian hospital in Esfahan, hospital staff gave him a Bible booklet that introduced him to Christianity. He formally converted at Luke Episcopal Church, after which his family expelled him from home and Christians in Tehran took him in. He later worked in a Christian bookshop, trained for ministry, and became an Assemblies of God evangelist who preached across Iran and served in Afghanistan. Arrested in 1983, he spent nine years in prison and was sentenced to death for apostasy in December 1993; international pressure secured his release in January 1994. He was kidnapped and murdered on 24 June 1994 for refusing to return to Islam.
sources: Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran — 'Mehdi Dibaj' memorial
Article18 — reporting on Dibaj's conversion at age 14 (1953), https://articleeighteen.com/news/4189/

name: Haik Hovsepian Mehr
summary: Born into an Armenian family in Iran, Haik Hovsepian Mehr began attending home prayer meetings at about age thirteen after a neighbor invited him — the beginning of his devotion to Christ. He joined the Assemblies of God around age fifteen and rose to become superintendent of the Assemblies of God churches in Iran, planting churches and defending Muslim-background converts. He led the international campaign that freed Mehdi Dibaj from a death sentence in January 1994. Three days later he disappeared en route to the Tehran airport; his stabbed body was found on 20 January 1994. He is widely regarded as a martyr of the Iranian church.
sources: Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran — 'Haik Hovsepian Mehr' memorial

name: Youcef Nadarkhani
summary: Nadarkhani converted to Christianity at age 19 and became a house-church pastor in Rasht, Iran. Arrested in October 2009 after objecting to his children being forced to read the Quran in school, he was sentenced to death for apostasy in 2010 and refused three court-ordered chances to recant. After 1,000 days in prison and global outcry he was acquitted of apostasy in September 2012 (though convicted of evangelizing) and released. He was rearrested in 2018 and faced further charges in 2023. Sources establish that Youcef Nadarkhani embraced Christianity around age 19, but none documents how he first encountered the gospel or what led to his conversion.

name: Ghorban Dordi Tourani
summary: Born to a devout Sunni Muslim Turkmen family near the Turkmenistan border, Ghorban Dordi Tourani had wanted to study Islamic theology but became disillusioned, abandoned religion, and fell into violence. Imprisoned in Turkmenistan in 1983 after a fatal fight, he attempted suicide in 1986 and then met a Russian Christian prisoner, Constantine, who shared Christ with him and obtained a New Testament for him. Tourani read it in two weeks and declared himself ready to become a Christian; his transformed life was so evident that prison authorities allowed Christian meetings. After his release in 1998 he returned to Iran, evangelized among the Turkmen, and planted an independent house church of converts in Gonbad-e-Kavus. A week after refusing Turkmen religious leaders' demand to deny Jesus and return to Islam, he was kidnapped from his home on 22 November 2005 and stabbed to death — the first Turkmen in Iran known to have been martyred for his Christian faith.
sources: Compass Direct News via Worthy News — 'Iranian Christians Mourn Martyred Convert'

name: Hassan (name withheld for security)
summary: Hassan grew up in a devout Iranian Muslim family and left Iran in 2005 on a personal mission to convert Europeans to Islam. A Christian man repeatedly invited him and his wife Shirin to an Iranian church, which Hassan finally visited only to confront the Muslim converts there. Confronted by their joy and testimony, he gave his life to Christ. His story is documented by Elam Ministries, a ministry serving the Persian-speaking church (name changed for security).
sources: Elam Ministries — testimonies: 'Hassan: I wanted to win Europe for Islam. But then I was invited to a church' — name changed for security

name: Attieh (name withheld for security)
summary: Attieh, an Iranian woman, received a New Testament while visiting a country near Iran. As she read, the Word of God spoke to her heart, and she traveled two hours to the nearest Persian-language church, where she gave her heart to Jesus. She became an irrepressible evangelist among Iranian women. Her story is documented by Elam Ministries (name changed for security).
sources: Elam Ministries — testimonies: 'Attieh' — name changed for security, via Evangelicals Now in-depth profile

name: Brother Rachid
summary: Born in Morocco in the 1970s to an imam, Rachid heard the gospel as a boy through a late-night radio broadcast, did four years of Bible correspondence courses, and converted around age 12. His devout parents expelled him, leaving him homeless for two years before a missionary family took him in. After fleeing Morocco in 2005 he began hosting 'Daring Questions' on Al-Hayat TV, a call-in program through which thousands of Muslims have come to Christ.
sources: Christian Aid Mission report, 'Christian Man Once Persecuted by Muslims Risks Life to Share Gospel' — via Gospel Herald

name: Farid Messaoudi (name changed for security)
summary: Farid came to Christ in 1983 at age 17 after receiving the Gospel through a friend — the first believer in his Kabyle village. His witness led his five siblings and his parents to the Lord, and he became pastor of a congregation of more than 75 Kabyle believers during the great Kabylie revival of the 1980s-90s. His story was documented by the International Mission Board (name changed for security).
sources: International Mission Board — 'Week of Prayer: Despite persecution, N. Africa's Kabylie churches flourish' — Baptist Press; name changed for security

name: Nawal (alias, name withheld for security)
summary: As a young Saudi woman searching for meaning and dignity, Nawal encountered a foreign female Christian preacher online who taught about God's love, his acceptance of sinners, and his fatherhood. An online follow-up network connected her with Christians and Bible material; gradually she sensed God speaking to her, and one day she gave her life to Christ, experiencing joy and peace — Matthew 28 spoke to her especially. She now lives two separate lives: a Muslim housewife and mother by day, and a closeted follower of Christ under Sharia rule, where her faith could get her killed by her own family. Her only contact with other believers is through brief, coded WhatsApp messages.
sources: Open Doors USA — story reported by the Christian Post, 8 Feb 2018; alias 'Nawal' used for security
Open Doors USA via Christian Post, 8 Feb 2018 — fuller conversion account

name: John Ghanim
summary: Born in Yemen to a devout Muslim family, John Ghanim had already abandoned Islam years earlier — reportedly while walking around the Kaaba in Mecca — but lived publicly as a Muslim from 2014 to 2017 to protect himself. After a period as an agnostic, he grew curious about Jesus; fleeing to Europe, he lived as a refugee in Greece, where he met Syrian Christian refugees and came to faith in Christ. He later moved to the United Kingdom, founded the evangelistic media ministry Faith and Love Media, and became an Arabic-speaking evangelist to Muslims. His family largely disowned him, and his former mosque issued a fatwa against him.
sources: International Christian Concern — 'No Going Back: Living Openly as a Christian Convert from Yemen' (24 June 2026)

name: Taysir 'Tass' Abu Saada
summary: Born in Gaza in 1951, Tass ran away at 17 to join Fatah under Yasser Arafat, becoming a sniper, assassin, and Arafat's personal driver, consumed by hatred of Jews. After moving to America he befriended a Christian and underwent a radical conversion to Christ in 1993. He founded the ministry Hope for Ishmael in Jericho, reconciling Arabs and Jews, and wrote the memoir 'Once an Arafat Man' (2008).
sources: Tass Saada with Dean Merrill, 'Once an Arafat Man' — Tyndale, 2008

name: Eman Sami Maghdid ('Maria')
summary: Eman, a 20-year-old Iraqi Kurdish woman whose father is a prominent local imam, publicly announced her conversion to Christianity on social media, where she sang Christian hymns to nearly 50,000 followers. In March 2022 her bound, stabbed body was found near Erbil International Airport in a suspected family honor killing just weeks before her planned baptism. Her case was documented by Middle East Concern and Morning Star News. Eman Sami Maghdid's conversion was publicly announced on social media but disputed by her family, and no source documents how she encountered the gospel or whether a genuine conversion occurred before her death.
sources: Middle East Concern and Morning Star News — 'Young Woman Who Left Islam Killed in Iraq'

name: Maxim Ahmed
summary: A 22-year-old Kurd from Kobani, Syria, Maxim lost an arm in an explosion during the war with ISIS and fled to Turkey for medical treatment, where he met Kurdish and Turkish Christian converts. Struck by their joy and talk of love, he decided to follow Jesus, joined the new church in Kobani, and saw friends and family grow interested in Christ. His conversion was documented by Reuters in 2019.
sources: Reuters — 'Christianity grows in Syrian town once besieged by Islamic State' (3 Apr 2019)

name: Zani Bakr
summary: Zani Bakr, 34, converted to Christianity in 2007 after disillusionment with how ISIS painted the conflict as religious. He moved from Afrin to Kobani, Syria, where he became pastor of a church of some 80-100 Kurdish converts meeting openly on Tuesdays and Fridays. His ministry was documented by Reuters in 2019 as part of the post-ISIS growth of Christianity in the Syrian Kurdish heartland. The only documented fact about Zani Bakr's conversion is that it occurred in 2007; the cited Reuters report does not say how he encountered the gospel or what led him to convert, and its mention of ISIS-era disillusionment refers to other Kurds, not to his own 2007 conversion.
sources: Reuters — 'Christianity grows in Syrian town once besieged by Islamic State' (3 Apr 2019)

name: Turgay Ucal
summary: Turgay Ucal grew up in Istanbul's Old Town in a Muslim family, praying five times a day and joining the Nurcu Islamic youth group — yet as a high school student he was curious about Jesus, slipping secretly into a Catholic church to learn what the Bible said about him. At university he studied Islamic literature and belonged to an Islamic youth group, but his real purpose was to learn more about Jesus: 'The Bible became my fate.' He embraced Christianity, finding in it a freedom that transcended the legalism of his upbringing, and quietly registered his new religious identity despite his military-officer father's fury. In 1986 he started a church for Muslim-background Turks in Istanbul; within a year it had twenty converts, and his Istanbul Presbyterian Church became one of Turkey's largest.

name: Abdul Rahman
summary: In 1990 Abdul Rahman worked with a Catholic medical-aid NGO serving Afghan refugees in Peshawar, Pakistan, where conversations about religion with his Catholic coworkers and reading the Bible 'opened my heart and my mind.' He converted 'in small steps,' was baptized into the Roman Catholic Church, and took the name Joel; his wife divorced him and his family rejected him. Back in Afghanistan, his conversion was revealed in a 2006 custody dispute, and he was put on trial for apostasy — a capital crime under Afghan law. His case drew worldwide condemnation, including from Western leaders and the Pope; he was released and granted asylum in Italy.
sources: Wikipedia — 'Abdul Rahman (convert)'; international press coverage 2006 (BBC, Associated Press, The New York Times)
WorldWide Religious News — 'Afghan Christian convert' reporting (WW RN articles/20973)
Baptist Press — 'Afghan Christian convert released; asylum reportedly requested' (2006)

name: Hamouda Teya Kaffi and Nada Hamad Koko
summary: Hamouda came to faith in Christ in 2018; his Muslim wife Nada's family forced an annulment of their marriage, and after apostasy was decriminalized in Sudan the couple reunited in 2021, with Nada also becoming a Christian. Under family pressure, apostasy charges were laid against them again in 2022 despite the law's repeal — an intimidation tactic widely condemned by human-rights advocates. Their case was documented by Open Doors and the Voice of the Martyrs Canada. Sources document that Hamouda put his faith in Christ in 2018 and Nada converted in 2021 (published sources spell their names Hamouda Tia Kafi and Nada Hamad Shukralah), but no source describes how either of them heard the gospel or what led to their conversions.
sources: Voice of the Martyrs Canada — 'Apostasy Charges Added to Christian Couple's Case' (20 Oct 2022), citing Open Doors

name: Pocahontas (Rebecca Rolfe)
summary: Daughter of the Powhatan paramount chief Wahunsenacawh, Pocahontas was taken captive by English colonists in 1613 and held at Henrico, where she learned English, professed Christian faith, and was baptized as Rebecca. She married tobacco planter John Rolfe in April 1614, a union the English celebrated as a diplomatic and spiritual triumph. She died in England in 1617 at about age twenty, leaving a contested legacy as one of the earliest documented Native converts in English America.
sources: U.S. National Park Service — Historic Jamestowne (https://nps.gov/jame/learn/historyculture/john-rolfe.htm)
Camilla Townsend, Pocahontas and the Powhatan Dilemma (2004)

name: Kateri Tekakwitha
summary: Orphaned by smallpox at age four, Tekakwitha was raised by her Mohawk uncle and instructed by Jesuit missionaries; she asked for baptism herself and was baptized Catherine at Easter 1676 at age twenty. Facing ridicule and accusations in her village, she moved to the Jesuit mission town of Kahnawake near Montreal, where she lived a life of prayer, fasting, and service until her death in 1680. Canonized in 2012, she is venerated as the first Indigenous North American saint.
sources: The Canadian Encyclopedia — Saint Kateri Tekakwitha (https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/tekakwitha-kateri)
New-York Historical Society — Life Story: Kateri Tekakwitha (https://wams.nyhistory.org/early-encounters/french-colonies/kateri-tekakwitha/)

name: Samson Occom
summary: Around age sixteen to eighteen, during the Great Awakening (about 1741), the young Mohegan Samson Occom heard evangelical sermons stressing the equality of all people before God. In his autobiography he described finding salvation through Jesus Christ, trusting in Christ alone, and gaining serenity and joy in serving God. He studied theology under Eleazar Wheelock and was ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1759. He became a renowned Native preacher and fundraiser whose sermons drew large audiences in New England and Britain. His success helped inspire the founding of Dartmouth College, though the school later shifted away from its original mission to educate Native youth.
sources: The Alabama Baptist — 'Heroes of the Faith: Samson Occom, Mohegan Missionary'
Connecticut History — 'Samson Occom and the Brotherton Indians'

name: John Marrant
summary: A free Black youth in Charleston, South Carolina, Marrant went to George Whitefield's 1769 sermon intending to disrupt it but fell under deep conviction of sin instead. He described being set free through prayer and joy in Christ, recording his experience in his 1785 Narrative. He went on to preach among both Black and Native American communities in North America and Nova Scotia.
sources: John Marrant, A Narrative of the Lord's Wonderful Dealings with John Marrant, a Black (1785) — via HathiTrust (https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/102267425)
Christianity Today — Early black evangelicals of the Great Awakening (https://www.christianitytoday.com/2025/05/early-black-evangelicals-great-awakening/)

name: William Apess
summary: After a childhood of poverty, indenture, and service as a drummer in the War of 1812, Apess was drawn to the egalitarian spirit of Methodist camp revivals and chose baptism as a Methodist. He became an itinerant preacher to mixed Native, Black, and white congregations and was ordained in 1829. His autobiography A Son of the Forest (1829) — built on his conversion narrative — was the first published by a Native American author, and he became a leading voice against Indian removal and for Native rights.
sources: William Apess, A Son of the Forest (1829)
Newberry Library — Digital Collections for the Classroom (https://dcc.newberry.org/?p=19732)

name: Peter Jones (Kahkewaquonaby)
summary: Raised in Mississauga Ojibwe tradition until age fourteen, Jones was baptized Anglican at his father's urging but later said it left him 'the same wild Indian youth as before.' Out of curiosity he attended a Methodist camp meeting in June 1823 with his half-sister and was genuinely converted there at age twenty-one. He became a Methodist minister, translator of hymns and Scripture into Ojibwe, chief of his people, and an advocate for Native land rights.
sources: Dictionary of Canadian Biography — Jones, Peter (https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/3992?revision_id=27607)
Donald B. Smith, Sacred Feathers: The Reverend Peter Jones (Kahkewaquonaby) and the Mississauga Indians (https://archive.org/details/sacredfeathersre0000smit)

name: Elias Boudinot (Gallegina Uwati)
summary: Educated at the Moravian mission school and the Foreign Mission School in Connecticut — founded expressly to train Native youth as missionaries — Gallegina Uwati was drawn by Christianity's message of universal love and converted around 1818–1820 (sources differ on the exact year). He professed Christian faith, was baptized with the name Elias Boudinot, and worked as a missionary, schoolmaster, and translator. He became the founding editor of the bilingual Cherokee Phoenix, the first Native American newspaper. Though his later support of the Treaty of New Echota divided the Cherokee Nation, his conversion and early ministry remain a landmark in Cherokee Christian history.
sources: Middlebury College Library — 'Elias Boudinot, Cherokee Writer You Should Know' (conversion 1818)

name: Jarena Lee
summary: Born free in New Jersey, Lee described herself as a 'wretched sinner' until she heard Richard Allen preach around 1804 and experienced pardon through prayer, later testifying to sanctification as well. Feeling called to preach, she overcame the objections of the young African Methodist Episcopal Church and became the denomination's first authorized woman preacher. Her autobiography (1836, expanded 1849) made her the first African American woman to publish an autobiography.
sources: Gilder Lehrman Institute — Richard Allen, Jarena Lee, and the Second Great Awakening (https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/richard-allen-jarena-lee-and-second-great-awakening)
Christianity Today — Black Christianity before the Civil War (https://www.christianitytoday.com/1999/04/black-christianity-before-civil-war-gallery-fruit-of/)

name: Sojourner Truth
summary: Born into slavery in New York as Isabella Baumfree, she experienced a spiritual awakening in 1827 while living with the Van Wagenen family and fighting in court to recover her illegally sold son. In her narrated account she described becoming conscious of her sin under God's judgment, then encountering Jesus as the loving mediator between her and divine wrath. She dedicated herself to God, joined the Methodist church in Kingston, and later the AME Zion Church. Her faith strengthened her legal fight for her son, and in 1843 she understood God to be calling her to itinerant gospel preaching, took the name Sojourner Truth, and walked out to preach. She became one of America's most famous Black evangelists and abolitionists, remembered for sermons including 'Ain't I a Woman?'

name: Dwight L. Moody
summary: A barely literate shoe clerk in Boston, Moody attended Mount Vernon Congregational Church only because his uncle required it. On April 21, 1855, his Sunday school teacher Edward Kimball visited him in the shoe store's stockroom, put a hand on his shoulder, and spoke of Christ's love — and Moody was converted. He went on to become the most famous evangelist of the nineteenth century, founding the Moody Bible Institute and preaching to millions on both sides of the Atlantic.
sources: Christian History Institute — Dwight L. Moody timeline (https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/uploaded/50cf79ab726927.41671672.pdf)
Christianity Today — The Life and Times of D. L. Moody (https://www.christianitytoday.com/1990/01/life-times-of-d-l-moody/)

name: Shingwaukonse
summary: A respected Ojibwe chief and War of 1812 veteran, Shingwaukonse had long adhered to the Midewiwin tradition when, in the early 1830s, he deliberately sought Christian teaching for his people. He led a delegation by canoe to York (Toronto) to petition the lieutenant-governor and the Anglican bishop for missionary support, and Anglican missionary William McMurray arrived at Garden River in the fall of 1832. Around 1833, during McMurray's deaconate — having weighed the competing Baptist, Catholic, Methodist and Anglican missions at work in the region — Shingwaukonse and his family converted to Anglicanism. He envisioned a 'Teaching Wigwam' at Garden River where Ojibwe youth could learn Christian faith alongside practical skills. His descendants' later founding of the Shingwauk Indian Residential School is a painful and complex legacy, but his own conversion reflected a sincere Indigenous embrace of Christianity.
sources: Carleton University ALGQP — Shingwauk family article (https://ojs.library.carleton.ca/index.php/ALGQP/article/download/577/477/1548)

name: Peter the Aleut (Cungagnaq)
summary: Cungagnaq, a native of Kodiak Island in Alaska, encountered the gospel through the Russian Orthodox missionaries — the Valaam monks of St. Herman's missionary party — who arrived on Kodiak in September 1794 and baptized thousands of Sugpiaq-Alutiiq people within two years. He was baptized into the Orthodox faith and received the Christian name Peter. He then worked as a fur hunter for the Russian-American Company, and in 1815 was among fourteen Aleut hunters captured by Spanish sailors near San Pedro, California, and taken for a mock trial. According to the original account — relayed by an escaped comrade to St. Herman — Peter was tortured and killed for refusing to renounce his Orthodox confession. Historians debate details of the account, including who his persecutors were, but he is venerated as the first Orthodox martyr of America.
