name: Nicky Cruz
summary: A feared leader of the Mau Mau street gang in 1950s New York, Cruz threatened to kill preacher David Wilkerson when Wilkerson came to the gangs with the gospel. Wilkerson's persistent answer — 'Jesus loves you, Nicky' — broke through, and Cruz surrendered his life to Christ in 1958. His testimony, told in the bestselling Run Baby Run, launched a decades-long evangelistic ministry to gangs and troubled youth worldwide.

name: Stephen Tong (Tang Chongrong)
summary: Born in Xiamen, China in 1940, Stephen Tong moved to Indonesia as a child. His mother had practiced ancestor worship before converting to Christianity after her eldest son was healed through prayer. As a teenager Tong rebelled: at 15 he embraced communism and socialism, dismissing Christianity as an unenlightened belief. In January 1957 his mother persuaded him to attend a Christian Youth Conference run by the Southeast Asia Bible Seminary in Malang. On January 9, the last day of the conference, evangelist Andrew Gih preached a revival sermon and Tong gave his life to Christ. He began preaching at 17, founded Stephen Tong Evangelistic Ministries International, and in 1989 planted the Reformed Evangelical Church of Indonesia, eventually preaching to tens of millions worldwide.

name: Chuck Colson
summary: A hard-driving Nixon White House operative, Colson was confronted by his friend Tom Phillips, who read to him from Lewis's Mere Christianity on the nature of pride. In 1973, alone in his car, Colson surrendered his life to Christ in tears. He later pleaded guilty in the Watergate scandal, served prison time, and founded Prison Fellowship, now one of the world's largest prison ministries.
sources: Christianity Today — The legacy of prisoner 23226 (https://www.christianitytoday.com/2001/07/legacy-of-prisoner-23226/)
Wheaton College — Charles W. Colson recollections (https://recollections.wheaton.edu/2012/04/charles-w-colson/)

name: Lee Strobel
summary: An award-winning legal journalist and self-described atheist, Strobel was dismayed when his wife became a Christian and set out to use his investigative skills to disprove the faith. Interviewing scholars and examining the historical evidence for Jesus' resurrection, he found the case for Christ more compelling than the case against — and became a Christian in 1981. His investigation became the bestselling book The Case for Christ.
sources: Lee Strobel, The Case for Christ (Zondervan, 1998)
Patheos FilmChat — Exclusive: Case for Christ author Lee Strobel (https://www.patheos.com/blogs/filmchat/2017/04/exclusive-case-christ-author-lee-strobel-facts-feelings-seeing-life-turned-movie.html)

name: Nicholas Black Elk
summary: A revered Lakota holy man and survivor of Wounded Knee, Black Elk was baptized Catholic in 1904 and became a catechist in 1907, teaching the faith for more than three decades. His life story, told to John Neihardt in Black Elk Speaks, made him famous worldwide — though he regretted aspects of how it was told. He sought to hold together his Lakota identity and his Christian faith, and his cause for Catholic sainthood is now underway.
sources: National Catholic Reporter — Walking the Good Red Road (https://www.ncronline.org/opinion/walking-good-red-road-takes-intriguing-look-nicholas-black-elk)
Diocese of Rapid City — Black Elk Mass homily (https://www.rapidcitydiocese.org/sosa-homily-blackelk-mass/)

name: Richard Twiss
summary: A former drug user who despised Christianity, Twiss hit bottom after a mushroom overdose on Maui in 1974. Alone on a beach, he experienced the presence of God and found peace through Jesus in the words of the Sermon on the Mount. He became a leading voice for contextualized Native Christian faith, co-founding Wiconi International and authoring One Church, Many Tribes before his death in 2013.
sources: Belmont University News — Lakota author challenges audience (https://news.belmont.edu/lakota-author-challenges-audience-to-broaden-perspective/)
Richard Twiss, One Church, Many Tribes (2000)

name: Henry ʻŌpūkahaʻia
summary: Left orphaned by warfare in Hawaiʻi, ʻŌpūkahaʻia left the islands as a youth aboard an American ship and reached New England, where he encountered Christian teachers and became a Congregationalist. He studied at the Foreign Mission School in Cornwall, Connecticut, and prepared to return as a missionary to his own people. He died of typhus in 1818 at about twenty-six, but his published Memoirs helped inspire the American Board's first mission to Hawaiʻi in 1820.

name: Queen Kaʻahumanu
summary: The powerful kuhina nui (co-regent) of the Hawaiian Kingdom, Kaʻahumanu publicly professed Protestant Christianity in 1824 and was baptized Elizabeth in 1825. Her conversion reshaped the kingdom: she promoted literacy and Christian marriage while also using her authority to enforce Protestant norms, including bans on traditional practices that modern Hawaiians view with painful complexity. Her story is both a genuine conversion and a caution about power joined to faith.
sources: Bishop Museum — Moʻolelo of Elizabeta Kaʻahumanu by S. M. Kamakau (https://blog.bishopmuseum.org/nupepa/mo%ca%bbolelo-of-elizabeta-ka%ca%bbahumanu-by-s-m-kamakau/)

Candid Native Philanthropy timeline — Christianity is enforced and cultural practices banned in Hawaii (https://nativephilanthropy.candid.org/events/christianity-is-enforced-and-cultural-practices-banned-in-hawaii)

name: Papeiha
summary: A Polynesian convert discipled under the London Missionary Society in Tahiti, Papeiha was trained as one of the first Indigenous evangelists to the Cook Islands. He helped establish Christianity on Aitutaki and in 1823 volunteered to be put ashore at Rarotonga, whose people had killed previous visitors — a courageous landing that opened the island to the gospel. His ministry made him one of the most celebrated Pacific Islander missionaries of the nineteenth century. Papeiha's personal conversion account is not documented in the published record: he is attested only as a Society Islands convert trained by John Williams at the Uturoa mission station in Raiatea before his posting to Aitutaki in 1821.
sources: John Williams, Memoirs of the Life of the Rev. John Williams, Missionary to Polynesia — via Cambridge (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/memoirs-of-the-life-of-the-rev-john-williams-missionary-to-polynesia/B7DFDC4D4B4F500A1839FC690C923B6C/listing)

name: Pōmare II
summary: Exiled and defeated, King Pōmare II received Christian instruction from LMS missionary Henry Nott and began professing Christianity around 1812. After his decisive victory at Fei Pi in 1815 — a battle he credited to the Christian God — he showed notable clemency to his enemies and was baptized in 1819. His conversion marked the turning point for Christianity in Tahiti, though, like other royal conversions, it was entangled with political consolidation.
sources: University of Edinburgh thesis — Pōmare II and the mission (https://era.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/30555)

name: Malietoa Vainuʻupo
summary: The paramount chief (tupu) of Samoa, Malietoa Vainuʻupo had just conquered the islands — avenging the death of his rival Tamafaiga — when LMS missionaries John Williams and Charles Barff landed at Sapapaliʻi, Savaiʻi, on 24 August 1830, accompanied by the Samoan couple Fauea and Puaseisei. Malietoa promised Williams he would become a Christian once he had fully avenged Tamafaiga's death, and sent one of his sons to help the Tahitian teachers build their chapel. When the chapel opened, he publicly announced his intention to keep his promise, taking the Christian name Tavita (David) — an act many Samoans saw as fulfilling the prophecy of the goddess Nafanua. He placed the Indigenous teachers under his protection, and his public embrace of the gospel gave the new faith legitimacy across the Samoan islands. Samoan Christianity thus began not only with foreign missionaries but with a Samoan chief's conversion.
sources: Constance Gordon-Cumming, A Lady's Cruise in a French Man-of-War, ch. 9 — Malietoa's promise and public profession (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/A_Lady%27s_Cruise_in_a_French_Man-of-War/Chapter_9)

name: Taufaʻahau (King George Tupou I)
summary: The ambitious young Tongan chief Taufaʻahau was baptized by Wesleyan missionaries in August 1831, taking the name George after the British king. His conversion preceded his unification of Tonga's warring chiefdoms, and as King George Tupou I he embedded Christianity in the new nation's constitution, laws, and public life. Tonga remains one of the most Christian nations on earth, a legacy traced to his 1831 baptism.

name: Seru Epenisa Cakobau
summary: The powerful Bauan chief Cakobau, who had resisted Christianity for years amid Tonga-backed wars and political turmoil, was baptized in 1854 after sustained Wesleyan missionary influence. His conversion — however mixed its political motives — broke the resistance of Fiji's most powerful chiefdom and accelerated Christianity's spread through the islands. He later ceded Fiji to Britain in 1874, ending his reign but not the church's growth.
sources: History Today — The British acquisition of Fiji (https://www.Historytoday.com/archive/feature/british-acquisition-fiji)
Yale eHRAF World Cultures — Fiji documents (https://ehrafworldcultures.yale.edu/cultures/oq12/documents/003)

name: Wiremu Tāmihana Tarapīpipi Te Waharoa
summary: A formidable Māori rangatira (chief) raised in warfare, Tāmihana was influenced by the teaching of missionary Alfred Brown and used Christian arguments to resist calls to war. He was baptized Wiremu Tāmihana on 23 June 1839 and founded Christian settlements governed by the Ten Commandments. Known as the 'kingmaker,' he later championed the Māori King movement as a Christian project of Māori unity and justice.
sources: Te Ara — The Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Te Waharoa, Wiremu Tāmihana Tarapīpipi (https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1t82/te-waharoa-wiremu-tamihana-tarapipipi)

name: Djiniyini Gondarra
summary: A Yolŋu man of the Golumala clan, Djiniyini Gondarra grew up in the Methodist missions at Milingimbi, where he embraced the Christian faith and trained for ministry, becoming Australia's first Aboriginal Methodist minister. Serving at Galiwin'ku (Elcho Island), he and his family returned from leave on 14 March 1979 to find a revival breaking out in his parish — he had prayed over a list of hopes for the church, and found God already answering them. He taught on the Holy Spirit from the Bible and led nightly prayer gatherings that drew hundreds: active church attendance leapt from about 25 to over 200 within weeks. He helped root the revival in Yolŋu culture and language, embodying an Indigenous Australian Christianity that is both deeply biblical and deeply Yolŋu. He went on to become a leading advocate for reconciliation and justice for his people.
sources: John Blacket — essay on Aboriginal revival history (https://www.chr.org.au/documents/5.-Essays-on-the-history-and-experience/John-Blacket.pdf)

name: Nan Inta
summary: A respected former Buddhist abbot from Sarapee District, Chiang Mai, Nan Inta was convinced of the truth of Christianity when missionary Daniel McGilvary correctly predicted the solar eclipse of 17 August 1868. Baptized on 3 January 1869, he became the first baptized Christian convert in northern Thailand, taught northern Thai to the missionaries, wrote Christian tracts, and was ordained the first northern Thai elder in 1875. He fled the 1869 persecution of Christians but returned to lead the Bethlehem Church in Sarapee until his death in 1882.
sources: Thai Missions biographical entry: 'Nan Inta (1804-1882) ... the first baptized Christian convert in northern Thailand, baptized by the Rev. Daniel McGilvary of the Presbyterian Laos Mission.' — https://thaimissions.info/gsdl/collect/thaimiss/index/assoc/HASH0105/834b9875.dir/doc.pdf

name: Noi Sunya
summary: Noi Sunya was a subject of Chao Kawilorot, the prince of Chiang Mai, who heard the gospel through the newly arrived Presbyterian Laos Mission — founded by Daniel and Sophia McGilvary in April 1867, with Chiang Mai's first church planted in 1868. He was among the seven Lao men who had converted by August 1868, and was baptized into the tiny fledgling church. When the prince demanded that his corvée laborers work on Sundays, Noi Sunya refused to break the Sabbath, and he was executed — beaten to death — on 14 September 1869 on the prince's order. Challenged publicly by McGilvary, Prince Kawilorot openly acknowledged that the two men had been killed simply because they were Christians. Noi Sunya is remembered as one of northern Thailand's first Protestant martyrs, and his martyrdom — though it scattered the young church — became a landmark of costly discipleship in Thai church history.

name: Boon Tuan Boon-Itt
summary: Born in Ratchaburi in 1865 and taken to America at age eleven by medical missionary Dr. Samuel Reynolds House, Boon Tuan had an evangelical conversion experience while studying at Williams College. After graduating from Auburn Theological Seminary, he returned to Siam in 1893 and became the first Thai Christian to establish a church in Thailand — the Suebsampantawong Church in Bangkok (1902), the first church planted and supported entirely by Thai Christians. He also founded Padoongrasdra School in Phitsanulok, declining royal offers of governorship and nobility to remain in Christian service.
sources: Wikipedia biography: 'the first Thai Christian to establish a church in Thailand' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boon_Tuan_Boon-Itt

name: Boon Mark Gittisarn
summary: Born in Ratchaburi in 1898, Boon Mark converted to Christianity while a student at Bangkok Christian College. He became an American Presbyterian Mission evangelist, was elected General Secretary of the Church of Christ in Thailand in 1938, and served as translator for the Chinese revivalist John Sung in 1938–39. After World War II he helped pioneer Pentecostalism in Thailand, founded the country's first independent church (Bangkok Church, 1957), and was a key figure in the 1956 T. L. Osborn evangelistic campaign.
sources: Thai Missions biographical entry: 'Boon Mark is one of the most important figures in 20th century Thai Protestant history... He converted to Christianity while at BCC' — https://thaimissions.info/gsdl/collect/thaimiss/index/assoc/HASHd3fb.dir/doc.pdf

name: Kaing Guek Eav (Duch)
summary: Duch, the former Khmer Rouge commandant of the S-21 (Tuol Sleng) prison, converted to Christianity around 1993 and was baptized in 1996 by pastor Christopher LaPel while living under an assumed name. At his trial before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, he publicly invoked his conversion, saying he had to 'kneel down and pray for forgiveness from those souls.' His daughter Ky Siev Kim also became a Christian through his witness.
sources: LiCAS.news: 'In 1993 Duch converted to Christianity... In 1996, the former prison chief was baptized by Christopher LaPel' — https://www.licas.news/2020/11/26/cambodians-consider-life-after-death-for-comrade-duch/

Academic paper 'Faith in Forgiveness' (Univ. of Bath) on former Khmer Rouge members' conversions, incl. Duch — http://purehost.bath.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/187504059/Faith_in_forgivness._Green_access_copy.pdf

name: Navy Chann
summary: After the Khmer Rouge seized power, Navy Chann fled Cambodia on foot with her family for four months to reach the Thai border, settling in a UN refugee camp. There, Cambodian friends who had recently become Christians shared the gospel with her, and she accepted Christ in 1982, followed by her husband and other family members. The family later returned to Cambodia with World Renew, where they train and support pastors and their families.
sources: Christianity Today, 'Born Again and Again: Cambodian Evangelicals Celebrate 100 Years' — https://www.christianitytoday.com/2023/01/cambodia-evangelicals-100-anniversary-protestant-missionary/

name: Chhric Taing
summary: Chhric Taing, a colonel in the Cambodian army, was among the influential Khmer leaders converted during the 1972 Phnom Penh evangelistic campaign led by Stanley Mooneyham of World Vision, when some 2,000 Cambodians responded to the gospel in a single week. Weeks before the fall of Phnom Penh, believers gathered in his home for a small-group Bible study and foot-washing service, sensing that 'for some of us there will be death.'
sources: Christianity Today (1978): 'The new Christians included influential leaders like Men Ny Borinn, president of the Supreme Court, and Chhric Taing, a colonel in the Cambodian army' — https://christianitytoday.com/ct/1978/november-17/editorials-indifference-to-cambodia.html

name: Thira Siengsukon
tribe: Lao (ethnic Chinese, raised in Thai culture)
summary: Born in Bangkok to non-Christian Chinese parents and raised Buddhist, Thira Siengsukon first heard the gospel through an American missionary's youth program near his home. After three years of comparing Christianity with the Buddhism of his upbringing, he surrendered to Christ at Bangkok's Sacred Light Baptist Church on 29 October 1967. He went on to found the Lao School of Ministry in Kansas City in 1988, training first-generation Lao Christian pastors and church leaders.
sources: Baptist Press: 'After three years, I surrendered to Christ, admitted I was a sinner and Christ gave me a brand new life in Him' — https://www.baptistpress.com/resource-library/news/chinese-by-birth-thai-by-culture-laotians-are-his-passion/

name: Bounchan
summary: A former communist soldier who rose to become an assistant district governor in Laos, Bounchan came to Christ and began witnessing boldly for his new faith. He was imprisoned and tortured for his Christian witness; while in prison, the thing he wanted more than food was a Bible. His perseverance under torture, documented by The Voice of the Martyrs, made his testimony widely known among the persecuted church. The documented record confirms that Bounchan came to Christ and witnessed boldly under torture, but no published account gives how or when he first heard the gospel.
sources: The Voice of the Martyrs documentary: 'Laos: Former Soldier Jailed for Christian Witness' — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TbqgssIKx_U

name: Saiyasak (surname not reported)
summary: As a boy, Saiyasak fled Laos with his family in the 1970s and spent two years in a Thai refugee camp before resettlement in Nashville, Tennessee. A nominal Buddhist, he was drawn by the love shown by members of Lighthouse Christian Fellowship, and one Sunday a Scripture passage about the love of Christ broke through: 'I opened up my heart to God. That was the transformation — it was like eternity had touched reality.' He earned three postgraduate seminary degrees and returned to Thailand in 1992 to lead a ministry overseeing churches, a seminary, a radio ministry, an orphanage, and a school.
sources: Christianity Today, 'The Refugee Pastor That Could' (2010) — https://www.christianitytoday.com/2010/09/refugee-pastor-that-could/

name: Temenggong Koh
summary: Temenggong Koh was an Iban leader who had led his followers to settle in the Baleh region of Sarawak. He was among the first group of Ibans baptized as Methodists — 29 persons baptized by the Rev. Burr Baughman on Christmas Day 1949 — and his conversion was of great importance in the initial growth of the church, leading many of his followers to accept the Christian faith.
sources: Academic article 'The Methodist church in Sarawak and its work among the Iban, 1939-1968': 'One of the first converts was the Iban leader, Temenggong Koh... his conversion was a factor of great importance in the initial growth of the Church' — https://www.thefreelibrary.com/The+Methodist+church+in+Sarawak+and+its+work+among+the+Iban%2C...-a0290733359

name: Lillian Bulan-Dorai (née Bulan)
summary: Lillian Bulan grew up in Bario, the remote Kelabit highland village in Sarawak where Australian missionary Hudson Southwell had reported the tribe's first known conversion in 1940. Raised with only nominal prayers before meals, she was transformed by the Bario revival of 1973, when a pervasive sense of the fear of God and his holiness swept the village — she recalls daily confessing her sins, holding her own prayer meetings with friends, and encountering God 'like a mother hen' protecting her. The revival's effects reshaped the whole Kelabit community.
sources: Christianity Today, 'A Call to Wake Up 50 Years After Malaysia's Bario Revival' (2024) — https://www.christianitytoday.com/2024/02/malaysia-revival-bario-kelabit-tribe-borneo/

name: Michael (surname not reported)
summary: Michael, from the Murut people of the hills of north Sarawak, lived a life marked by drunkenness, gambling, and violence — he had killed a man and had five children from three wives. About five years before a Langham Partnership report, he met Jesus and his heart and life were transformed. He completed two years of Bible school, became a pastor, and was sent to minister in Stalun, an Iban longhouse village near Sibu. The documented account records only that Michael 'met Jesus' about five years before the report and was transformed; it gives no details of how he heard the gospel or the circumstances of his conversion.
sources: Langham Partnership: 'He met Jesus five years ago and his heart and life were transformed' — https://langham.org/news-and-updates/langham-trains-drunken-gambler-turned-pastor-in-remote-east-malaysia/

name: Lionel Jayasinghe
summary: A former Buddhist monk, Lionel Jayasinghe came to know the Lord through a discarded gospel tract. After graduating from Bible college, he became the first Christian worker to venture into Tissamaharama in the deep south of Sri Lanka, an area with no Christian presence. He served there for five years before being brutally murdered — two intruders thrust a shotgun into his mouth and pulled the trigger in his own home — making him a modern martyr of the Sri Lankan church.
sources: International Journal of Religious Freedom, Vol 1:1 (2008), Godfrey Yogarajah: 'A former Buddhist monk, who came to know the Lord through a discarded tract... was brutally murdered' — https://www.ijrf.org/index.php/home/article/download/157/191

name: Silva (given name not reported)
summary: Silva, a Sri Lankan Buddhist who had never heard about Jesus, returned home from working in Saudi Arabia after the 2004 tsunami, when Southern Baptist disaster-relief workers cared for his family. For months he quietly watched the Christians pray and serve; after watching the 'JESUS' film with his brother-in-law he concluded, 'in Jesus' character and reading the Bible stories, there is something we can get for our lives.' Other new Sri Lankan believers baptized him in the Indian Ocean in September 2005, and he began leadership training and sharing his faith with family and friends.
sources: Baptist Press: 'Other new Sri Lankan believers baptized Silva in the Indian Ocean in mid-September' — https://www.baptistpress.com/resource-library/news/tsunami-brings-sri-lankan-home-to-meet-jesus/

name: Giam Chheng Hoa (A Hoa)
summary: A young Taiwanese intellectual, Giam Chheng Hoa sought out Canadian Presbyterian missionary George Leslie Mackay shortly after his arrival in Tamsui in 1872, bringing scholars to debate him. Intrigued by Christianity, Giam agreed to teach Mackay Chinese in exchange for instruction in the faith — and became Mackay's first convert. Mackay immediately began training him for ministry, and Giam later became the first native pastor in the northern synod of the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan.
sources: Christianity Today: 'Mackay's first convert was a young intellectual named Giam Chheng Hoâ... Giam later became the first native pastor in the northern synod' — https://www.christianitytoday.com/2022/07/george-leslie-mackay-taiwan-missionary-canada/
Academic article 'Thirty Years of Mission in Taiwan' (MDPI, Religions 12/3/190) — https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/12/3/190

name: Dalisen
summary: Dalisen was the first Pinuyumayan (Puyuma) person to become a Christian, coming to faith in Jesus in 1928 when he heard the gospel in Japanese at a Holiness Church in Taipei. After seminary training in Japan, he returned to his homeland in southeastern Taiwan, where from 1934 to 1938 he and Canadian Anglican missionary Narcissus Peter Yates evangelized in Japanese — singing 'Jesus Loves Me' and telling Bible stories to children and families — laying the foundation for the Pinuyumayan church.
sources: Presbyterian Church in Canada Mission Blog: 'The first Pinuyumayan person to become a Christian was a man named Dalisen who came to faith in Jesus in 1928' — https://pccweb.ca/missionblog/2023/11/27/the-pinuyumayan-new-testament-and-65th-anniversary-of-christian-mission-nov-26-2023/

name: Vang Atu
summary: Vang Atu, a Hmong man who once worshipped spirits for luck, wealth, health, and food, surrendered his life to Jesus and completely abandoned his animistic beliefs — becoming the first Christian convert in his village in northwest Vietnam. His house became the place of worship for at least four families who came to follow Jesus through his evangelism. In 2016 local authorities and villagers destroyed his house and forced his family out of the village for their faith. Note: 'Vang Atu' is a pseudonym used by Open Doors for security, and the published account records his conversion and persecution but not how he first heard the gospel.
sources: Open Doors USA via Christian News Network: 'Vang Atu... was the first Christian convert in his village in Vietnam... He comes from the Hmong tribe' — http://christiannews.net/2018/02/11/vietnamese-christian-persecuted-by-authorities-own-brother-desires-to-one-day-preach-to-his-oppressors/

name: Hilario Castillo
summary: Blind since the age of four, Hilario Castillo was taken in at age seven by American Baptist missionaries at their mission station in Capiz, where he worked as their masseur and pounded rice. As he labored, he was given Bible verses to memorize and came to faith; he memorized many verses by heart. Despite his blindness, he became an itinerant evangelist, rising at 4 a.m. to walk the hills and rugged roads of Romblon, Mindoro, Capiz, and Mindanao to preach the gospel — once fainting from hunger in front of a store and then evangelizing its owner upon recovering.
sources: 'A History of Philippine Baptist Pastors 1898–2002' (Central Philippine University repository): 'Hilario Castillo had been blind since he was 4 years old... This blind boy was the masseur of the American missionaries' — https://repository.cpu.edu.ph/bitstream/handle/20.500.12852/1658/A history of philippine baptist pastors 1898-2002(1).pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y

name: Diosdado P. Menor
summary: Diosdado P. Menor of Calapan, Oriental Mindoro, was converted by a native preacher named Adap in the early years of the Churches of Christ movement in the Philippines. He went on to become a well-known preacher in his own right, touring the nation and converting hundreds — if not thousands — to the faith, continuing to preach into his advanced years. The documented record states only that he was converted by the native preacher Adap in the early Churches of Christ movement in the Philippines; the circumstances of his conversion are not further documented.
sources: Truth Magazine, 'The Gospel in the Philippines': 'Adap preached and was able to convert a young man... the young man's name was Diosdado P. Menor' — https://www.truthmagazine.com/archives/volume34/GOT034092.html

name: Batdorj "Bataa" Juvaa
summary: Batdorj Juvaa grew up in communist Mongolia as the son of a Communist Trade Union leader, and first heard of the Bible from a high-school teacher who warned it was a dangerous 'book of horror.' After Mongolia's peaceful 1990 revolution, he and his friends wandered into a 400-person Christian church in Ulaanbaatar in March 1993 and were struck when the congregation sang 'Amazing Grace' in Mongolian. Within a few months Bataa became a follower of Jesus, and he went on to pioneer Cru's campus ministry, mentoring a team of Mongolian staff reaching tens of thousands of students.

name: Enkhsarul
summary: Enkhsarul had been a Buddhist her entire life in a remote area of Mongolia and knew nothing of Christianity until a team of Christians visited, shared about Jesus, and gave her a New Testament. When she discovered Jesus had power to deliver, she confessed her sins and received His salvation. Later, when her seven-year-old son Chinbatar's kidney failure was declared hopeless by doctors, she prayed through the night in Jesus' name and he was healed by morning — after which her entire family became followers of Christ.

name: Tohar Haydarov
summary: Tohar Haydarov, an Uzbek Baptist convert from Islam, was arrested in January 2010 after police tried to pressure him to renounce Christ and return to Islam. When he refused, he was charged with drug possession — charges his fellow Christians and Forum 18 insisted were fabricated — and sentenced to ten years in a labor camp near Qarshi. After serving nearly seven years as a prisoner of conscience, supported by prayer and letter-writing campaigns worldwide, he was released on parole in November 2016. The documented record confirms that he became a Christian after 2001 and joined a Council of Churches Baptist church, but no published account gives how or when he heard the gospel.

name: Makset Djabbarbergenov
summary: Makset Djabbarbergenov became a Christian in 2000 and soon became an active church leader in Nukus, the capital of Karakalpakstan, where no Protestant church has official registration. Arrested six times for his faith, he fled with his family to Kazakhstan in 2007 after a police raid, only to be detained in Almaty at Uzbekistan's request on charges of practicing religion outside state regulation. After international advocacy involving Open Doors and UNHCR, he was released and reunited with his family. The documented record confirms that he became a Christian in 2000 and soon led a church in Nukus, but no published account gives how he heard the gospel or the circumstances of his conversion.

name: Kaldibek Primbetov
summary: Kaldibek Primbetov was the first man in the Karakalpak village of Janbashkala, near Turtkul in Karakalpakstan, to become a Christian, and he became pastor of its small Protestant congregation. A wealthy village strongman mounted a campaign against the believers, warning 'there is no place here for Christians,' and Christian villagers were beaten, threatened with broken limbs, and expelled from their homes for abandoning the Muslim faith of their parents. More than half of the village's Christian families fled, but Primbetov and a remnant continued to meet for worship. No published account of how Primbetov first heard the gospel or came to faith survives; he is documented only as the first Christian of Janbashkala (circa 2000) and pastor of its small congregation.

name: Saktinbai Usmanov
summary: Saktinbai Usmanov was an ethnic Kyrgyz convert to Christianity and the only Christian in his village in eastern Kyrgyzstan. After his conversion the village mullah had him banned from community events — deeply painful for the community-centered Kyrgyz — and barred him from burial in the village cemetery. In late December 2006 he was murdered, the culmination of a long series of intolerant incidents; his son Ruslan Usmanov, a Protestant pastor, rejected claims that Protestants killed him for wanting to return to Islam as 'monstrous slander.' No documented account of how Usmanov heard the gospel or was converted survives beyond the record that he became a Protestant Christian in 1990; the published sources document only his ostracism and murder.

name: Eldos
summary: Eldos, a Kyrgyz convert from Islam in his mid-20s, was cornered by three Muslim men in the village of Tamchi, Issyk-Kul, in October 2018 and beaten nearly to death for refusing to recite the shahada — suffering a fractured jaw, smashed teeth, concussion, and suspected brain hemorrhage. Police tried to disguise the religious motive, and the attackers' lawyer later held him captive for ten hours in a prosecutor's office, threatening him with prison if he did not drop the charges. Fearing for their lives, Eldos and his Christian uncle fled to another country. How Eldos first heard the gospel is not documented in the published reports, which record only his beating in October 2018 for refusing to recite the shahada.

name: Takhir Talipov
summary: Takhir Talipov, a Russian-born ethnic Tatar, became a Baptist church planter in Kazan, the capital of the mainly Muslim republic of Tatarstan, where he had been based since 1992. When he applied for a residency permit, the local FSB assessed his missionary work — trying 'to convert Muslims to his faith' — as 'extremist' and a threat to interconfessional stability, and a Kazan court upheld the refusal of his permit in 2004. His case became a documented example of pressure on ethnic Tatar evangelical believers in post-Soviet Russia. No documented account of Talipov's own conversion survives; the sources describe only his Baptist church-planting in Kazan from 1992 and the 2004 court case over his residency permit.

name: Emil Panahov
summary: Emil Panahov was raised in an Azeri Muslim family with a communist father and came to faith at age 12 in 1989 through a local Russian Baptist church, but fell away as he pursued a professional dancing career around the world. In 2007, after a knee injury in Turkey ended his dancing and doctors said he would never dance again, he recalled Jesus — whom he says spoke a word of healing to him — and was recommissioned through his Turkish pastor to return to Azerbaijan. He founded the Vineyard church in Baku, whose home fellowships baptize dozens of Azeri Muslim-background converts each year.

name: Hamid Shabanov
summary: Hamid Shabanov, of the Ingiloy ethnic Georgian Muslim minority in Azerbaijan's Zaqatala region, converted to Christianity from Islam in 1994 and became a Baptist pastor in the town of Aliabad. After his conversion he was summoned to the secret police and beaten, and he and other Baptists were fired from state jobs for their faith. In 2009 he was convicted on weapons charges and sentenced to two years of hard labor — a case his supporters said involved a planted weapon aimed at closing the Aliabad church. No documented account of how Shabanov heard the gospel survives beyond the record that he converted from Islam in 1994; the sources document his subsequent persecution and imprisonment.

name: Zaur Balayev
summary: Zaur Balayev pastors a Baptist congregation in Aliabad, a town in northwestern Azerbaijan populated almost entirely by the Ingiloy (ethnic Georgian Muslim) minority. He was first imprisoned for 16 days in 1995 on accusations of preparing a revolt, and in 2007 was sentenced to two years in prison on charges of violently resisting arrest — charges witnesses called fabricated, noting his slight build against five police officers. After global Baptist appeals, including from former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, Azerbaijan's president pardoned and released him in March 2008 after ten months. No documented account of how Balayev heard the gospel survives beyond the record that he became a Christian in 1992; the sources document his church leadership and imprisonment.

name: Rena
summary: Rena, a young woman in Azerbaijan, was furious when her sister and mother became Christians, scorning them for shaming the family. After losing her cow and searching three days in vain, she prayed: 'They say Jesus Christ is alive. If this is true let my cow return to me, and I will believe in Him.' That evening the cow came running toward her in the headlights of cars, and she declared, 'My cow has been found and Jesus Christ made it happen' — from that day she followed Jesus and joined the growing church her family attended.

name: Alexander Kasimovich Kazembek
summary: Born in Rasht, Qajar Iran, to a prominent Derbent family, Alexander Kazembek was the son of a Muslim cleric and qazi who trained him in Arabic, logic, and jurisprudence for a clerical career. In Astrakhan he encountered Scottish missionaries, taught them Tatar, Persian, and Arabic, and converted from Islam to Christianity — declaring to his father, 'I cannot recant; my flesh would willingly become a Mahomedan, but my conscience will not allow me.' Despite beatings, imprisonment, and disownment, he was baptized by the Scottish mission in July 1823 and became a renowned professor of Oriental studies at Kazan and St. Petersburg universities.

name: Bakhytzhan Kashkumbayev
summary: Bakhytzhan Kashkumbayev, a Kazakh pastor who led the Presbyterian Grace Church in Astana, was arrested in May 2013 on bizarre charges of lacing communion tea with hallucinogens and 'propaganda of extremism.' He spent nine months in jail, including forced detention in a psychiatric hospital with psychotropic drugs — a notorious Soviet-era punishment — and wrote a desperate plea to the UN Human Rights Committee. Released in February 2014 with a four-year suspended sentence, his case drew international advocacy from the U.S. Congress Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission and Forum 18. No published account of Kashkumbayev's conversion is known; the sources document only his pastoral ministry in Astana and his 2013-2014 imprisonment.

name: Gulya
summary: Gulya, an ethnic Kazakh woman, came to faith in Christ through dreams and began a small fellowship when she was one of only three ethnic Kazakhs in her church and felt out of place. The fellowship she started grew into the 'Senim' (Faith) church with more than 200 baptized believers, worshipping in Kazakh, Russian, and Uzbek, with new converts added nearly every week. She and her team showed the 'Jesus' film in Kazakh and Uzbek villages, enduring threats on their lives and newspaper accusations of betraying Islam, yet remained determined to introduce Kazakhs to the Savior she had found.

name: Yqylas Qabduaqasov
summary: Yqylas Qabduaqasov, a 54-year-old Kazakh Christian convert and active member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church in Astana, was detained in August 2015 and put on trial in handcuffs. Several witnesses testified that during Bible study sessions he had expressed ideas sounding 'insulting to Muslims and the Prophet Muhammad,' and he faced up to ten years in prison on charges of 'inciting religious hatred.' His prosecution became a widely reported example of the pressure on Muslim-background converts in Kazakhstan, whom Open Doors identifies as facing the harshest persecution from both family and the state. No documented account of how Qabduaqasov heard the gospel or was converted is publicly available; the sources document only his 2015 prosecution for discussing his faith.

name: Bakhrom Kholmatov
summary: Bakhrom Kholmatov, identified by the U.S. Congress Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission as a Tajik pastor, led the Sunmin Sunbogym (Full Gospel) Protestant Church in Khujand. In April 2017 the secret police raided his church, and he was jailed for 'singing extremist songs in church' — worship songs the authorities claimed incited religious hatred, alongside Josh McDowell's 'More Than a Carpenter,' which they labeled extremist. Sentenced to three years in Yavan Prison, he was freed early in December 2019, thanking supporters whose prayers 'helped me to stand.' No documented account of how Kholmatov heard the gospel or was converted is publicly available; the sources document only his pastoral ministry in Khujand and his 2017-2019 imprisonment.

name: Shageldy Atakov
summary: Shageldy Atakov, a Turkmen Baptist in the Caspian port city of Turkmenbashi, was imprisoned, as the U.S. Congressional Record put it, 'simply because he decided to change his religion from Muslim to Christian' — arrested in December 1998 and sentenced on trumped-up swindling charges. Amnesty International took up his case as Turkmenistan's only known Christian prisoner of conscience, and the European Parliament condemned his unjust treatment. His wife Artygul and five children were pressured by authorities and mullahs to convert to Islam, and he was finally released in January 2002, declaring, 'Jesus has given me a Christmas gift.' No documented account of how Atakov heard the gospel or was converted is publicly available; the sources document only his 1998-2002 imprisonment and steadfastness.

name: Joanes Leizarraga
summary: Born in the Northern Basque Country (Labourd), Leizarraga was a Catholic priest who converted to Protestantism around 1560, at the same time the Queen of Navarre embraced the Reformation. He placed himself under the Synod of Pau, which commissioned him to give the gospel to his people in their own tongue. He produced the first New Testament translation in Basque, published in La Rochelle in 1571, laying the foundation of written Basque prose.

name: Samuel Vila Ventura
summary: Born in 1902 in Rubí, Catalonia, into a prosperous Catalan merchant family that had converted to Protestantism through English missionaries. As a boy he attended a Methodist church, printing Bible verses and tossing them from train windows in hopes someone would find Jesus. He made the faith his own, wrote his first apologetic book at a young age, founded the evangelical publisher CLIE in 1924, helped plant 52 churches across Spain, and defended persecuted Protestants under the Franco dictatorship — which branded him 'one of the most dangerous agitators in Spain.'

name: Lukash Dzekut-Malei
summary: Born in 1888 in Slonim into an Orthodox family and orphaned at four, Dzekut-Malei encountered Baptists while serving in the Russian army in Białystok. On 31 December 1912 he was baptized in the Supraśl river by preacher Roman Chomiak. For his open preaching he was arrested by the Tsarists and forced to walk some 170 km tied to a horse to a prison in Brest. He became the leading Baptist pastor of the Belarusian evangelical awakening, founded numerous congregations, and translated the first complete New Testament into Belarusian (1931), earning the title 'father of the Belarusian Bible.'

name: Victor Danielsen
summary: Born in 1894 in Søldarfjørður, Danielsen was a gifted teacher whose spiritual life was decisively shaped by the evangelical preacher J.C.V. Ryving-Jensen. In 1915 he left the Lutheran state church and joined the Brethren congregation, being baptized in the fjord in 1916. He spent the rest of his life as an itinerant missionary and preacher across the islands, and between 1934 and 1949 he translated the entire Bible into Faroese — a landmark achievement for the language and the Christian faith of the islands.

name: Menno Simons
summary: Born in 1496 in Witmarsum, Friesland, Menno was ordained a Catholic priest in his mid-twenties and served at Pingjum and Witmarsum. Troubled by doubts about transubstantiation and by the execution of the Anabaptist Sicke Freerks at Leeuwarden in 1531, he studied the New Testament and came to reject infant baptism and Catholic dogma. On 12 January 1536 he resigned his priesthood, was rebaptized at Leeuwarden, and became the organizing leader of the peaceful Anabaptists — the movement that took the name Mennonite from him — living as a fugitive with a price on his head.

name: Evan Roberts
summary: Born in 1878 at Loughor, Wales, Roberts was a collier who had been converted as a boy and prayed for revival for eleven years as a member of Moriah Calvinistic Methodist Church. While preparing for ministry at Newcastle Emlyn in the autumn of 1904 he experienced a deep work of the Spirit and returned to Moriah to share it with the young people. The meetings that followed sparked the 1904–1905 Welsh revival, in which some 100,000 people were converted, with lasting influence on Pentecostal and charismatic movements worldwide. The details of Roberts's own childhood conversion are not documented — even his sympathetic biographer gives no certain account; what is documented is the 1904-1905 Welsh revival he catalyzed.

name: Howell Harris
summary: Born in 1714 at Trevecca, Breconshire, Harris was a schoolmaster of uncertain spiritual state until Palm Sunday 1735, when a parish sermon by the Rev. Pryce Davies on the necessity of partaking of Holy Communion pierced him. After weeks of self-examination he received Communion on Whit Sunday convinced he had received mercy through the blood of Christ. He at once began holding meetings in his home, became the catalyst of the Welsh Methodist revival, preached through Wales for decades despite mob violence, and founded what became the Calvinistic Methodist movement.

name: William Williams Pantycelyn
summary: Born in 1717 in Carmarthenshire, Wales, Williams had been studying for the Anglican ministry when in 1737 he heard the newly converted Howell Harris preaching in Talgarth churchyard. The preaching convicted him, and he was converted on the spot, redirecting his whole vocation. He became the great hymn-writer of the Welsh Methodist revival — author of 'Guide me, O thou great Jehovah' and hundreds of Welsh hymns — spreading the gospel of the revival through song across Wales for over fifty years.

name: Billy Bray
summary: Born in 1794 at Twelveheads, Cornwall, William 'Billy' Bray grew up to be a hard-drinking tin miner notorious for riotous behaviour. In 1823, after a narrow escape from a mining accident, he read John Bunyan's 'Visions of Heaven and Hell' and was converted in November of that year, later saying he 'shouted for joy and did not stop until the day he died.' He became a joyful, unconventional Bible Christian preacher, built three Methodist chapels, raised two orphans alongside his own children, and became one of the most beloved figures of Cornish Methodism.

name: Johannes King
summary: Born Adiri among the Matawai Maroons, King suffered a prolonged illness during which, beginning in 1855, he reported visions directing him toward Christianity. He taught himself to read using Moravian mission materials, built a church in his village, and was baptized as Johannes King in 1861, becoming the first Maroon missionary. His diaries, kept from 1864 until his death in 1898, are a unique firsthand record of an African-descended Maroon embracing and spreading the Christian faith.

name: Johannes Alabi
summary: Born around 1743 at Munyawoyokiiki in the Upper Suriname, Alabi (also spelled Arabi) was of Yoruba West African descent and the son of a man who would become granman (paramount chief) of the Saramaka Maroons. When his father was killed by the Matawai in 1767, Alabi swore revenge, but the tribe's elders persuaded him to make peace since he stood to become granman himself. He then came into contact with Moravian missionaries, who taught him to read and write, and he aided them in developing a Saramaccan-German dictionary — one of the earliest written records of the language. He was christened Johannes on 6 January 1771, was elected granman of the Saramaka in 1783, and lived until 1820, remembered in Richard Price's 'Alabi's World' as a bridge between Maroon society and the Christian mission.
sources: College of Charleston — anthropologist Richard Price, author of 'Alabi's World' (https://today.cofc.edu/2016/02/01/anthropologist-richard-price/)

name: Elka
summary: Elka was a Wai Wai chief and witchdoctor (shaman) in what was then British Guiana who took an interest in spiritual things as a youth and rose to be one of his people's most respected witchdoctors. Beginning in the late 1940s, missionaries of the Unevangelized Fields Mission (now Crossworld) — including brothers Neill, Rader and Bob Hawkins — brought the gospel to the Wai Wai, and in the 1950s Elka became the first Christian convert of his tribe. He renounced witchcraft and became a jungle missionary, traveling with evangelist Neville (Kedu) to preach among the Wai Wai and neighboring groups. His story is told as a firsthand account in Homer E. Dowdy's 1963 'Christ's Witchdoctor'; he died in August 1994, credited with leading many Wai Wai to faith and opening contact with tribes no foreign missionary could reach.
sources: Mission Nexus — 'Christ's Witchdoctor' by Homer E. Dowdy (https://missionexus.org/books/leaders-edge/christs-witchdoctor-dowdy/)
Beacon Media — 'Christ's Witchdoctor' full text, part 1 (https://beaconmedia.com.au/beaconmedia/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Christs-witchdoctor-part-1.pdf)

name: Sir Lionel Luckhoo
summary: Lionel Luckhoo was a celebrated Guyanese lawyer and diplomat — twice listed in the Guinness Book of Records for the most successful criminal lawyer — who had been only nominally Christian. On November 7, 1978, at age 64, he experienced a profound conversion at a Full Gospel Business Men's Fellowship meeting in Guyana. He spent his remaining years as an evangelical speaker and author, known especially for his public defense of Christ's resurrection.
sources: Christianity Today — 'Evangelicals Win Breakthrough on Asian Refugee Resettlement' (1980) (https://www.christianitytoday.com/1980/03/evangelicals-win-breakthrough-on-asian-refugee-resettlement/)

name: Eduard
summary: George Eduard, a Saramaka Maroon of Suriname, became a Christian as a youth and as a teenager accompanied his grandfather preaching the gospel along the Suriname River. After a witch doctor accepted Christ in one village, the villagers stoned them; that night the persecutors dragged his grandfather from his hut, beat him with a chain and poured tar on him while Eduard watched hidden in the darkness. After he grew up and left home, Eduard strayed from the faith — until one night Jesus appeared to him in a dream, saying, 'I'm getting ready to do a great work on the Suriname River. I need you to help.' He returned to the river as a guide and evangelist, teaming with Southern Baptist IMB missionaries Tim McClard and Chip Collins; when volunteers renovated the Dang Village school in 1997, about 175 Saramaccans accepted Christ after viewing the 'Jesus' film.
sources: Baptist Press — 'Descendants of African slaves find freedom from power of evil' (https://www.baptistpress.com/resource-library/news/descendants-of-african-slaves-find-freedom-from-power-of-evil/)

name: Magdala
summary: Magdala, a Saramaka Maroon woman, heard Eduard preach about the love of Jesus and accepted Christ, renouncing the Kunu practices of her village. Despite pressure from her community, she prepared for public baptism as a testimony of her new faith. Her conversion was reported by Baptist Press alongside Eduard's, as part of the gospel's advance among the Saramaka of the Suriname River.
sources: Baptist Press — 'Descendants of African slaves find freedom from power of evil' (https://www.baptistpress.com/resource-library/news/descendants-of-african-slaves-find-freedom-from-power-of-evil/)

name: José Cabrera
summary: José Cabrera was the Chocó associate of Foursquare missionary Dick Scott, who began Bible translation among the Emberá of Panama's Darién in 1960. Cabrera became a believer after his son Ricardo was miraculously healed of a sickness so severe he could neither sit up nor eat; afterward he asked whether the same God could cure him of his drinking habit — and he was delivered. He went on to serve as Scott's language informant and co-translator for the Emberá Bible, published in 2013.
sources: Foursquare News — 'Dick Scott, missionary, college president and Bible translator, with the Lord' (https://resources.foursquare.org/dick-scott-missionary-college-president-and-bible-translator-with-the-lord/)
Foursquare News — 'Longtime Dream of Bible Translation Nears Completion' (https://resources.foursquare.org/?p=25374)

name: Norberto Chipiage
tribe: Indigenous Venezuelan (people group not named in source)
summary: Norberto Chipiage, an indigenous chief (cacique) in the Atures municipality of Amazonas state, had already accepted Jesus when he began listening to an Adventist radio program for a year. He contacted the station, and he, his wife, and their six children received Bible studies and were baptized together in June 2023. He then donated a house for the area's first Adventist church, becoming a local leader of the new congregation.
sources: Adventist News — 'Un programa de radio lleva a un cacique indígena a convertirse en adventista' (https://adventist.news/es/news/un-programa-de-radio-lleva-a-un-cacique-indigena-a-convertirse-en-adventista)

name: Pedro Quintrequeo
summary: Pedro Quintrequeo testified that as a young man of about eighteen to twenty he had been 'an enemy of the Gospel.' After his mother accepted the Gospel during a serious illness, he too was converted and went on to become a Pentecostal pastor among the Mapuche. His first-person testimony is recorded in an academic thesis on Mapuche Pentecostalism at the University of Chile. The details of Quintrequeo's conversion are not documented beyond his own brief testimony — recorded in a University of Chile thesis — that after his mother accepted the gospel during a serious illness, he too was converted.
sources: University of Chile repository — Lafferte, thesis on Mapuche Pentecostalism (https://repositorio.uchile.cl/bitstream/handle/2250/106524/lafferte_m.pdf?sequence=3)

name: Helen Reynolds
summary: Helen Reynolds was among the early converts in Belize, baptized on November 22, 1980, after a healing that she and local members described as a great manifestation of faith. Her baptism testimony was reported by the Church News as part of the first fruits of missionary work in Belize. (Note: her conversion was into the Latter-day Saint tradition; included here as a documented Belizean conversion testimony.)
sources: Church News — 'Belize: Great Manifestations of Faith' (1998) (https://www.thechurchnews.com/1998/2/7/23251109/belize-great-manifestations-of-faith/)

name: Pooq
summary: Pooq was among the first Inuit converts of Hans Egede's Danish mission; in 1724 Egede gave him a handwritten catechism booklet that survives today as one of the first written samples of the Greenlandic language. He and his friend Qiperoq became the first Inuit to travel voluntarily on a European ship, sailing to Copenhagen in 1724 to present the Greenland Mission to the Danish-Norwegian king and public. Their witness so moved Count Zinzendorf that it helped inspire the Moravian missions to Greenland and Labrador. No documented account of how Pooq came to faith survives beyond his 1724 baptism by Hans Egede; the sources record his catechism, his voyage to Denmark, and his witness that moved Count Zinzendorf.
sources: Springer — Martin Luther's Small Catechism in Greenlandic, ch. 13 (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-662-72538-2_13)

name: Arnarsaq
summary: Arnarsaq came to the Danish mission asking to be taught how to come to the Christian God; she converted and was baptized in 1737, and was unusually permitted to keep her original Inuk name instead of taking a biblical one. She became a translator, interpreter, and critical debate partner of theologian Paul Egede, and with Hans Punngujooq helped translate the New Testament into Greenlandic. Sent as a missionary to Greenland in 1741, she remained the vital link between the Danish missionaries and the Inuit for decades.

name: Kajarnak (Kayarnak)
summary: Kajarnak was untouched by the Moravians' abstract theological preaching until he heard the story of Gethsemane and Calvary, which thrilled and transformed him. On 30 March 1739 he was publicly baptized as the firstfruit of the Moravian Greenland Mission, with his wife and children. He endured persecution — his brother-in-law was murdered — yet conducted prayer meetings, reasoned with his people, and helped the Brethren with their Greenlandic translation work.
sources: J. E. Hutton, History of Moravian Missions (e-book) (https://missiology.org.uk/pdf/e-books/hutton/moravian-missions_hutton.pdf)

name: Karpik
summary: Born around 1754 at Arbatok near Hamilton Inlet in southern Labrador, Karpik lost his mother as a small child and his father was killed in 1767 during a melee between the British and Inuit. In 1769 Governor Hugh Palliser placed the orphaned boy in the care of Moravian missionaries Jens Haven and Christian Drachardt, who took him to Fulneck, Yorkshire, where he attended school with British boys — Karpik had remembered Drachardt's preaching at Chateau Bay back in 1765. He embraced Christianity and was baptized on his sickbed by Drachardt on 4 October 1769, 'departing very happily' the next day, 5 October, when he died of smallpox. He was the first baptized Inuk from Labrador, carrying the missionaries' hopes that he would help open the Labrador mission — hopes his death cut short, making him, in mission historian Thompson's phrase, 'the Henry Obookiah of Labrador.'
sources: Hans Rollmann — Hopedale: Inuit Gateway to the South and Moravian Settlement (https://www.thefreelibrary.com/Hopedale%3A+Inuit+gateway+to+the+south+and+Moravian+settlement-a0360993790)
Durham e-theses — history of the Moravian church in the North of England, quoting the Fulneck record of Karpick's sickbed baptism (http://etheses.dur.ac.uk/9715/1/9715_6508.PDF)
Thompson, 'Moravian Missions' — on Karpik as the 'Henry Obookiah of Labrador' (https://www.gospelstudies.org.uk/missiology/pdf/e-books/thompson-a-c/moravian-missions_thompson.pdf)

name: Kippinguk (Jonathan)
summary: Born in Chateau Bay in southern Labrador, Kippinguk first heard the gospel from the Moravians after their Hopedale station was founded in 1782. Traveling together in a boat with missionary William Turner, he heard Turner speak 'so much to me about the state of my soul' — words, he later wrote, that he never forgot. On 25 January 1784 he was baptized at Hopedale, receiving the Christian name Jonathan; he and his wife Sibylla were the first Esquimaux baptized at the station, marking the beginning of the Moravian congregation on the southern Labrador coast. In an October 1804 letter to Turner he confessed he had 'walked in darkness' even after baptism, but testified: 'since you left us, I have turned with my whole heart to Jesus, and all my thoughts and desires are drawn towards him.' He later piloted missionaries Kohlmeister and Kmoch on their 1811 exploration to Ungava Bay, and died in 1812 while traveling from Hopedale to Okak.
sources: Hans Rollmann — Hopedale: Inuit Gateway to the South and Moravian Settlement (https://www.thefreelibrary.com/Hopedale%3A+Inuit+gateway+to+the+south+and+Moravian+settlement-a0360993790)
The Moravians in Labrador (Project Gutenberg) — Jonathan's October 1804 letter to William Turner (https://www.gutenberg.org/files/18391/18391-h/18391-h.htm)
Hans Rollmann — 'Hopedale: Inuit Gateway to the South and Moravian Settlement,' Newfoundland Studies (https://www.erudit.org/fr/revues/nflds/2013-v28-n2-nflds28_2/nflds28_2art01/)

name: Chinnik
summary: Chinnik was a warlike Chukchi chief in the 1830s whom neighboring Koryak and Itelmen tribes feared for his ruthlessness — the priest Gromov described his 'animal-like behavior.' The first active Orthodox evangelization of the Chukchi came in the 1830s-40s as natives and Russians reinforced trade relations, with missionaries such as Trifonov and Roman Vereshchagin preaching at the annual trade fairs; at Gizhiga only one Chukchi was baptized in 1831 and four more in 1835. In 1839 Chinnik came with a group of fifteen Chukchi to the trade fair at the Gizhiga fort and, to everyone's astonishment, asked the local priest Roman Vereshchagin for baptism — news that reportedly reached Tsar Nicholas I, who exclaimed, 'Good God, at last.' No account survives of what moved the chief to ask for baptism.
sources: Andrei Znamenski, Shamanism and Christianity (academic text, hosted) (https://www.scribd.com/document/249291539/Shamanism-and-Christianity)

name: Yatargin
summary: Yatargin was a toion (headman) of the reindeer Chukchi who encountered the gospel through the Orthodox missionaries working the annual trade fairs, where Trifonov and others preached to the Chukchi who came to trade. In 1840 he brought ninety-three of his people to the annual fair at the Gizhiga fort and asked for baptism for them all — the first collective Chukchi embrace of Christianity. Missionary Trifonov baptized the group, and the later missionary Suvorov described Yatargin as 'the first' and 'the best' Christian among the Chukchi, a report that led Bishop Veniaminov to conclude the Chukchi actively sought conversion. No record survives of what prompted Yatargin's request, and the hold of Christianity on the group later proved shallow.
sources: Andrei Znamenski, Shamanism and Christianity (academic text, hosted) (https://www.scribd.com/document/249291539/Shamanism-and-Christianity)

name: Uyaquq (Helper Neck)
summary: Born in the mid-1860s into a family of shamans in the lower Kuskokwim River valley, Uyaquq became a shaman himself in early adulthood but converted to Christianity after his father's conversion, joining the Alaskan Moravian Church. As a Moravian Helper — English speakers called him "Helper Neck" — he is said to have converted whole Yup'ik villages in the lower Kuskokwim valley. Fascinated by written Scripture, he invented the Yugtun writing system in five documented stages and produced Bible translations and religious works within five years, all while refusing English literacy so as not to lose his Yupik identity.

name: Nedercook ("Grandma Tucker")
summary: Born in the 1850s at Rocky Point on the Bering Sea coast, Nedercook grew up among the Inupiat in the old ways and did not see a white person until adulthood. In her oral-history interview preserved at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, she recalled first learning 'the religion of the white man' from missionaries — whom, she said, her people at first disliked and shunned. She came to Christian faith late in life, converted at age eighty-three (around 1938), and at 113 gave her testimony at the 1971 Alaska Baptist crusade in Anchorage. Her interviews remain a firsthand account of an Inupiaq woman's journey from the old ways to faith in Christ.
sources: Baptist Press — Bill Hunke, former Alaska exec & historian, dies (https://www.baptistpress.com/resource-library/news/bill-hunke-former-alaska-exec-historian-dies/)
UAF Oral History Archives — interview with Grandma Minnie Tucker (https://oharchives.library.uaf.edu/74/74-06_SIDE_A_T01.pdf)
Dogear Diary — review of Once Upon an Eskimo Time by Edna Wilder (https://dogeardiary.com/2018/04/once-upon-an-eskimo-time/)

name: Mosab Hassan Yousef
summary: Born in Ramallah, West Bank, Mosab is the eldest son of Hamas co-founder Sheikh Hassan Yousef and was groomed as his father's successor in the militant movement. Around 1999, a stranger invited him to a Bible study in Jerusalem's Old City; over four years of reading Scripture he grew disillusioned with Hamas's violence and gave his life to Christ, secretly baptized in 2005 at a beach near Tel Aviv. He publicly announced his faith in 2008, the same year he came to the US seeking asylum, which was granted in 2010 after his former Shin Bet handler testified that Yousef's information had saved hundreds of lives. Disowned and threatened with death by Hamas, he authored the bestselling memoir 'Son of Hamas' (2010) and now speaks openly as a Christian advocate for reconciliation and against radical Islam.

name: Afshin Javid
summary: Raised in a strict Iranian Shiite Muslim family, Afshin was declared the spiritual heir of his grandfather, a respected Islamic leader; he studied the Quran with passion and joined Hezbollah's Basij ranks as a teen to prove his devotion and convert Christians. While imprisoned in Malaysia's Pudu prison for passport offenses, he faced a terrifying spiritual crisis and, desperate, cried out to God — hearing a voice tell him to call on the name of Jesus. Jesus then appeared to him, speaking forgiveness over him and commissioning him; he miraculously obtained a Bible, supernaturally gained the ability to read English, and began preaching Christ to fellow inmates. Now leading the Cyrus Call ministry and author of 'As Easy as Drinking Water, A Muslim Forgiven' (2010), he travels the world evangelizing Muslims.

name: Daniel Shayesteh
summary: A practicing Muslim raised in Iran, Daniel became a teacher of Islamic philosophy and a leading Muslim politician in Khomeini's 1979 Islamic Revolution. When he fell out with the regime he was kidnapped by the Revolutionary Military, placed on death row awaiting execution, then miraculously released — escaping to Turkey. While pursuing doctoral studies in Istanbul, a failed business relationship brought him into contact with Christians; as he compared religions he was shocked by Christianity's message of freedom, love and unconditional forgiveness, and he gave his life to Christ. He founded Exodus from Darkness ministry and authored 'The House I Left Behind' (2012), now traveling the world preaching the gospel to Muslims.

name: Hormoz Shariat
summary: Born into a devout Muslim family in Iran, Hormoz chanted 'Death to America' as a teenager during the 1979 Islamic Revolution, then moved to the US for a PhD in artificial intelligence. In a season of spiritual questioning he read the Quran cover to back and found it added nothing; prompted to also study the Bible, he compared the two books and was transformed by the gospel around 1980. His calling was sealed when his brother Hamraz was executed by firing squad on a minor political charge — 'OK, I'm going to start sharing the Gospel with Muslims.' In 1987 he planted a church in San Jose that became one of the largest Muslim-convert churches in America, and in 2001 founded Iran Alive Ministries, which now broadcasts the gospel 24/7 by satellite into Iran, where Shariat is called 'the Billy Graham of Iran.'

name: Saeed Abedini
summary: Raised a strong Muslim in Iran — at 14 he wanted to join Hezbollah to fight Israel — Saeed sank into depression and planned to kill a church pastor near his home before taking his own life. At 20, kneeling with a Bible in one hand and a Quran in the other, he prayed for God to show him the true way; he heard a voice, 'Saeed, I'm coming back soon; go preach my gospel,' saw a light filling his room, and gave his life to Christ (2000). He became a house-church pastor; arrested in 2012, he was sentenced to eight years in Tehran's Evin Prison for his faith, enduring beatings, solitary confinement and relentless pressure to deny Christ — which he refused. In prison he evangelized fellow inmates, with at least ten converting in his first year, and was finally released in 2016.

name: Maryam Rostampour
summary: Born into a Muslim family in Iran, Maryam grew unsatisfied with the teachings of the Quran and converted to Christianity as a young woman after personal encounters with Jesus; she studied theology in Turkey. Returning to Iran with her friend Marziyeh Amirizadeh, she helped distribute more than 20,000 Farsi New Testaments across the country and started two secret house churches. Arrested on 5 March 2009, she spent 259 days in Tehran's notorious Evin Prison, where she was urged before a Revolutionary Court to recant her faith and return to Islam — she refused, even sharing the gospel with fellow inmates. Released in November 2009 after international pressure from Amnesty International and the UN, she co-authored the memoir 'Captive in Iran' (2013).

name: Marziyeh Amirizadeh
summary: Born into a Muslim family in Iran, Marziyeh converted to Christianity as a young woman after personal encounters with Jesus, having grown dissatisfied with the Quran's teachings; she studied theology in Turkey, where she met Maryam Rostampour. The two returned to Iran on a shared evangelistic vision, covertly putting New Testaments into the hands of twenty thousand Iranians and planting two underground churches. Arrested on 5 March 2009, she spent 259 days in Evin Prison facing charges of apostasy and propagation of Christianity, refusing repeated demands to renounce Christ and instead witnessing to prisoners around her. Released in November 2009 following international pressure, she co-authored 'Captive in Iran' (2013), a searing account of faith under fire.

name: Majed El Shafie
summary: Born in Cairo to a prominent Muslim family of judges and lawyers, Majed converted to Christianity as a young law student and began advocating equal rights for Egypt's Christians, building a ministry and human rights organization that grew to 24,000 members. Arrested in 1998 and taken to Cairo's Abu Zabal Prison, he endured days of brutal torture — electrocution, beatings, cigarette burns, dogs released into his cell — and was sentenced to death on three charges. He escaped Egypt by driving a stolen jet-ski from Taba to Eilat, Israel, and was resettled in Canada in 2002. There he founded One Free World International, testified before the US Congress on religious freedom, authored 'Freedom Fighter,' and received the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012.

name: Magdi Cristiano Allam
summary: Born in Cairo in 1952 as Magdi Muhammad Allam, he became Italy's most prominent Muslim journalist — deputy editor of Corriere della Sera and a fierce critic of Islamic extremism — having made the hajj pilgrimage in 1991 though otherwise non-practicing. After a years-long interior journey culminating in reflection on the value of life following Hamas death threats, he converted to Catholicism and was personally baptized by Pope Benedict XVI at the 2008 Easter Vigil in St. Peter's Basilica, taking the name 'Cristiano,' later writing 'Thank You Jesus: My Conversion from Islam to Christianity.' He lived under police protection after receiving death threats from radical Islamic groups. In 2013 he publicly left the Catholic Church over its stance toward Islam while insisting he remains a Christian.

name: Mark A. Gabriel
summary: A devout Egyptian Muslim who memorized the entire Quran by age 12, earned a PhD in Islamic history at Cairo's Al-Azhar University — the premier university of Islamic teaching — and taught there while serving as a mosque imam. His exhaustive study of Islamic history and the Quran's internal contradictions (on jihad, alcohol, and the treatment of Christians) convinced him the Quran was a man-made book rather than God's revelation. When he voiced his doubts he was fired, kidnapped and tortured by Egyptian secret police, nearly killed by his own father, and survived assassination attempts. He fled Egypt, changed his name (Gabriel is a pseudonym), and received asylum in the United States, where he now writes and lectures, authoring 'Islam and Terrorism' and 'Jesus and Muhammad.'

name: Mohammed Hegazy (Bishoy Armia Boulous)
summary: Raised in Port Said on the Suez Canal, Mohammed converted to Coptic Orthodox Christianity at age 16 in 1998 after 'readings and comparative studies in religions,' saying 'Islam wasn't promoting love as Christianity did'; he took the name Bishoy after a Coptic saint, and his wife also converted. In 2007 he became the first Egyptian to sue for legal recognition of his conversion on his government ID card — the request was rejected and the case stalled. He was repeatedly detained and tortured, arrested again in 2013, and sentenced to five years in 2014 on charges his lawyers called retaliation for his apostasy; his wife and children fled to Germany. NEEDS VERIFICATION: in 2016 a video surfaced of him reciting the Shahada and declaring a return to Islam; his attorney said the video was recorded under duress while imprisoned to secure his release.

name: Necati Aydin
summary: A Turkish convert from Islam, Necati became the pastor of a small Protestant church in Malatya, eastern Turkey. On 18 April 2007, five young Muslim-Turkish nationalists stormed the office of the Zirve Christian publishing house and demanded that the Christians pray the Islamic prayer of conversion; when Necati, Ugur Yuksel and their German colleague refused, they were bound, interrogated about their Christian activities, tortured with knives, and had their throats slit. Necati was dead at the scene; the five killers were convicted of premeditated murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. His widow publicly forgave the killers, and his story is told in the Voice of the Martyrs documentary 'Malatya.'

name: Ugur Yuksel
summary: A Turkish convert from Islam, Ugur worked alongside pastor Necati Aydin at the Zirve Christian publishing office in Malatya, eastern Turkey. On 18 April 2007, five young Muslim-Turkish nationalists broke into the office, demanded the three Christians pray the Islamic conversion prayer, and when they refused — bound them, interrogated them about their evangelistic activities, tortured them, and slit their throats. Ugur was rushed to hospital alive but died during surgery; the five killers were later convicted and sentenced to life in prison. His death alongside Aydin became one of modern Turkey's most widely reported martyrdoms of converts from Islam, documented in the Voice of the Martyrs film 'Malatya.'

name: Nihad Hassan
summary: A Kurdish Muslim from a small village near Afrin, Syria, Nihad was already on a spiritual journey when he was jailed as a political prisoner in 2008. He spent 55 days in a 90-by-90-centimetre solitary confinement cell, where — as he told SAT-7 — 'I heard the voice of the Lord... He told me he loved me,' experiencing physical and emotional healing and a profound, personal faith in Christ. He became pastor of a Kurdish church in Lebanon, where his testimony inspired other Kurds to follow Christ. In July 2026 he was detained again while visiting Afrin and questioned about his Christian faith; during two weeks of detention he evangelized fellow inmates and prison staff, with a SAT-7 clip of his testimony drawing tens of thousands of responses.

name: Mohammed Christophe Bilek
summary: Born in 1950 into a Muslim Kabyle (Berber) family in Algeria, Bilek moved to France in 1961. In the 1960s, while living in Paris, he first heard of Jesus Christ and the Gospel on the radio, took a correspondence catechism course with Swiss Protestants, and visited medieval churches; fascinated by Jesus, he was baptized in 1970 and later entered the Catholic Church, drawn by saints such as Francis of Assisi and Therese. He became a published author ('Un Algerien pas tres catholique', 1999; 'Saint Augustin raconte a ma fille', 2011) and in the 1990s founded the website Notre-Dame de Kabylie, devoted to evangelization among Muslims and Muslim-Christian dialogue. He has testified publicly about his conversion in the French press (e.g., Famille Chretienne) and in academic interviews, and is a prominent public voice for North African converts.

name: Said Oujibou
summary: Born in Morocco to a Muslim family, Oujibou left his native Morocco for France at the age of three and a half with his mother and siblings. Raised in a strongly Islamic milieu in France under Islamist pressure, he drifted into violence and trafficking as a youth while feeling a deep spiritual thirst. At about age 21 his life was overturned by an encounter with what he calls 'a God of love,' and he converted to Christianity. He became a pastor, consultant on urban violence, conference speaker and teacher of Islamic studies; in 2008 he founded the Union des Nord-Africains Chretiens de France to give a voice to North African converts, and authored the book 'Fier d'etre arabe et chretien' (Proud to be Arab and Christian). He has given his testimony publicly in churches, on television and in the press.

name: Jamaa Ait Bakrim
summary: A Moroccan convert from Islam living in the Massa area near Agadir in the Souss region, Bakrim refused to hide his Christian faith. Authorities jailed him and confined him in a psychiatric facility; between 2001 and 2005 he painted crosses and wrote Bible verses in public at his business (which was also his home) and openly displayed a cross, earning another year in jail. On December 28, 2005, an Agadir court sentenced him to 15 years in prison for 'proselytism' (and for burning two disused utility poles), after he proclaimed in court that he was 'the son of Christ' and wished Moroccans would become Christians. He did not appeal the sentence; fellow believers said it was meant to silence him, and he preached the gospel even in prison and in the psychiatric ward.

name: Rachid (of Agadir)
summary: Born and living in Agadir, Morocco, Rachid grew up in a very Islamic Sufi family around a zaouia (his father is a well-known fiqh) and used to mock Christianity. At age 12 he grew curious after hearing a Monte Carlo radio program in Darija (Moroccan Arabic); he later read the Arabic Gospel, shed his mistaken ideas, and came to see Christianity as a religion of love, peace and humility, converting in the 1990s. After years of hiding his faith, he now publicly confesses it, giving interviews to the Moroccan outlet H24info and to Evangelical Focus. He lost his job as an accountant because of his conversion and now works freelance; relations with his parents are restored though tension remains with his extended family.

name: Krimo Siaghi (also reported as Karim Siaghi)
summary: An Algerian convert from Islam living in Oran, in northwestern Algeria. In April 2011 he was arrested after a phone-shop merchant, angered that Siaghi would not recant his Christianity or recite the shahada, accused him of insulting Islam; Siaghi had given a Christian CD to a Muslim. In May 2011 he was sentenced to five years in prison and a fine of 200,000 dinars under Algeria's blasphemy law, even though prosecutors presented no evidence or witnesses, and he appealed the verdict. His case was documented internationally by Baptist Press, Open Doors, International Christian Concern and Morning Star News as a landmark prosecution of a convert, and he faced the sentence as a husband and father who would not deny Christ.
