name: Mohamed Ibaouene
summary: A convert from Islam working as a company manager in Tindouf, western Algeria. When a machine operator at his company pressured him to renounce Christ and return to Islam, Ibaouene refused; the colleague then filed a complaint accusing Ibaouene of pressuring him to abandon Islam. Ibaouene was convicted in absentia under Algeria's Law 03/06 (one year in prison plus a fine), and on appeal in February 2013 the prison term was revoked but the fine was doubled to 100,000 dinars. The president of the Protestant Church of Algeria (EPA), Mustapha Krim, publicly denounced the ruling and the church planned a further appeal, calling the law a standing threat to all converts.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: the cited sources document his trial and refusal to recant, but give almost no detail on his Muslim background or how he came to faith.

name: Seyfao Madi
summary: Born in Libya in 1977 into a Muslim family, Madi was introduced in 2016 by a friend to Christian friends, including an American; after discussions he converted to Christianity in 2017 and was baptized by the American. He began sharing his faith with other Libyans. Arrested by Libya's Internal Security Agency, he appeared in an interrogation video the ISA published online, in which he stated his conversion and evangelism in his own words. He was among six Libyans reported in 2023 to face the death penalty under penal code article 207 for converting to Christianity and proselytizing.
sources: NOTE: his name and confession are public only because Libya's Internal Security Agency recorded and published his interrogation video; The Guardian also reported the case via activists. Handle with care.

name: Mohamed Ali
summary: A 22-year-old from Kairouan, Tunisia, Mohamed Ali was raised in an orphanage from a very young age; he was not deeply religious but felt drawn to Christianity, while stumbling over doctrines such as the Trinity and the death of Christ. Through the Arabic 'Miracle' page of Miracle Connect, a counselor led him step by step through how God created man, why He created us, and how and why God came in the flesh. His mind and soul accepted that Jesus Christ came to redeem lives and bring people from darkness into light; he accepted Jesus as Lord and Savior, confessing himself a sinner in need of Christ's cleansing blood. His written testimony was published by Miracle Connect's Arabic outreach ministry.

name: Nabil
summary: Nabil was a young Salafist imam in Kairouan, Tunisia's holy city and the fourth holiest city in Islam; after the 2011 revolution he used the political chaos to impose a radical form of Islam in his neighborhood and preached the destruction of Tunisia's pre-Islamic heritage. A Franco-Tunisian Christian archaeologist then showed him, beneath the very foundations of his mosque, the remains of a 4th-century Christian basilica - a discovery that sparked a quest through the history of Roman Christian Africa. That journey led him from the ruins to the living Christ, and he now gives his testimony publicly on video. Only his first name is public in the available testimony.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: single-name video testimony on the 'Faith Without Limits - Testimonies' YouTube channel; independent corroboration not found.

name: Mustapha (surname withheld by source)
summary: A 29-year-old Tunisian believer interviewed by Open Doors in 2017, Mustapha grew up in a country that was 99 percent Muslim with, in his words, 'no Christianity' visible until after 2000. He was among those reached through satellite television and the internet, the means by which many Tunisians first encountered the Gospel. He now works full time for a church in Tunis that began as a handful of believers in house churches, was given use of a church building in 2006, and has grown to about 90 members; he is married with two children. His story illustrates the quiet, media-driven growth of the Tunisian church from a Muslim background.
sources: NOTE: Open Doors published only his first name; conversion details in the interview are limited.

name: Rustam Begaliev
summary: Rustam Begaliev grew up in a nominally Muslim Tajik family with ten siblings. When he was 14, his father was lethally poisoned by someone who wanted his factory, and Rustam turned to robbery to fund his dream of studying medicine in the poverty of post-Soviet Tajikistan around 1990. The turning point came through a Korean Tae Kwon Do instructor who was also a Christian missionary and began each class with a Bible reading; one day the instructor told Rustam that Jesus Christ is the risen Lord who wants a personal relationship with him. That night Rustam awoke to find his bedroom bathed in light and saw a figure clothed in white who said, 'I am Jesus Christ, the risen Lord.' Gripped by his own sinfulness, he asked Jesus to forgive him and received the charge, 'Do not be afraid. Serve me and spread my word in the whole world.' He trained at a Moscow seminary, served nine years in Christian ministry in Afghanistan (2001–2010), and returned to Tajikistan to pastor two congregations — one in his home village of 30–40 members and one in Dushanbe of 20 — and recorded SAT-7's first Tajik-language discipleship television series, 'Foundations of Christian Faith.'

name: Fariza Gulomikova
summary: Fariza Gulomikova was born and raised in post-Soviet Tajikistan in a Shia Ismaili Muslim family. As a child she began questioning her faith — notably why prayers had to be said in Arabic — and was struck by the transformed life of a cousin and the love and kindness of Christians she encountered. At age 11 she had a supernatural encounter with Jesus and became a Christian. Facing intense family pressure and the realities of apostasy — losing nearly everyone in her life for her faith — she held firm, immigrated to the United States at age 18 in pursuit of religious freedom and higher education, and now publicly advocates for ex-Muslims, religious liberty, and women's rights as an entrepreneur and host of the Christ-centered podcast 'The Royal Remnant.'

name: Assett (Aset)
summary: Assett, born in Almaty into a Muslim family, grew up making frequent trips to mosques, learning Arabic, and even exploring Buddhism — but found none of these paths satisfying. At age 15 he formed close friendships with missionary priests of the Communion and Liberation movement, whom he considered like fathers; he learned Italian with them and slowly came to know Jesus as the one he had been searching for all his life. At 21 he decided to be baptized and shared the decision with his mother, who replied, 'I would never do it, but you have to do what is best for you.' He married Mayra, a Muslim from Uzbekistan, and their two children are baptized; the interfaith family attended the Holy Mass presided over by the Pope in Nur-Sultan on 14 September 2022 together. His story was published by Vatican News ahead of the papal visit to Kazakhstan.

name: Gulnisa
summary: Gulnisa is an Uyghur woman in eastern Kazakhstan, part of a community that has held to Islamic traditions for centuries. She endured five years of chronic illness that kept her confined to her home, seeking help through Quranic prayers, fortune-tellers, and mullahs — all without relief. Then one night Jesus himself appeared to her in a dream: she held something like a ball and a white cord that was unraveling along a white road, and Jesus said, 'It is ours,' and smiled at her. Searching online afterward, she recognized the radiant figure from her dream, which led her into a house church where she came to faith. She is among a few hundred Uyghur evangelical believers in Kazakhstan reached by missionaries such as Marat and Nurlikiz Urazov, amid a quiet movement of Uyghur villages hearing the gospel, with about 25 villages in the region now hearing it for the first time.

name: Faruq (name changed)
tribe: Central Asian (specific people group withheld by source) — NEEDS VERIFICATION
country: Central Asia (country withheld by source for security) — NEEDS VERIFICATION
summary: Faruq grew up in the Muslim tradition of his parents in Central Asia; as a boy of 12 to 14 he would go to the mosque alone at midnight to pray and fast. Disillusioned by the emptiness he found studying the Quran at a local madrassa, he abandoned Islam at 18 to find what he calls the 'real God.' A chance encounter with a foreign believer put a Bible in his hands, and reading Jesus' words in John 10:10 — 'I have come that they may have life and have it in abundance' — he believed, having never known such love. While engaged he led his fiancée Jamilah to Christ. After a police informant infiltrated the small discipleship group in his home, Faruq was arrested in a night raid, interrogated at police headquarters, and held for days in a crowded central jail among criminals and Islamic radicals; he refused to recant, saying, 'Even if it is wrong [in your eyes] I still want to believe in this … my country needs it.' Released without charge, he fled with his family, returned, and now trains a new generation of leaders with the goal of spreading house churches across the nation. The Baptist Courier published his story under a changed name for his protection; his tribe and country were not specified.

name: Jamilah (name changed)
tribe: Central Asian (specific people group withheld by source) — NEEDS VERIFICATION

summary: Jamilah was raised in a Muslim family in Central Asia. While engaged to Faruq, he told her about his Christian faith and warned her plainly: 'It will be a tough life. … I might go to jail, I might be killed, many things will happen to me. I might be kicked out of the family … Do you want to still be with me?' She said yes, and he led her to faith in Jesus before their marriage. When Faruq was arrested in a night raid and his conversion became known, her father's terms for returning their family were that Faruq forsake Jesus, embrace Islam, and remarry her in a traditional Muslim ceremony. Jamilah chose to stay with her husband; they escaped the city in the middle of the night, left the country, and later returned to serve in house-church ministry alongside him. Her story was documented in the Baptist Courier's 2012 report under a changed name for security.

name: Murat (name changed)
tribe: Central Asian (specific people group withheld by source) — NEEDS VERIFICATION
country: Central Asia (country withheld by source for security) — NEEDS VERIFICATION
summary: Murat grew up in Central Asia with the impression that Allah cared more about people praying the right way, at the right time, in the right place. Through Bible studies with Central Asian Christians he heard that Jesus is God's Son who died for sins and is God himself — claims he found impossible to make sense of. Challenged to pray and ask God to show him whether he was real, Murat prayed and that night dreamed of demons tormenting children, which he tried and failed to drive out. After further dreams and prayer, he prayed a third time; that night he dreamed of his grandparents' former caretaker returning pregnant from her home country — a detail he knew nothing of until his mother called that morning confirming it exactly. Convinced God was real and listening, he prayed to be accepted into God's family. He became a Christian brother and a leader in a church he helped plant. His first-person account was published by Baptist Press under a changed name for security; his tribe and country were not specified.

name: Bilquis Sheikh
summary: Born in 1912 into the powerful Punjabi Muslim Hayat Khattar feudal family of Wah, near Rawalpindi, Bilquis Sheikh married a high-ranking Pakistani government official and lived as a prominent, politically connected Muslim woman. In 1966 a series of vivid, prophetic dreams launched her on a spiritual quest; a Christian missionary friend gave her a Bible, and through reading it she became convinced that Jesus was the Son of God. She gave her life to Christ in 1966, a conversion that put her life in danger and alienated her from her elite Muslim circles. She told her story in the autobiography 'I Dared to Call Him Father' (1978), a classic of Muslim evangelism that has sold over 300,000 copies; in 1972 she resettled in the United States with Samaritan's Purse sponsorship, spoke widely about her faith, later returned to Pakistan, and died there in 1997 with a Christian funeral.

name: Gulshan Esther
summary: Gulshan Esther was born into a devout Muslim family in Pakistan and was crippled by typhoid at six months old; her father took her from Pakistan to England seeking a cure and even made pilgrimage to Mecca begging Allah for her healing, all without success. After her father's untimely death, in her grief she cried out to God and heard a gentle voice say, 'I am Jesus, son of Mary'; as she read the Quran her interest in Jesus grew until one night he appeared to her in her bedroom in a blaze of light, miraculously restored her crippled arm and leg, taught her the Lord's Prayer, and told her to go to his people and tell them what he had done. She became a joyous disciple of Christ and has spent decades as a traveling evangelist. Her autobiography 'The Torn Veil' (1984), written with Thelma Sangster, has sold over 200,000 copies worldwide; she now lives in Oxford, England.

name: Sabatina James
summary: Born in November 1984 in Dhadar, Pakistan, into a devout Muslim family — the granddaughter of a mullah — Sabatina James was raised reading the Quran in Arabic and praying five times a day. After her family moved to Austria when she was ten, they dragged her back to Pakistan under false pretences, announced her engagement to a cousin, and, when she resisted the forced marriage, sent her to a strict Quran school where she endured beatings and abuse. She fled, refused the marriage, and converted to Christianity, for which her family condemned her for apostasy and issued death threats, forcing her into hiding under a new identity and police protection in Europe. She became a human-rights activist and founder of Sabatina e.V., rescuing persecuted Christians in Pakistan and Muslim girls fleeing forced marriage; her memoir 'My Fight for Faith and Freedom' was a German bestseller, followed by 'The Price of Love' (2025).

name: Esther John (born Qamar Zia)
summary: Born Qamar Zia on 14 October 1929 into a Muslim family in British India (her family migrated from Madras to the new state of Pakistan in 1947), she began attending a Christian school at seventeen and was deeply moved by the Book of Isaiah, especially chapter 53. A missionary gave her a pocket New Testament which she read twenty-seven times in secret, and she became convinced of Christ. In 1954, fearing her family would force her into a Muslim marriage, she ran away from home, changed her name to Esther John, worked in an orphanage and a mission hospital in Sahiwal, and trained as a teacher at the United Bible Training Centre in Gujranwala. She spent her remaining years evangelizing in villages around Chichawatni until she was murdered in her bed on 2 February 1960 for her evangelism; she is recognized as Pakistan's first modern Christian martyr and was honored in 1998 with a statue above the great west door of Westminster Abbey among ten 20th-century martyrs.

name: Nasir Siddiki
tribe: Not publicly specified (South Asian Muslim heritage — NEEDS VERIFICATION)
summary: Nasir Siddiki was born in 1953 in London, Ontario, Canada, into a Muslim family and became a successful, wealthy businessman who knew Allah only as a distant God. In 1987 he was admitted to Toronto General Hospital with what was called the worst case of shingles ever seen there; his immune system shut down, his fever hit 107.6, and doctors left him to die. On his deathbed he cried out, 'God, help me!' — and, as he testifies, Jesus appeared in his hospital room, identified himself as 'the God of the Christians, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob,' and miraculously healed him. After leaving the hospital he saw a television program asking 'Is Jesus the Son of God?', prayed to receive Christ, devoured the Bible, and in 1998 founded Wisdom Ministries in Tulsa, Oklahoma; he now hosts the TBN program 'Winning with Wisdom' and holds crusades worldwide.

name: Faruk al-Ahmed
summary: Faruk al-Ahmed is a Bengali Christian convert from Islam in northern Bangladesh who has been preaching the gospel since the mid-1990s. When he began his ministry in Kurigram, there was only one traditional Christian family and one Muslim-background family in his area; today, by his account, nearly 1,500 believers from Muslim backgrounds worship there. His ministry has grown in one of the most hostile environments for converts in South Asia, where apostates face social retaliation and violence. He has publicly stated that more persecution will come but that he and the believers are ready to face it.

name: Hossain Ali
summary: Hossain Ali was a Bengali Muslim who converted to Christianity in 1999 and became a Christian preacher in Kurigram District, northern Bangladesh. On 22 March 2016, at age 68, he was hacked to death by at least two assailants as he went about his day in Garialpara; the Islamic State claimed responsibility, calling him an apostate who had become 'a preacher for the polytheist Christianity,' though Bangladeshi police disputed the IS claim and blamed local militants. His murder was part of a wave of killings of converts from Islam and religious minorities in Bangladesh in 2015–2016. His son told reporters the family had faced local hostility over their faith.

name: Khaza Somiruddin
summary: Khaza Somiruddin was a 75-year-old Bengali pastor in Jhenaidah (Jenaidah) District, Bangladesh, and a Christian convert from Islam who was active in evangelism. He had received repeated threats from Islamic extremists for his preaching. On 6 January 2016 he was slain, one of several converts from Islam murdered in Bangladesh during the 2015–2016 wave of militant attacks on religious minorities and secular figures.

name: Imad-ud-din Lahiz
summary: Born in 1830 into a fourth-generation family of maulvis (Muslim scholars) from Panipat, Imad-ud-din Lahiz was a Sufi and staunch Sunni apologist who assisted the Muslim side at the famous Agra debate of 1854 against the German missionary Karl Gottlieb Pfander. Through years of restless seeking after Allah and close study of Pfander's 'Mizan al-Haqq,' he became convinced of the truth of Christianity and was baptized on 29 April 1866 at Amritsar. He became one of the most famous — and notorious — Christian apologists in 19th-century South Asia: he translated the Quran into Urdu, wrote some 53 books defending Christianity and refuting Islam (including the first scholarly refutation of Rahmatullah Kairanawi), endured constant death threats, became the first Indian to receive a Lambeth Doctor of Divinity (1884), and addressed the Chicago Parliament of Religions in 1893; he died in 1900 as the best-known Indian pastor and scholar of his day.

name: Safdar Ali
summary: Born in 1830 in Dholpur (Rajputana) to an orthodox Syed gentleman who served as qazi, Safdar Ali received a deep Islamic education from his father and other scholars, but his studies led him to philosophical and theological questioning of Islam. He spent three years in intense struggle, comparing the Christian and Muslim scriptures and controversial literature of both faiths, until he attained what he called full assurance of salvation; he was baptized on Christmas Day 1864. A close friend of Imad-ud-din Lahiz who also attended the 1854 Agra debate, he became a prominent indigenous Christian apologist and writer in Urdu (his 'Naya Zamana' drew published Muslim rebuttals), while also serving in government employment; he died in 1899.

name: Abdullah Atham
summary: Born in 1828 into a Muslim household in Ambala, Punjab, Abdullah Atham (born Aathim) converted from Islam to Christianity and was baptized in Karachi on 28 March 1853, adding 'Atham' ('the one that sins') to his name. He rose to become an Extra Assistant Commissioner in British Indian public service and one of the earliest living Indian converts from Islam, making Muslim-Christian controversy his life's study and writing books such as 'Andruna Bible' and 'Asliyat-e-Quran.' In 1893 the missionary Dr. Henry Martyn Clark chose him as the Christian champion to debate Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, founder of the Ahmadiyya movement, in the famous 15-day Jang-e-Muqaddas (Holy War) debate at Amritsar. He died on 27 July 1896 in Firozpur, still a controversial figure claimed by both sides' narratives.

name: Kyai Sadrach (born Radin Abas)
summary: Born Radin around 1835 in the Jepara region of Central Java into a devout Javanese Muslim family, Sadrach was educated in pesantren (Islamic boarding schools), including in Jombang, and added 'Abas' to his name as a mark of devout Islam. In Semarang he met the evangelist Hoezoo and Kyai Ibrahim Tunggul Wulung, a fellow Javanese convert from Islam, whose teaching drew him to Christianity; he traveled to Batavia and was baptized on 14 April 1867 in the Zion Church, taking the Christian name Sadrach. Returning to Central Java, he became an indigenous evangelist who founded Javanese Christian communities that wove Javanese culture together with Reformed faith — the 'Golongane Wong Kristen Kang Mardika' (free Javanese Christians) — building his own joglo-style church at Karangjasa in 1871. Though distrusted by Dutch missionaries for his independence and opposed by Muslim society, his network grew to some 20,000 people by his death in 1924, one of the largest indigenous Javanese churches of the 19th century.

name: Albertus Soegijapranata
summary: Born Soegija on 25 November 1896 in Surakarta to a Muslim courtier (abdi dalem) of the Sunanate of Surakarta, he was raised in a Muslim Javanese court family. Enrolled at the Catholic Xaverius College in Muntilan, he encountered the Christian faith there and was baptized in 1910 at about age fourteen, taking the name Albertus — a remarkable conversion for the son of a Muslim court official in colonial Java. He joined the Jesuits, was ordained a priest in 1931, and in 1940 became the first native Indonesian bishop (Apostolic Vicar, later Archbishop, of Semarang). Through the Japanese occupation and Indonesia's war of independence he shepherded the Church through persecution and chaos, famously declaring himself '100% Catholic, 100% Indonesian.' Named a National Hero of Indonesia, he died on 22 July 1963 and was buried with military honors.

name: Justinus Darmojuwono (born Djamin)
summary: Born Djamin on 2 November 1914 in Klewonan, Godean, Yogyakarta, into a poor Javanese Muslim farming family. Following his elder brother's conversion, he too converted to Catholicism in 1932, taking the baptismal name Justinus. Against his father's initial wishes, his persistence won him permission to enter the seminary in 1935; he was ordained a priest in 1947 by Soegijapranata and served parishes across Central Java. In 1963 he was appointed Archbishop of Semarang, and in 1967 Pope Paul VI created him Indonesia's first cardinal — the Muslim-born village boy becoming the highest-ranking Catholic in the nation's history, and an elector in the conclaves that chose John Paul I and John Paul II. He retired in 1981 and died in 1994.

name: Yusuf Roni (Pdt. Jusuf Roni)
summary: A former Islamic dawah missionary, kyai/ustaz, and chairman of an Islamic youth organization in Indonesia who became one of the country's best-known Muslim-background Christian preachers. According to his widely circulated public testimony, he first picked up a Bible to refute Christianity, but reading it — he points to three key verses — convinced him of Christ instead, and he converted. He was imprisoned for abandoning Islam, and after his release became a pastor (Pdt. Jusuf Roni), preaching and publishing his testimony across Indonesia for decades until his death; his sermons and 'Kesaksian Yusuf Roni' videos remain widely shared in Indonesian Christian media.

name: Ahmad Quraisy (pen name; birth name withheld)
summary: A commander of the Negara Islam Indonesia (NII) militant movement, radicalized after Indonesia's late-1990s economic crisis. He once carried a bag with a time bomb to a Protestant church in Jakarta intending to kill worshippers — but hearing the pastor preach 'love your enemies' stopped him; he abandoned the attack and was detained for a month by furious NII leaders. Soon after, through a series of visions (including a vision of hell and of Jesus healing his typhus), his secretly Christian wife's prayers, and reading a Bible borrowed from a Christian neighbor, he gave his life to Christ in 2001. His father disowned him, and the young family lived for two months in a bus station. He now leads an underground movement of some 7,000 former Muslims meeting in house churches across Indonesia and has published his testimony in self-published books under the name Ahmad Quraisy.

name: Muhammad Kace (also spelled Muhammad Kece)
tribe: Sundanese (inferred from West Java origin; ethnicity not explicitly documented)
summary: A former Muslim cleric from West Java who publicly proclaimed his conversion to Christianity on YouTube in 2014, going on to post some 400 video sermons critiquing Islam and preaching Christ while dressed in clerical attire. His outspoken apostasy drew nationwide outrage: arrested in Bali in August 2021 on blasphemy charges, he was beaten and smeared with excrement by fellow inmates on his first night in detention. In April 2022 the Ciamis District Court sentenced him to ten years' imprisonment (later reduced to six on appeal) as thousands of protesters surrounded the courthouse demanding harsher punishment. His case, documented by the U.S. State Department, Christian Post, Barnabas Aid, and Jubilee Campaign, became an international symbol of Indonesia's blasphemy laws and the cost of public apostasy.

name: Lina Joy (born Azlina Jailani)
summary: Born Azlina Jailani on 28 July 1964 to Malay Muslim parents of Javanese descent. She embraced the Christian faith at age 26 in 1990 and was baptized a Catholic in 1998; she later sought to marry a Christian man. When Malaysia's National Registration Department refused to remove 'Islam' from her identity card without an apostasy certificate from a Sharia court, she took her case through the civil courts, arguing her constitutional right to profess her religion. In a landmark 2–1 Federal Court ruling on 30 May 2007, her appeal was dismissed — the court held a Muslim could only leave Islam through Sharia procedures. Forced into hiding by threats and publicity, she remains Malaysia's most famous convert, her case defining the legal plight of Malay apostates.

name: Syarifah Nooraffyzza (seeks name Vanessa Elizabeth)
summary: An ethnic Malay woman raised as a Muslim who came to Christian faith and was baptized in 2009. Like Lina Joy, she petitioned Malaysia's courts to change her national identity card from Muslim to Christian and her name to Vanessa Elizabeth, filing a formal declaration that she no longer practices Islam. Her case was joined with three others before Malaysia's Federal Court in 2018, testing whether converts out of Islam can ever obtain legal recognition in a system where civil courts defer to Sharia courts and Sharia courts refuse to certify apostasy. Publicly named in court reporting by Morning Star News, she represents a new generation of Malay converts seeking legal existence as Christians.

name: Pastor Mocsin Hasim (also reported as 'Harsim')
summary: A former Muslim from Mindanao who became a pastor with the Christian and Missionary Alliance Church, evangelizing among Muslim tribes in Zamboanga del Norte despite receiving death threats for months. On 3 June 2006, hours after receiving a death threat by text message and shortly after leading a wedding service, he and his daughter Mercilyn were ambushed on an empty road and shot — he at least nineteen times, she five times; both died. Local police linked the attack to the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. His widow Evelyn and surviving children went into hiding amid continued threats. Reported by Open Doors via BosNewsLife.

name: Datu (alias; birth name withheld)
summary: A devout Muslim man in Mindanao known publicly only as 'Datu' (a traditional title, used to protect his identity) who violently opposed Christianity — he once hurled stones at a local pastor, his church building, and his home after learning his daughter was courting the pastor's son Efren. At the couple's church wedding, hearing Pastor Bagwis preach 'Jesus Christ crucified,' Datu and his family repented and accepted Christ; he and his oldest son were baptized a month later. Muslim relatives threatened and harassed them, and his son had to be relocated for safety. As Datu grew bolder in sharing the Gospel in the predominantly Muslim area, the persecution he had once inflicted came back on him — he was stabbed to death on Mindanao on 2 January 2016. Documented via Christian Aid Mission and reported by Gospel Herald and Today's Martyrs.

name: Nurta Mohamed Farah
summary: Nurta Mohamed Farah was a 17-year-old Somali girl from Bardher in the Gedo Region who converted to Christianity from Islam. When her Muslim parents discovered her faith in May 2010, they beat her severely, regularly shackled her to a tree at their home, confined her indoors, had a doctor prescribe her medication for supposed 'mental illness,' and had the Quran recited over her twice a week to cure her. She refused her family's offer of forgiveness in exchange for renouncing Christ and fled to live with relatives in the Galgadud Region. On November 25, 2010, she was shot dead in the chest and head in Abudwaq in an apparent 'honor killing' by two men strongly suspected to be relatives acting on her family's behest.

name: Ayaan Hirsi Ali
summary: Ayaan Hirsi Ali was born in Mogadishu in 1969 and raised as a Muslim in Somalia, Saudi Arabia, and Kenya, where she suffered female genital mutilation. In 1992 she fled an arranged marriage to the Netherlands, renounced Islam in 2002, and became one of the world's best-known atheist critics of Islam, later moving to the United States. In November 2023 she published the essay 'Why I am now a Christian' in UnHerd, declaring herself a Christian: she wrote that atheism failed to answer the question of life's meaning and purpose, that she found life without spiritual solace 'unendurable,' and that Christianity offered the answer. NOTE: her profession is public and well documented, but she frames it largely in philosophical and civilizational terms (defending Western civilization against Islamism, authoritarianism, and 'woke ideology'), and she came to Christianity via atheism rather than directly from Islam; include with this honest caveat.
sources: Ayaan Hirsi Ali, 'Why I am now a Christian,' UnHerd, Nov 11, 2023 (essay cited via Heritage Foundation bio)

name: Osman Jama
summary: Osman Jama was a Muslim Somali refugee who came to Christ in 2007 while living in Minnesota. When his family learned of his conversion, they disowned him and cut off all communication. Rather than hiding his faith, Jama became a Christian missionary, serving with the Presbyterian Church in America's Mission to North America Refugee and Immigrant Ministry, reaching Muslim immigrants and refugees in the United States. In June 2024 he spoke at the PCA's 51st General Assembly in Richmond, Virginia, in a seminar titled 'From Islam to Christian Ministries,' urging American churches to evangelize their Muslim neighbors more actively.

name: Bashir Musa Ahmed
summary: Bashir Musa Ahmed was an Ethiopian national of Somali origin from the predominantly Muslim Somali Region of eastern Ethiopia, a convert from Islam who became known as a bold preacher of Christianity and a scholar of Islam. He led efforts at Muslim-Christian dialogue in the region and distributed Somali-language Bibles to Muslims. On May 23, 2009, zonal police arrested him in Jijiga, the regional capital, after he was accused of providing Muslims with Somali-language Bibles; Christian sources said his own relatives and tribe instigated the arrest to stop him spreading Christianity. Contrary to Ethiopian law he was held nearly four months without formal charge, and authorities planned to transfer him to a more remote jail to prevent other Christians from visiting him.

name: Charles Yabaga Diarra
summary: Charles Yabaga Diarra grew up in a Muslim family in Lere, Mali, where he was taught that Christians do not pray, drink alcohol, and eat pork. After running away from his strict father, he took refuge with his uncle, a Christian pastor, and was stunned to hear the man pray before a meal in his own mother tongue; his uncle took him to a Vacation Bible School, and Diarra even tried to convert his uncle back to Islam. In November 1981, exhausted from seeking the truth, he prayed for God to show him the way and a Bible verse from VBS came to mind - he dates his conversion to that night. His father summoned a family council to make him recant, and he became the lone Christian among 400 high school classmates; after his father's death he raised all 14 of his siblings, most of whom are now Christians, and perhaps 100 members of his extended family have come to faith. Now a husband, father, educational administrator, and preacher, he is internally displaced by Mali's conflict and endures daily insults and discrimination as a Christian.

name: John (name withheld for security)
summary: Born to a Hausa Fulani family in Kaduna State, Nigeria, 'John' (a pseudonym used for his security) became a banker and a congregational prayer leader - an imam - at his mosque; he even converted a Christian woman to Islam and married her. His wife later reclaimed her Christian faith after an encounter with Jesus in a dream, and their community condemned her as an apostate while pressuring John to divorce her; confident he could reconvert her, he drove her to a church crusade in 1995. There he encountered a theological reality about Jesus as the Son of God present in both the Bible and the Quran, and he himself converted to Christianity. His family forced the couple into hiding across different Nigerian states, one of their sons was murdered, and the family eventually fled to the United States to seek asylum, where he told his story to The Christian Post in 2018.
sources: NOTE: subject's real name withheld by source for security; identity is publicly documented only under the pseudonym 'John.'

name: Eli Abdullah Tinau
summary: Eli Abdullah Tinau is a former Islamic Fulani Nigerian who converted to Christianity and is now a pastor and missionary of the Evangelical Church Winning All (ECWA) in Nkiendoro, about 60 miles from Jos in Plateau State's Bassa Local Government Area. He evangelizes Fulani Muslims - the very community whose militants have burned his home and terrorized Christians across Nigeria's Middle Belt - and has led at least two Fulani to Christ. Despite terror threats from militants of his own people, he declares, 'I will never go back to Islam' and 'I will continue to preach and bring additional souls to Christ.'

name: Abubakar Diallo Sulemana
summary: Abubakar Diallo Sulemana is a Fulani man from a Muslim background in Ghana who came to faith in Christ and was embraced, discipled, and trained for ministry by The Church of Pentecost's Home and Urban Missions (HUM), which reaches marginalized and unreached peoples including the Muslim-majority Fulani. In July 2022 he was commissioned into full-time ministry at the Pentecost Convention Centre in Gomoa Fetteh, becoming the first Fulani minister in the history of The Church of Pentecost - a milestone reported by the church's official news outlet and GhanaWeb. He and his wife, Mariam Diallo Sulemana, were posted to Nkwanta as HUM pastor for the Volta and Oti sectors, where his ministry focuses on evangelism, discipleship, and church planting among Fulani and other unreached communities.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: his personal conversion narrative is reported by secondary/social-media accounts; the official church source confirms his Fulani identity, commissioning, and ministry among Muslim-majority Fulani.

name: Halima Mohammed Ali
summary: Halima Mohammed Ali is a Sudanese Muslim-background mother of five, aged 1.5 to 14, living at the Gorom Refugee Settlement in South Sudan after fleeing Sudan's war. She put her faith in Christ in June 2024 and began attending discipleship classes and worship services at a church in the refugee camp. On the night of September 8, her Muslim husband stabbed her on the right side of her head after learning she had become a Christian, and his relatives pressured him to drive her away, saying, 'We cannot stay with a Christian woman.' She briefly left but returned to care for her children, refusing to renounce her faith despite ongoing threats: 'But I refuse.'
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: tribe listed as Sudanese Arab based on name and context; Morning Star News does not state her ethnicity explicitly.

name: Gueye Ndiougour
summary: Gueye Ndiougour was born on August 18, 1987, in Niakhar, Senegal, and grew up in a mixed-faith Wolof household with a Muslim father and a Catholic mother. A pastor friend of his father's told him about Jesus Christ, gave him a Bible, and shared Matthew 11:28 - 'Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest' - the verse through which Gueye decided to accept Jesus. He began ministry in 2009, completed leadership, discipleship, and theology training, and is now a church planter whose stated goal is to evangelize the Wolof people of Senegal and build churches among them; he is married to Daba Diouf and they have six children. NOTE: his background is mixed Muslim/Catholic rather than strictly Muslim, included here as a Wolof convert from a Muslim household reaching an overwhelmingly Muslim people group.

name: Barack Hussein Kedir
summary: Barack Hussein Kedir was born to Muslim community leaders in Arsi Negelle district in southern Ethiopia and had been a zealous Islamic youth coordinator who once harassed Christians before his long process of conversion to Christ - a commitment for which his own father shot him in the leg. He fled hostilities in Ethiopia to Kenya in 2003, but secretly returned home in June 2009 to help establish three new churches; when local Muslims discovered his work they hunted him with intent to kill, forcing him back to Kenya. In July 2010 Somali Muslim extremists in Nairobi slipped a threatening CD and letter under his door and rammed his car, and after a December death threat his wife fled the country with their two children - yet he told Compass Direct News, 'I have never given up or lost my hope in serving the Lord.'
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: tribe inferred from his Arsi Negelle origin in Oromo-majority southern Ethiopia; Compass Direct does not state his ethnicity explicitly.

name: Taha Abduraman Dinka
summary: As a child in Gawo Kebe, Ethiopia, Taha Abduraman Dinka faithfully attended the mosque and adhered to his community's Islamic beliefs, never imagining his life would take a different direction. In 2019 he heard the gospel and decided to follow Jesus, experiencing what he described as spiritual freedom and peace: 'When I accepted Christ, I felt peace in my life. I believed God had rescued me from darkness.' His decision brought rejection and threats from family and community members who accused him of betraying his family and religion and warned he would suffer or die. In August 2025 he was violently attacked and forcefully removed from his home for refusing to renounce Christianity, and he fled to Dembi Dollo town; he told International Christian Concern, 'I was beaten because I would not deny Jesus.'
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: tribe inferred from Gawo Kebe in Oromia, western Ethiopia; ICC does not state his ethnicity explicitly.

name: Rahma
summary: Rahma was a young Kenyan Muslim woman from the coast who was introduced to Christianity by her friend Amina and met a local pastor, who mentored her after she expressed readiness to put her faith in Christ and be baptized. In the early hours of October 29 she was caught by her aunt reading a Swahili Bible during her devotions; when confronted, she gathered her courage and told the whole household she had given her life to Christ and would continue in the Christian faith. Her family treated her as an apostate and infidel: they chased her out of the house, stripped her of her possessions including her clothes and shoes, and essentially disowned her for the shame her conversion brought in the Muslim community. She now lives with her friend Amina in Mombasa and is growing in a church mentorship of Bible reading, prayer, and fellowship.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: tribe listed as Swahili based on coastal Kenyan Muslim context; the ICC/Christian Post report does not state her ethnicity explicitly.

name: Isa El-Buba
summary: Isa El-Buba was born into a Muslim family in northern Nigeria and grew up as an Islamic occultist, serving 'the queen of heaven' from childhood and later training as a militant jihadist with a hatred of Christianity. In 1982 he experienced what he describes as the exceeding grace of the Lord Jesus Christ bringing him salvation - preceded by a series of revelations of the reality of hell - was baptized in the Holy Spirit, and was commissioned to preach the gospel. He is now president of El-Buba Outreach Ministries International, headquartered in Jos, Plateau State, with a special burden to reach the Muslim world through publications and media; he has survived attempts on his life and preaches openly about his past as a former jihadist turned evangelist.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: ethnicity listed as Hausa based on northern Nigerian Muslim-family background; public profiles emphasize his Islamic past rather than his ethnicity.

name: Afshin Ziafat
summary: Born in Houston to an Iranian Muslim family, Afshin Ziafat moved to Iran at age two and fled back to America with his family during the 1979 Islamic Revolution, growing up Muslim in Houston amid the hostility of the Iran hostage crisis. As an elementary-school child, a Christian tutor his family had hired to teach him English gave him a New Testament and told him to read it later in life. He rediscovered that Bible as a high-school senior, read the entire Gospel of Matthew in one sitting, and gave his life to Christ at a Jay Strack evangelistic campaign — a decision for which his family, led by his prominent Muslim father, disowned him. He is now the lead pastor of Providence Church in Frisco, Texas, and speaks widely on loving Muslims with the gospel that converted him.

name: Annahita Parsan
summary: Raised in a Muslim home in Iran, Annahita Parsan was married at sixteen, widowed soon after, and then trapped in an abusive second marriage from which divorce was impossible. Fleeing Iran in 1984 during the Iran-Iraq war, she endured a month in a Turkish prison before reaching Denmark, where a woman who came to her door gave her a small Bible; reading it in secret, and after a suicide attempt following a beating by her husband, she and her children knelt in a church and prayed, 'God, from this day on we are Christians.' Settling in Sweden, she became an ordained minister in the Church of Sweden and has since baptized hundreds of former Muslims — reportedly leading some 1,500 Muslims to Christ — despite a church bombing and ongoing murder threats. She told her story in the memoir 'Stranger No More: A Muslim Refugee's Harrowing Escape, Miraculous Rescue, and the Quiet Call of Jesus' (Thomas Nelson, 2017).

name: Mona Walter
summary: Mona Walter grew up in Mogadishu, Somalia, as a 'cultural' Sufi Sunni Muslim who had never read the Quran for herself. Fleeing the war, she arrived in Sweden as a refugee around age nineteen in the early 1990s, where local imams pressed her to cover herself and attend the mosque; reading the Quran for the first time there left her upset and disillusioned, and she became an atheist for a time. A family member later encouraged her to read the Bible, and Jesus' words in Matthew 5:44 — 'love your enemies' — stunned her by contrast with what she had been taught; she became a Christian, married an ethnic Swede, and broke out of the immigrant enclave in Gothenburg. She is now a well-known public activist for religious freedom in Sweden, speaking openly against Islam at great personal risk, including criticism and death threats.

name: Rifqa Bary
summary: The only daughter of devout Sri Lankan Muslim immigrants Mohamed and Aysha Bary, Fathima Rifqa Bary grew up in Columbus, Ohio, after the family moved to the U.S. in 2000. She converted to Christianity at age thirteen in 2005 and was secretly baptized in July 2009 in Big Walnut Creek by her mentor Brian Michael Williams, worshipping at Columbus Korean United Methodist Church and an Ohio State prayer house. In July 2009, at seventeen, she fled Ohio on a Greyhound bus to Orlando, Florida, saying she feared an honor killing after her father discovered her faith; she was sheltered by an evangelical pastor couple, taken into Florida state custody, and became the center of a nationally covered custody battle before being returned to Ohio foster care. The case made her one of the most publicly documented young Muslim-background converts in America.

name: Joseph Fadelle
summary: Born Mohammed al-Sayyid al-Moussawi in 1964 into a wealthy, aristocratic Shiite family in Iraq, Joseph Fadelle encountered Christianity during his 1987 military service when he was roomed with a Christian, Massoud, whom he set out to convert — and found himself intrigued instead. A dream, a rigorous comparative reading of the Quran and the Bible, and a phase of atheism led to his secret conversion, which his wife soon shared; when his brothers discovered a Bible, the family sought his death and Saddam Hussein's regime tortured him for months. Shot by his own relatives and left for dead, he survived, fled through Jordan — narrowly escaping an assassination attempt organized by his brothers and uncle — and reached France in 2001, where he became a French citizen. His autobiography 'The Price to Pay: A Muslim Risks All to Follow Christ' (French 2010; Ignatius Press, 2012) is a European bestseller, and he travels under police escort because of continuing death threats.

name: Joshua Milton Blahyi ("General Butt Naked")
summary: Born in 1971 in Monrovia into a Krahn family, Joshua Milton Blahyi claims he was taken at age seven to Krahn elders in Sinoe County and inducted as a high priest of a secret society, performing monthly child sacrifices and black magic in service of President Samuel Doe's regime. During the First Liberian Civil War (c. 1993-1996) he became the feared warlord "General Butt Naked," leading the child-soldier "Naked Base Commandos" of ULIMO-J into battle naked, convinced the ritual made him bulletproof. In July 1996 he says a radiant figure appeared to him in battle saying "repent and live or refuse and die"; he abandoned his fighters on the spot and became a street preacher. He later testified before Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2008), confessing to some 20,000 deaths, and now serves as an evangelical preacher of reconciliation; his story is told in the documentary "The Redemption of General Butt Naked" (2011). Note: his relatives dispute his account of the childhood priesthood, though the conversion itself is extensively documented.

name: Josiah Olufemi Akindayomi
summary: Born in 1909 in Ondo, southwestern Nigeria, Olufemi Akindayomi was raised by parents who worshipped Ogun, the Yoruba god of iron and warfare, and was apprenticed as a blacksmith rather than sent to school. Drawn by a hunger to know the Supreme Being beyond the gods of his people, he was baptized into the Anglican Church by the Church Missionary Society in 1927, taking the name Josiah. Still spiritually unfulfilled, he joined the Cherubim and Seraphim movement in 1931, where his zeal in prayer, fasting and healing earned him recognition as a prophet. After business failures brought him to repentance and a decisive call to ministry, he broke with C&S in 1952 and founded the fellowship that became the Redeemed Christian Church of God, which he led until his death in 1980 and which has since grown into one of the world's largest Pentecostal denominations.

name: Khama III
summary: Khama III (c. 1837-1923), eldest son of the traditionalist chief Sekgoma I of the Bamangwato, converted to Christianity around 1860 together with his brother, a step fiercely opposed by their father. Succeeding as kgosi in 1875, he made his new faith the law of the land: he banned liquor from tribal territory, abolished polygamy, promoted schools and gave preference to educated Christians, working closely with London Missionary Society missionaries. In 1895 he traveled to Britain with chiefs Bathoen I and Sebele I - a missionary-organized tour at which his Christianity was the centerpiece - and won public and parliamentary support against Cecil Rhodes's scheme to absorb Bechuanaland, securing the protectorate that became Botswana. Remembered as "Khama the Good," he ruled as a Christian king until his death in 1923.

name: Ham Mukasa
summary: Born around 1870 in Buddu, Buganda, the son of a minor clan chief, Ham Mukasa was placed as a page in Kabaka Mutesa I's palace at age nine. There he first received instruction from the Muslim teachers influential at court, but was then drawn to the Protestant missionaries and baptized with the name Ham. As a young Protestant he survived the 1886 anti-Christian massacres of Mwanga II with a lasting leg injury, and fought in Buganda's religious wars of 1888-1892 on the Protestant side. He rose to become secretary to Katikiro Apolo Kagwa and ssaza (county) chief of Kyaggwe (1905-1935), a licensed lay reader who wrote a Luganda commentary on Matthew's Gospel. His memoir "Uganda's Katikiro in England" (1904), written after accompanying Kagwa to Edward VII's coronation in 1902, is one of the earliest published books by an African author describing Europe from an African Christian point of view.

name: Gudina Tumsa
summary: Born in 1929 at Boji in Wollega, Ethiopia, Gudina Tumsa grew up in a family that observed the traditional religion of the Oromo. When he began attending the local school in 1938 he was converted to Christianity, and his first response to the old faith was to cut down the ritual Hommi tree his parents held sacred - an act widely condemned but which he faced down fearlessly - before preaching the gospel to his family and village. Educated under the Swedish Evangelical Mission at Nejo (1955-1958) and at Luther Seminary in St. Paul, Minnesota (1963-1966), he became General Secretary of the Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus (1966-1979), giving the young church its decisive push toward independent African theological thought. Abducted and murdered on July 28, 1979 under the Marxist Derg regime, he is remembered as "Ethiopia's Bonhoeffer."

name: Kapi'olani (High Chiefess)
summary: High Chiefess Kapi'olani (c. 1781-1841) was raised in the kapu system of traditional Hawaiian religion, in which the volcano goddess Pele was deeply feared. After converting to Christianity through the American missionaries, she resolved to demonstrate the powerlessness of the old gods: in December 1824 she walked nearly a hundred miles to Kilauea, descended alone into the crater of Halema'uma'u, and - instead of the traditional prayers and offerings to Pele - prayed aloud to Jehovah, ate the 'ohelo berries sacred to Pele, and threw stones into the lava. She emerged unharmed. Witnesses declared Pele powerless, and missionaries reported that her act of moral courage broke the fear of idolatry across the islands and drew multitudes to hear the gospel. Alfred, Lord Tennyson later commemorated the episode in verse (1892).

name: Keōpūolani
summary: Keōpūolani (1778-1823) was the highest-ranking ali'i of her generation - born with the kapu moe, sacred wife of Kamehameha I and mother of Kamehameha II and III - a living embodiment of the old Hawaiian religious order. After Kamehameha I's death she helped end the 'ai kapu system (1819), welcomed the first American missionaries at Kailua in 1820, and in 1823 invited missionaries William Richards and Charles Stewart to Lahaina, Maui, where she studied Scripture under their guidance. In obedience to Christian teaching she confirmed her marriage to Hoapili and renounced her other husband, publicly ending royal polygamy. Falling mortally ill, she asked for baptism; the missionary William Ellis baptized her "Harriet" on September 16, 1823, an hour before she died - remembered as the first Hawaiian convert, whose dying charge was that her children be raised Christian.

name: Kalanimoku (William Pitt Kalanimoku)
summary: Kalanimoku, called "the iron cable of Hawai'i," was premier and the most powerful chief under Kamehameha I, raised entirely within the kapu religious system. In August 1819, months after Kamehameha's death and before any resident missionaries had arrived, he boarded the French corvette Uranie at Kawaihae Bay and asked its chaplain, Abbé de Quélen, to baptize him, saying he had long wished to become a Christian and that his baptized mother had urged it on her deathbed. The baptism - witnessed by King Kamehameha II and the court - was the first recorded Christian baptism in the Hawaiian Islands. That December Kalanimoku led the royal forces at the Battle of Kuamo'o, defeating Kekuaokalani's defenders of the old gods and priesthood. He later served as regent of the kingdom and died a Christian in 1827.

name: Maputeoa (Gregorio I)
summary: Te Maputeoa (c. 1814-1857) became 'akariki (paramount chief and king) of Mangareva and the Gambier Islands around 1830, ruling a society rooted in the worship of gods enshrined in marae temples, with cannibalism still practiced. When French Picpus missionaries Honoré Laval and François Caret landed in 1834, they were first rebuffed, but won over his uncle Matua, the high priest of the local temple. Maputeoa then consented to the dismantling of the great Te Keika marae at Rikitea - the largest in the islands - and on August 25, 1836 was baptized a Roman Catholic with 160 of his people, taking the name Gregorio after Pope Gregory XVI. On the marae's site rose St. Michael's Cathedral, the largest church in the South Pacific; the kingdom's idols were destroyed and the islands became a Catholic community within a few years. He reigned as the Christian king Gregorio I until his death in 1857.

name: Wang Zhiming
summary: Born in 1907 in Wuding County, Yunnan, Wang Zhiming grew up among the Miao (Hmong) people, whose traditional religion centered on ghost worship and spirit appeasement. From 1913 he attended a China Inland Mission school for Miao children, where he came to faith, and went on to teach, preach (from 1940), lead the Shapushan General Assembly, and be ordained a pastor in 1951, also compiling a Miao hymnal. When Communist authorities demanded he subordinate Christ to Mao and the state church, he refused; arrested in 1954 and again in 1969, he was tortured in Wuding County Detention Center, answering "Do you trust Mao Zedong or Jesus?" with "I believe in Jesus." On December 29, 1973 he was executed by firing squad before 10,000 people at a denunciation rally. The government later admitted wrongdoing and compensated his family; in 1998 his statue joined ten 20th-century martyrs above the Great West Door of Westminster Abbey, and his church grew from 2,795 members at his arrest to over 12,000 within seven years.

name: Chief Seattle (Sealth)
summary: Sealth (c. 1786-1866), chief of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples of Puget Sound, was raised in the traditional Coast Salish religion - completing a vision quest, gaining Thunder power, and leading successful raids as a warrior. After the death of a son in battle he sought out Catholic missionaries and was baptized, taking the prophet Noah as his baptismal name (recorded as "Noe Siattle" in the Oblate register); his children were baptized as well. His conversion ended his fighting days: he became renowned as a peacemaker and friend to incoming settlers, guiding them along the Duwamish River and sharing food and labor, and was the first to sign the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott. He observed morning and evening prayers for the rest of his life, and the city of Seattle bears his name.

name: Red Cloud
summary: Red Cloud (c. 1822-1909) was the Oglala Lakota chief who led Red Cloud's War (1866-1868) - the only Indian war in which the United States sued for peace - and signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie, raised wholly within the Lakota spiritual tradition of Wakan Tanka. As his people were confined to the Pine Ridge Reservation, he concluded the Oglala must seek peace. In 1884 he, his family, and five other Lakota leaders were baptized as Roman Catholics by Father Joseph Bushman. He remained a steadfast advocate for his people, opposing the Dawes Act of 1887 and later land cessions, and died at Pine Ridge in 1909 at about 87, the last of the great Lakota leaders of the Indian Wars, buried in the cemetery that bears his name.

name: Charles Eastman (Ohiyesa)
summary: Born Ohiyesa in Minnesota in 1858, Charles Eastman fled with his family to Canada during the 1862 U.S.-Dakota War and was raised there in the traditional Dakota way by his grandmother and uncle until age fifteen. His father, Many Lightnings - long presumed dead - had converted to Christianity while imprisoned after the war, taken the name Jacob Eastman, and returned to fetch his son in 1873, plunging the boy from a "wild boyhood" into mission schooling at Flandreau. Soon baptized as Charles Alexander Eastman, he excelled academically: Dartmouth College (1887) and a Boston University medical degree (1890), among the first Native Americans to earn an M.D. He served as agency physician at Pine Ridge, treating the wounded of the 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre, and became a nationally known author of eleven books - including "Indian Boyhood" and "The Soul of the Indian" - and co-founder of the Society of American Indians, bridging Dakota heritage and Christian faith until his death in 1939.

name: Whittaker Chambers
summary: Whittaker Chambers (1901–1961) was an American writer who became a committed Communist in the 1920s and served from 1932 to 1938 as a courier and agent for Soviet military intelligence in the United States. Disillusioned by the purges and the cruelty of the system he served, he broke with the Party in 1938 and, through reading and the influence of Christian friends, came to see communism as a rival faith built on a lie about man. His conversion to Christianity was sealed by baptism and confirmation in the Episcopal Church and, in 1943, by joining the Pipe Creek Friends Meeting (Quakers) in Maryland with his family. He recounted the journey in his 1952 memoir Witness, became the key witness against Soviet spy Alger Hiss, and spent his later years as a senior editor at Time magazine and a voice of Christian anti-communism.

name: Bella Dodd
summary: Bella Dodd (1904–1969), born Maria Asunta Isabella Visono in Italy and raised in New York, was a brilliant lawyer who rose to the National Committee of the Communist Party USA, organizing teachers and labor unions through the 1930s and 1940s. Expelled from the Party in 1949, she entered into conversations with Monsignor Fulton J. Sheen, who gave her weekly instruction and led her to confront the spiritual void of materialist ideology. She was received into the Roman Catholic Church at St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York in April 1952. She told her story in her 1954 autobiography School of Darkness and spent her remaining years as an outspoken Catholic anti-communist lecturer, testifying before Congress about communist subversion.

name: Malcolm Muggeridge
summary: Malcolm Muggeridge (1903–1990) was a celebrated English journalist and satirist who spent most of his life as an agnostic with socialist sympathies, traveling to the Soviet Union in the early 1930s hoping to find a workers' utopia. His reporting on the Ukrainian famine and Soviet reality cured him of communism, and decades of observing power, war, and human nature gradually drew him toward Christian faith, deepened by his encounter with Mother Teresa in Calcutta. He publicly embraced Christianity with Jesus Rediscovered (1969) and became a prominent Christian apologist, author, and BBC broadcaster. In 1982 he and his wife were received into the Catholic Church, and he spent his final years defending Christian moral teaching in Britain's public square.

name: Peter Hitchens
summary: Peter Hitchens (b. 1951) is an English journalist who burned his Bible at school at age fifteen, embraced atheism, and joined the Trotskyist International Socialists, confident that revolutionary politics would perfect the world. Posted as a foreign correspondent to Moscow in 1990, he watched the Soviet Union — history's great atheist utopia — collapse into moral and social ruin, an experience that shattered his faith in secular progress. Through philosophy, literature, and the witness of Christian faith surviving under communism, he returned to the Anglican Christianity of his childhood. He chronicled the journey in The Rage Against God (2010), written partly as a reply to his brother Christopher Hitchens's God Is Not Great, and remains a prominent British Christian conservative voice.

name: Francis Collins
summary: Francis S. Collins (b. 1950) was an atheist graduate student in physical chemistry who dismissed faith as an irrational relic — until, as a young medical student, a dying patient's simple question about his own beliefs unsettled him. Determined to refute Christianity intellectually, he read C. S. Lewis's Mere Christianity and found the moral argument for God unanswerable; on a hike in the Cascade Mountains he knelt in the dewy grass and gave his life to Christ. He went on to lead the Human Genome Project and to direct the U.S. National Institutes of Health from 2009 to 2021. In The Language of God (2006) he publicly described his conversion, and he founded the BioLogos Foundation to show the harmony of science and Christian faith.

name: Rosaria Butterfield
summary: Rosaria Champagne Butterfield was a tenured professor of English and women's studies at Syracuse University — an outspoken lesbian feminist activist and atheist who set out to write a book critiquing the religious right. A local Presbyterian pastor, Ken Smith, answered her critique with two years of patient hospitality, friendship, and Bible study alongside his wife, which forced her to read Scripture on its own terms. In 1999 she converted to Christianity in what she calls a 'train wreck' conversion, eventually leaving her academic career and her former way of life. She married Reformed Presbyterian pastor Kent Butterfield and told her story in The Secret Thoughts of an Unlikely Convert (2012), becoming a widely read author and speaker on repentance, hospitality, and the cost of discipleship.

name: Ran Yunfei
summary: Ran Yunfei (b. 1965) is a prominent writer and democracy activist from Sichuan, China, famous for his satirical blogs under Communist rule; a signer of Charter 08, he was detained in 2011 during the 'Jasmine' crackdown. Raised in China's officially atheist system, he became a Christian in 2015 and was baptized by Pastor Wang Yi of Chengdu's Early Rain Covenant Church. Since his conversion he has openly shared the gospel alongside his literary and activist work. In 2020 police held him at a station for hours to stop him delivering an online lecture series on Christianity and Chinese culture. He told supporters afterward that 'being in chains is sharing the gospel.'

name: Wang Yi
summary: Wang Yi (b. 1973) was a celebrated Chinese constitutional scholar, human rights lawyer, and public intellectual — named one of China's 50 most influential intellectuals in 2004 — who lived as a secular atheist. After his conversion and baptism in 2005 he left law for ministry and planted the Early Rain Covenant Church in Chengdu, which grew into one of China's most prominent unregistered house churches. His 2018 'Declaration of Faithful Disobedience' articulated a theology of nonviolent resistance to the Communist Party's religious controls. In December 2018 he was arrested, and in 2019 he was sentenced to nine years in prison for 'inciting subversion,' where he remains a globally recognized prisoner of conscience.

name: Chai Ling
summary: Chai Ling (b. 1966) was a commander of the student democracy movement in Tiananmen Square in 1989, raised in a People's Liberation Army family under China's official atheism; after the massacre she escaped to the United States via Operation Yellowbird. For twenty years she lived with the unanswered question of where God was during the killing, until she gave her life to Christ — a pastor at Boston's Park Street Church baptized her on Easter Sunday 2010. Her new faith redirected her activism: she founded All Girls Allowed to oppose China's one-child policy and forced abortion. She told her story in her autobiography A Heart for Freedom (2011) and has testified repeatedly before the U.S. Congress.

name: Yu Jie
summary: Yu Jie (b. 1973) is a Chinese essayist from Chengdu whose 1998 book Fire and Ice made him, at twenty-five, one of China's most famous dissident writers; an early signer of Charter 08, he was raised without faith under Communist rule. In 2003, after weighing Scripture and the claims of Christ — influenced by Calvin, Bonhoeffer, and Chinese house-church Christians — he was baptized and joined a Beijing house church. His faith gave theological grounding to his opposition to the regime, and he became an outspoken defender of religious freedom, which brought repeated detention and months of house arrest. In 2012 he fled to the United States with his family, where he continues to write as a Christian intellectual.

name: Bob Fu
summary: Fu Xiqiu, known as Bob Fu (b. 1968), was a student leader in the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests who went on to teach English at the Central Party School of the Chinese Communist Party in Beijing. An American teacher gave him a biography of a Chinese Christian convert; reading it, he became a Christian and began leading a house church at night while teaching in the communist school by day. He and his wife were imprisoned for their 'illegal' church activity before escaping to the United States as religious refugees in 1996–97. In 2002 he founded ChinaAid, which defends persecuted Christians and dissidents in China, and he recounted his conversion in God's Double Agent (2013).

name: Kim Sung-min
summary: Kim Seong-min is a North Korean defector who served as a military monitor of foreign broadcasts before fleeing across the Tumen River in 1996; recaptured, he was sentenced to death but escaped by jumping from a moving train in April 1997. While hiding in China he worked in a factory in Yanji, where he converted to Christianity, before reaching South Korea in 1999. In 2004 he co-founded Free North Korea Radio, the first defector-run station broadcasting news — and daily gospel programs, Bible readings, and Christian music — into the North. He has met with U.S. presidents and remains a leading advocate for North Korean human rights and for the underground church.

name: Kang Chol-hwan
summary: Kang Chol-hwan (b. 1968) spent ten years of his childhood in North Korea's Yodok political prison camp after his family was purged, enduring forced labor and starvation under the regime's enforced atheism; even there, he secretly listened to Christian radio broadcasts from the South, whose message of love he recalled as 'sweet as honey.' After his family's release he escaped to South Korea via China in 1992, where he found God and embraced the Christian faith. His memoir The Aquariums of Pyongyang (2001) was the first published survivor's account of the camps. He became a journalist and human rights advocate, co-founding the North Korea Strategy Center, and has described his faith as the ground of his activism.

name: Aleksandr Ogorodnikov
summary: Aleksandr Ogorodnikov (b. 1950) grew up as a Soviet Communist youth and studied philosophy and cinematography, but as a student his encounter with the film The Gospel According to St. Matthew and with underground believers drew him to Orthodox Christianity. In 1974 he founded the Christian Seminar, an underground network that gathered thousands of young Orthodox, Catholic, and Protestant converts across more than ten Soviet cities for Scripture study and fellowship. Arrested in 1978, he spent nine years in the Gulag, refusing the KGB's offer of exile because he wanted to change Russia from within. Released under Gorbachev, he founded the Christian-Democratic Union of Russia and charitable works for the poor; his biography Dissident for Life tells his story.

name: Tatiana Goricheva
summary: Tatiana Goricheva (1947–2025) was a Leningrad philosophy professor raised in thoroughgoing Soviet atheism who led her Communist youth group and moved through Marx, Nietzsche, Sartre, Heidegger, and yoga in search of truth. In 1974, at age twenty-six, she converted to the Russian Orthodox Church and began a religious-philosophical seminar that became the dissident circle '37,' publishing samizdat journals on faith and feminism. The KGB surveilled and interrogated the group, and in 1980 she was forced to choose between prison and exile; she emigrated to Paris. There she founded the journal Conversations and wrote Talking About God Is Dangerous, becoming one of the most influential Russian Christian thinkers of the dissident era.

name: David Yonggi Cho
summary: David Yonggi Cho (1936–2021) was raised in a devout Buddhist family in Korea, where his father taught him Buddhist chants as a boy. At 17, dying of tuberculosis in the aftermath of the Korean War, he prayed to Buddha without answer and then cried out to the Christian God he had heard about from a witnessing Christian girl. He received Christ, an experience he later described as being born again with a call to preach, and he recovered from his illness. He attended Bible college and went on to found Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul, which grew into one of the largest congregations in the world. His testimony of healing and conversion from Buddhism became central to his preaching ministry for the rest of his life.

name: Moung Nau
summary: Moung Nau was a Burman living in the Theravada Buddhist kingdom of Burma when the American missionary Adoniram Judson began preaching in Rangoon. He attended Judson's zayat discussions and heard the gospel in Burmese, weighing Christ's claims against the Buddhism he had always known. On June 27, 1819, he was baptized — the first Burman convert of the mission — declaring that while Buddhism offered no deliverance from the punishment of sin, Christ had died to deliver his disciples. He became Judson's assistant and evangelist, helped form the first Burmese Christian communion, and endured danger and social scorn for his faith. His baptism marked the beginning of an indigenous Burmese church.

name: Nantachai Mejudhon
summary: Nantachai Mejudhon grew up in a devout Theravada Buddhist home in Thailand and was ordained as a Buddhist monk for three months at age 18. His fiancée Ubolwan became a Christian while studying in New Zealand, and Nantachai wrote her hundreds of letters trying to argue her back into Buddhism. To sharpen his arguments he bought a Bible and read it intensively — and instead found himself falling in love with Jesus, committing his life to Christ after being pierced by 1 Corinthians 13. He and Ubolwan married and in 1972 began ministry among Thai university students, pioneering a respectful, culturally sensitive approach to witness in a Buddhist society. He later earned a doctorate and became a leading voice on meekness and mission in Thailand.

name: Ubolwan Mejudhon
summary: Ubolwan Mejudhon was raised Buddhist in Thailand and went on to study and teach Buddhist philosophy. While studying English in New Zealand in 1970, she encountered Christians and became a follower of Jesus — a decision that shocked her fiancé Nantachai back home. The two exchanged some 700 letters debating Buddhist and Christian theology as he tried to win her back to Buddhism. Instead, her witness — combined with his own intensive Bible reading — led Nantachai to Christ as well, and they married. Together they launched Thai student ministry in 1972, and Ubolwan later completed doctoral research on meekness as the heart of Christian witness in Buddhist Thailand.

name: Turk Pongsaowapak
summary: Turk Pongsaowapak was born in Chainat Province into a half-Chinese Buddhist family and spent much of his childhood in a Christian mission hospital, where two missionary doctors' kindness and quiet witness planted seeds he did not understand. As a young man he rejected all religion and proudly called himself an atheist, but in his first year at university he was haunted by the questions of why he was born and what life's purpose was. A Christian friend introduced him to Glory Church in Bangkok, where worship and Bible study convinced him that God is love, and he welcomed Jesus Christ into his life. Today he and his wife serve in their local church's missions department, and he leads student ministry. His story shows gospel seeds bearing fruit across generations in Buddhist Thailand.

name: Susan Khoo
summary: Susan Khoo grew up in Malaysia in a Buddhist Chinese family that practiced ancestor worship and spirit-medium rituals; as a child she was dedicated as a child of a god whose blessings had to be bought with offerings and contracts. When her beloved mother faced a fourth serious surgery, a Christian school friend named Phyllis prayed for her over the phone, and Susan slept in peace for the first time. Drawn to the love she saw at Phyllis's church and moved by the film Jesus of Nazareth, she compared Christ — who died for sinners — with gods who only took, and on September 14, 1981, she prayed to receive Jesus. Her parents disowned her, and her mother said she wished Susan had never been born, yet Susan stayed, witnessed to her brothers (who believed), and clung to Acts 16:31. While she studied in America, both parents became Christians, and she returned to a Malaysian home with no idols — a family that could kneel and pray together.

name: Ngoc Ha
summary: Ngoc Ha was born in 1954 in Bac-lieu, Vietnam, to a Buddhist family that participated in ancestor worship. After serving in the South Vietnamese military police, he endured a reeducation camp when Saigon fell in 1975, then fled Vietnam by boat in 1979 and resettled in Houston, Texas. There his Christian brother witnessed to him, but it was through English-as-a-Second-Language classes at Sagemont Baptist Church — and the friendship of a Christian man — that he professed faith in Christ and was baptized. Soon after, he sensed God's call to ministry, trained at East Texas Baptist University and Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, and was ordained in 1986. He went on to pastor Vietnamese congregations in Texas and Tennessee, preaching the gospel simply to fellow refugees, most of them — like him — converts from Buddhist backgrounds.

name: Inazo Nitobe
summary: Inazo Nitobe (1862–1933) was born into a samurai family in Morioka, Japan, and raised in the Buddhist milieu of late-Tokugawa and early-Meiji Japan. As a student at Sapporo Agricultural College, he joined the Sapporo Band of students who signed a covenant of belief in Jesus in 1877 under the influence of their Christian teachers. He was baptized and later, while studying in Baltimore in 1886, became the first Japanese member of the Society of Friends (Quakers). He went on to become an educator, the author of Bushido: The Soul of Japan, and an international diplomat and advocate of peace. His life bridged samurai Japan and the modern world as a Christian statesman.

name: Yoseb Gergan
summary: Yoseb Gergan (born Sonam Tsetan, c. 1878–1946) was a Ladakhi of the Tibetan Buddhist world of the western Himalayas who became a Christian in connection with the Moravian mission. Working with Moravian missionaries including August Hermann Francke, he devoted his life to giving the Scriptures to Tibetan-speaking peoples, preparing the landmark third revision of the Tibetan Bible. The complete Tibetan Bible — the Old Testament translated with Francke and colleagues — was published in 1948, the fruit of his decades of labor. Remembered as the father of the Tibetan Bible, his work put God's Word into the literary language of millions across Tibet, Ladakh, and the Himalayas.

name: Sawan
summary: Sawan was born into a Buddhist family in Thailand and spent four years studying for the Buddhist priesthood, yet remained spiritually empty. He became a noted painter and sculptor of Buddhist religious art — his depictions of the Buddha's life hang in temples even in the United States — and served his village as a fortune-teller and leader of ritual ceremonies. At 53, a Christian villager shared his testimony and gave Sawan a Bible; reading Scripture daily, he found the answers he had craved and became a Christian, immediately destroying his idols. Every Sunday evening more than 30 people now gather in his home for Bible study and worship of the living God. His story, reported by the Bible League, shows the gospel reaching deep into Thailand's folk-Buddhist heartland.

name: Jonnathan Zin Truong
summary: Jonnathan Zin Truong, a Vietnamese-American, describes himself as a former devout Buddhist who was once on the path toward becoming a Tibetan Buddhist lama. In a published video testimony, he recounts how an encounter with the gospel turned him from that trajectory to faith in Jesus Christ. He is now a Christian pastor — lead pastor of GodManifest in Houston, Texas — as well as an author and speaker. His public testimony presents his conversion as a decisive break with Tibetan Buddhism for Christian ministry.

name: True Nguyen
summary: True Nguyen, a Vietnamese-American ministry leader, shares that he became a Christian as a teenager and was disowned by his Buddhist family, experiencing homelessness at 18. In a published podcast interview, he describes obedience to Christ costing him family and security, and decades later, God's restoration of his family, career, and life. He now serves as chairman of the board of Christ's Body Ministries. His story is told as one of perseverance through rejection for the sake of the gospel.
