name: Krishna Pal
summary: A carpenter near Serampore, Krishna Pal had drifted from formal Hinduism into a theistic, egalitarian sect when he dislocated his shoulder and was treated by missionary doctor John Thomas, who spoke to him about the healing of his soul and gave him a Bengali tract. After reading Scripture with William Ward and Felix Carey, he confessed, 'I am a great sinner, but I have confessed my sin and I am free!' He broke caste by eating with Europeans, was mobbed and called 'traitor' by fellow Indians, and was baptized by William Carey in the Hoogli River on 28 December 1800 after seven childless years of missionary labor. His wife, sister, and four daughters soon followed him into the faith, forming the first indigenous Christian community in the region. He became the first native missionary to Calcutta, preaching at a dozen locations weekly, and the first writer of Christian hymns in Bengali, before his death in 1822.

name: Krishna Mohan Banerjee
summary: Born in 1813 into an orthodox Kulin Brahmin family of Calcutta and educated at Hindu College, Krishna Mohan Banerjee joined the radical Young Bengal movement and attended the lectures of Scottish missionary Alexander Duff. Excommunicated by his family in 1831 after defending friends who ate beef, he converted to Christianity in October 1832 and faced lasting familial ostracism. He trained at Bishop's College and became the first Indian ordained as an Anglican priest in Bengal (1839), preaching in Bengali at Christ Church, Calcutta. He emerged as 19th-century Bengal's leading Christian apologist, arguing in works like The Arian Witness (1875) that Christ is the fulfillment of the Vedic sacrificial system, and he influenced fellow converts including Michael Madhusudan Dutt. He also campaigned against sati, caste discrimination, and kulin polygamy, and served as the first president of the Bengal Christian Association.

name: Michael Madhusudan Dutt
summary: Born in 1824 in Sagardari, Bengal, to a Hindu lawyer's family and educated at Hindu College, Madhusudan Dutt grew averse to Indian custom and yearned for European culture, partly to escape an arranged marriage. On 9 February 1843 he embraced Christianity at the Old Mission Church in Calcutta despite the objections of his parents and relatives, writing of being 'long sunk in superstition's night' until God's grace shone. His conversion forced him out of Hindu College and his furious father cut him off financially, leaving him impoverished; he moved to Bishop's College and then to Madras, where he married Rebecca McTavish and took the name Michael. Though his early English poetry failed, he turned to Bengali and became the first great poet of modern Bengali literature, pioneering the sonnet and blank verse with his epic Meghnad Badh Kavya (1861).

name: Narayan Sheshadri
summary: A Deshastha Brahmin youth teaching at the Scottish Mission's English school in Bombay and caring for his twelve-year-old brother Sripat, Narayan Sheshadri came under the influence of missionaries John Wilson and Robert Nesbit. He embraced Christianity and was baptized in 1843, a conversion that caused a sensation and drew hostile Hindu mobs, requiring government protection of the missionaries' converts. Ordained as a Presbyterian minister, he established his base at Jalna and founded an extensive mission to the outcaste Mangs, building the 'Bethel' Christian village community on hundreds of acres granted for the work. His eloquence in English and Marathi won him support on fundraising visits to Scotland and America, and the mission grew into a cluster of churches, schools, and catechists across the region.

name: Baba Padmanji
summary: Born Baba Padmanji Mule in 1831 in Belgaum to a Konkani-Marathi Hindu family, he began attending a local mission high school at age twelve, and his journey toward Christianity began through missionary education. Mentored by Murray Mitchell, John Wilson, and Narayan Sheshadri, he converted to Christianity in his early twenties (1854) and was ordained a pastor of the Free Church in 1867, serving in Pune. He told his own story in the Marathi autobiography Arunodaya and in English as Once Hindu, Now Christian (1900), describing his former Hindu life and the causes of his conversion. He became the father of Christian literature in Marathi, publishing over a hundred books, including Yamuna Paryatan (1857), the first independent social novel in Marathi, which championed widows and women's dignity and drew fierce criticism from Hindu readers.

name: Henry Alfred Krishnapillai
summary: Born in 1827 into a Vaishnavite, non-Brahmin high-caste Hindu family, Krishnapillai worked as a teacher at the Church Mission Society College in Tirunelveli. In his early manhood he was gripped by the Gospel through his contact with the mission and embraced the Christian faith, breaking with his family's Vaishnavite tradition. He became one of the triumvirate of Tamil Christian poets alongside Vedanayagam Sastriar and N. Samuel, composing deeply indigenous Tamil verse. His masterpiece, Ratchanya Yathrigam, a Tamil rendering of Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, carried the Christian story into the poetic idiom of Tamil bhakti. He died in 1900, and new editions of his works continued to appear, recovering the voice of what scholars call 'the bard of an indigenous faith in the Gospel.'

name: Kali Charan Banerjee
summary: Born in 1847 at Jabalpur into a Brahmin family and educated at Calcutta University, Kali Charan Banerjee became a Christian in 1869 through the Free Church of Scotland and built a career as a leading pleader of the Calcutta High Court. Convinced that Indian Christians should not be denationalized by Western missions, he founded the Calcutta Christo Samaj in 1887, an indigenous church organized parallel to the Brahmo Samaj, and earlier helped organize the Bengal Christian Conference. He was also a founder of the Indian National Congress, represented Indian Christians at its early sessions, served as president of the Calcutta YMCA, and sat on the Bengal Legislative Council. His nephew Brahmabandhab Upadhyay first learned of Christ through him before his own celebrated conversion.

name: Brahmabandhab Upadhyay
summary: Born Bhavani Charan Banerjee in 1861 into a Bengali Brahmin family, he first passed through the Brahmo Samaj, drawn by Keshub Chandra Sen's devotional theism, and developed a fervent love for Jesus partly through his convert uncle Kali Charan Banerjee. He was baptized a Christian by the Anglican Rev. Heaton on 26 February 1891 and conditionally received into the Roman Catholic Church that September, taking the baptismal name Theophilus. In 1894 he declared himself a sannyasi, adopted saffron robes, and took the name Brahmabandhab Upadhyay, proclaiming himself a 'Hindu-Catholic' — Hindu in custom and culture, Catholic in faith. Through his journals Sophia, The Twentieth Century, and Sandhya he built an indigenous Indian theology, first on the Vedas and later on Advaita Vedanta wedded to Thomism, while also embracing the nationalist cause until his death in 1907.

name: Narayan Vaman Tilak and Lakshmibai Tilak
summary: Narayan Vaman Tilak, born in 1861 into a Kokanastha Chitpavan Brahmin family, was a celebrated Marathi poet, Hindu patriot, and Prarthana Samaj sympathizer when a missionary handed him a Bible on a train; reading the Sermon on the Mount answered his deepest religious questions. Without telling his wife, he was baptized in Bombay on 10 February 1895 by Rev. Tukaram Nathoji, a preacher of formerly untouchable background — a deliberate rejection of caste hierarchy that scandalized his Hindu followers, and two attempts were made on his life. His wife Lakshmibai, born in 1868 into a strict Brahmin family and married to him at eleven, endured five years of separation before she too was baptized with their son at Rahuri in 1900. Narayan served the American Marathi Mission at Ahmednagar for 24 years, composing hundreds of abhangas and kirtans and the Marathi verse Life of Christ, the Khristayan (completed by Lakshmibai after his 1919 death), while Lakshmibai's autobiography Smritichitre became a Marathi classic.

name: Vengal Chakkarai
summary: Born in 1880 into a Hindu Chettiar family of Chennai and educated at the Scottish Mission School and Madras Christian College, Chakkarai came under the influence of Principal William Miller, whose 'fulfillment theology' presented Christ as the answer to Hinduism's deepest longings. Studying the Bible led him to a personal experience of Christ that became the turning point of his life, and he was baptized in the college chapel on 22 February 1903. After practicing law, he joined the Danish Mission as a preacher in 1913 and served twenty years as a missionary while also becoming a disciple of Gandhi, Mayor of Madras (1941–42), and president of the All India Trade Union Congress. With his brother-in-law P. Chenchiah he joined the 'Rethinking Christianity' group, developing a theology of 'Jesus the Avatar' that interpreted the cross through the Hindu longing for moksha.

name: P. Chenchiah
summary: Pandipeddi Chenchiah was born in 1886 in Nellore into a Hindu Brahmin home — his father Adinarayaniah was a prominent Brahmin lawyer — and at the age of fifteen he converted to Christianity together with his entire family, being baptized by the Scottish missionary William Miller. He won a gold medal in philosophy at Madras Christian College, took law degrees, practiced at the Madras High Court, and served as a district judge, resigning rather than yield to government pressure for a favorable verdict. With his brother-in-law Vengal Chakkarai he founded the Madras Christo Samaj and became a leading voice of the 'Rethinking Christianity in India' group, publishing Rethinking Christianity in India (1938) as an Indian answer to Hendrik Kraemer. His theology centered on direct experience of Christ, the Holy Spirit as new cosmic energy, and an openness to Hindu insights, putting him in uneasy tension with the institutional church.

name: Manilal C. Parekh
summary: Born in 1885 at Rajkot, Gujarat, into a family following Jainism and Vaishnavism, Manilal Parekh was drawn toward God during a serious illness in 1903, after which he read the entire Bible alongside Gujarati devotional works and Thomas à Kempis's Imitation of Christ. At Bombay University he encountered Christ through the Christ-centered writings of Keshub Chunder Sen and served for some years in Sen's Church of the New Dispensation before being baptized into the Anglican Church on 6 February 1918. Calling himself a 'Christian Hindu' and a Hindu disciple of Christ, he founded the Hindu Church of Christ, free from Western institutional control, and developed a 'Jesus-Yogi' portrait of Christ from a Hindu point of view. He authored A Hindu's Portrait of Christ and a standard Gujarati church history, remaining a controversial bridge figure between the two faiths until his death in 1967.

name: Ram Gidoomal
summary: Born into a Sindhi Hindu family that had fled India during Partition, Ram Gidoomal was brought up in both Hindu and Sikh faiths and attended a Muslim school in Kenya before his family was forced to flee to London as refugees when he was sixteen. At Imperial College, removed from his family context and searching for a worldview that made sense of the wider world, he began reading about Jesus and was intrigued by the historical basis for his existence, becoming a follower of Christ during his university years. He went on to build a major business career, ran twice for Mayor of London, and after a 1985 visit to a Bombay slum devoted himself to philanthropy, founding the Christmas Cracker charitable trust that mobilized tens of thousands of young people. He has written books including Sari 'n Chips and Reaching Your Hindu Neighbour, ministering for decades among the South Asian diaspora in Britain.

name: Rahil Patel
summary: Rahil Patel served as a Hindu priest in London under a guru, but grew disillusioned, concluding he wanted 'a bigger God than my Hindu guru offered,' and after a tense confrontation he left the priesthood. Parking the whole idea of God while he searched for work, he wandered into a church on a Sunday morning in South Kensington, felt God's presence fall on him 'like a comforting blanket,' heard an inner whisper — 'You are home' — and gave his life to Jesus that day. The transition from a religion of spiritual effort to a relationship of grace required painful 'detox,' healing him, as he testifies, from shame, guilt, resentment, and anger. He has since authored Found by Love: A Hindu Priest Encounters Jesus Christ and serves as a speaker and tutor at the Oxford Centre for Christian Apologetics.

name: Hom Nath
summary: A devout Hindu man in Kathmandu, Hom Nath spent eight or nine months comparing the Hindu scriptures with the Bible, and was struck that in Christianity 'Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and salvation was a free gift,' whereas in Hinduism salvation must be earned — 'if you try to earn salvation, you will fail.' In November 1982 he gave his life to Jesus secretly, knowing his family, society, and the government would oppose him; his family first disbelieved, then grieved, fearing he would end up in prison. He joined an underground Kathmandu church of about thirty converts, which grew to 150–200 over a decade. His wife Sharada, a Brahmin scholar's daughter, converted at nursing college after organizing rival Hindu scripture studies, and their Christian wedding had to be brought forward for fear both would be arrested at the service; both later faced punitive job transfers meant to break their faith.

name: Deena Muthen
summary: Deena Muthen was a practicing Hindu priest in Durban, South Africa, before he converted to Christianity and became a pastor serving the large Indian township of Chatsworth. He has urged Indian Christians to stay proud of their Tamil language and culture, preaching and singing hymns in Tamil and calling churches to become more culturally involved so converts need not surrender their heritage. His stance provoked a public storm when a South African Hindu Maha Sabha leader declared that converts to Christianity 'lose their right to be Indian' and condemned Muthen's Tamil preaching as a trick to entice converts. Muthen rejected the charge, insisting that a hunger for Indian culture exists among Christian Indians and that 'this does not mean that we are not Indian or less than Indian.'

name: Moishe Rosen
summary: Born Martin Rosen (1932) in Kansas City and raised in an Orthodox-leaning but not deeply religious Jewish home in a Yiddish-speaking Denver neighborhood. As a teenager he married Ceil Starr in an Orthodox synagogue, intending to be 'modern American Jews'; about three years later Ceil befriended a Christian woman and converted. Rosen, displeased, began studying the New Testament to prove her wrong, and the study led to his own conversion in 1953. He trained at Northeastern Bible College, was ordained a Baptist minister, served as a missionary to the Jews (1957-1972), and founded the confrontational street-evangelism movement Jews for Jesus in 1973. His ministry made him one of the most controversial Jewish converts of the 20th century, denounced by Jewish communal leaders; he died of cancer in San Francisco in 2010.

name: Arnold Fruchtenbaum
summary: Born in 1943 in Siberia to Polish Jewish parents; his father had fled the Nazis only to be falsely accused of being a Nazi spy and imprisoned by the Communists. With the help of the Israeli underground the family escaped to Displaced Persons camps in Germany, where Arnold received Orthodox Jewish training from his father, before immigrating to New York in 1951. The family was befriended by a Lutheran minister, a contact that led Arnold and his mother to the American Board of Missions to the Jews. At age 13, through studying the Messianic prophecies of the Hebrew Bible, he came to saving faith in Yeshua (Jesus) as Messiah. He went on to earn a Th.M. from Dallas Theological Seminary and a Ph.D. from New York University, and in 1977 founded Ariel Ministries, dedicated to the evangelism of Jewish people; his 'Israelology' made him one of the foremost Messianic theologians.

name: Michael L. Brown
summary: Born in 1955 into a nominally observant Jewish family in New York City, Brown drifted into the rock-music scene as a teenager and became a heroin-shooting, LSD-using drummer. Friends brought him to a Pentecostal church, and in late 1971, at age 16, he converted to faith in Jesus, abandoning drugs virtually overnight. At his father's request he met with the local rabbi, whose challenges drove him to master Hebrew and study the Old Testament deeply to defend his new faith. He earned a Ph.D. in Near Eastern Languages from New York University and became one of the world's foremost Messianic Jewish apologists, author of the five-volume 'Answering Jewish Objections to Jesus' and host of the nationally syndicated 'Line of Fire' radio program.

name: Israel Zolli
summary: Born Israel Anton Zoller in 1881 in Brody (then Austria-Hungary) into a family with 130 years of rabbinical tradition on his mother's side, he became a renowned Scripture and Talmudic scholar. He served as Chief Rabbi of Trieste for 35 years and then as Chief Rabbi of Rome from 1940 to 1945; Catholic scholars had already recognized his learning by inviting him to assist the Pontifical Biblical Commission. After what he described as at least twelve years of serious study and prayer, he and his wife were baptized on February 17, 1945, and he took the Christian name Eugenio to honor Pope Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli) for sheltering Jews during the Nazi occupation. The conversion of the wartime Chief Rabbi of Rome shocked the Jewish world and provoked lasting anger in Italy's Jewish community. He spent his remaining years teaching philosophy at the Sapienza University of Rome and wrote the autobiographical 'Before the Dawn', describing his faith in Christ as the completion, not abandonment, of his Judaism; he died in 1956.
sources: Eugenio Zolli, 'Before the Dawn: Autobiographical Reflections' (book)

name: Jean-Marie Lustiger
summary: Born Aaron Lustiger in 1926 in Paris to non-practicing Polish Jewish immigrants from Bedzin, he encountered a Protestant Bible between the ages of ten and twelve and felt inexplicably drawn to it. Sent to hide with a Christian family in Orleans after the 1940 German occupation, the 13-year-old decided during Holy Week 1940 to convert to Catholicism and was baptized on August 21, 1940, by the Bishop of Orleans, taking the name Jean-Marie. His mother was deported and murdered in Auschwitz in 1943; his surviving father opposed the conversion and even sought the chief rabbi of Paris to annul the baptism. Ordained a priest in 1954, Lustiger became Bishop of Orleans (1979), Archbishop of Paris (1981-2005), and cardinal (1983), a close confidant of John Paul II. He insisted throughout his life, 'I was born Jewish and so I remain,' and co-founded Yahad-In Unum to advance Jewish-Catholic cooperation and document Holocaust mass graves in Ukraine; he died in 2007.

name: Oswald Rufeisen (Brother Daniel)
summary: Born Oswald Rufeisen in Poland in 1922 to a Jewish family, he was a Zionist youth who during World War II worked as a wartime resistance fighter, secretly saving Jewish lives while forced to labor for the Nazis. Sheltered by nuns in a convent, he converted to Catholicism and became the Carmelite monk Brother Daniel. After the war he immigrated to Israel, but the state refused him citizenship under the Law of Return. His 1962 appeal produced the landmark Supreme Court ruling Rufeisen v. Minister of the Interior, which held that a Jew who has voluntarily converted to another religion does not qualify as a Jew for the Law of Return, a precedent later codified in the 1970 amendment. He lived out his life as a monk at the Stella Maris Monastery in Haifa, a living embodiment of the Jewish-Christian identity conflict; he died in 1998.

name: Hugh Montefiore
summary: Born Hugh William Sebag-Montefiore in London in 1920 into one of Britain's best-known Anglo-Jewish families (Sephardic on his father's side, Lithuanian Jewish on his mother's), he converted from Judaism to Christianity at age 16 while still a schoolboy. He liked to describe himself as a 'Jewish Christian' and never disowned his Jewish roots. Ordained an Anglican deacon in 1949 and priest in 1950, he rose to become Bishop of Kingston (1970) and then Bishop of Birmingham (1977-1987). In his 1998 book 'On Being a Jewish Christian' he explored the blessings and problems of holding both identities and issued a heartfelt plea for the Church to formally apologize to the Jewish people for centuries of mistreatment; he died in 2005.
sources: Hugh Montefiore, 'On Being a Jewish Christian' (Hodder & Stoughton, 1998)

name: Leopold Cohn
summary: Born in 1862 in Berezna, Hungary, and orphaned at age seven, Cohn was raised in the Satmar Hasidic tradition and studied at the Pressburg Yeshiva; by his own account he received rabbinic ordination and served as an itinerant rabbi (claims about his surname and rabbinic past were contested in his own day, including by family members in court). After immigrating to the United States in 1892, he encountered the gospel in New York and converted to evangelical Christianity, training at a Presbyterian seminary and being ordained a Baptist minister. In 1894 he founded the Brownsville Mission to the Jews, which became Chosen People Ministries, pioneering the 'Messianic Judaism' approach of honoring Jewish identity within Christian faith and aiding poor Jewish immigrants with food, clothing, medical care, and English classes. He endured bitter, vehement persecution from the Jewish community throughout his ministry, received an honorary Doctor of Divinity from Wheaton College in 1930, and died in Brooklyn in 1937.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: Cohn's claims of rabbinic ordination and his family surname were publicly contested in his lifetime; his 1908 autobiography 'The Story of a Modern Missionary to an Ancient People' is the principal source for his pre-conversion life.

name: Adolph Saphir
summary: Born Aaron Adolph Saphir in 1831 in Pest (Budapest), son of the Jewish merchant Israel Saphir, he was raised in the synagogue on a strict, abstract monotheism that left his heart, in his own words, 'chilly and desolate'. As a boy he was electrified by finding a book titled 'Immanuel, God with Us' in his father's library. In 1843, through the Jewish mission of the Free Church of Scotland in Budapest, the entire Saphir family converted to Christianity. Sent to Edinburgh to train for the Free Church ministry, he studied at Glasgow and Aberdeen, was appointed a missionary to the Jews in Hamburg, and then served as a Presbyterian pastor in England (South Shields, Greenwich, Notting Hill, Belgrave), where his Thursday expository lectures drew crowds and he became a friend of Charles Spurgeon. A prolific theologian, he wrote 'Christ and the Scriptures', 'The Everlasting Nation', and 'The Hidden Life', received a D.D. from Glasgow in 1878, and died in 1891, days after his wife.

name: Joseph Rabinowitz
summary: Born in 1837 in Resina, Bessarabia, Rabinowitz was brought up as a Hasid, later mastered Russian and became a lawyer of wide influence among the Jews of Kishinev, known as a diligent student of the Hebrew Scriptures and Talmud. Around 1882, through study of Messianic prophecy, he confessed Jesus as the Messiah and founded the Novy Israel (New Israel) movement, preaching Christianity to the Jews of Kishinev to great public attention in the Russian press. He was baptized in Berlin on March 24, 1885, using a creed he had written himself in Hebrew, insisting on entering the universal church without losing his Jewish identity. His open conversion to Protestantism estranged many followers, and the Tsarist authorities, while licensing his meetings, forbade him to baptize or administer sacraments; the movement crumbled after his death in Odessa in 1899. The great Hebrew Christian scholar Franz Delitzsch regarded his conversion as the most remarkable since Saul of Tarsus and defended him in print.

name: Stan Telchin
summary: Born in 1924, Telchin was a U.S. Army World War II veteran who became a successful businessman in the Washington, D.C. area, living in a happy, close-knit Jewish family. His world was shaken when his 21-year-old daughter Judy called from college to say she had become a Christian. Determined to win her back, Telchin set out to disprove the Messiahship of Jesus, studying the Bible for the first time in his life; instead the Messianic prophecies convinced him, and he too came to faith. He chronicled the family's story in 'Betrayed!' (1981), which sold more than a million copies in 30 languages and was called by Jews for Jesus 'the single most-read testimony of a Jewish person who has come to faith in Jesus in recent history.' He pastored a nondenominational fellowship in suburban Washington for fourteen years and served with Jews for Jesus from 2003 until his death in 2012.

name: Lon Solomon
summary: Solomon describes his former self as 'a secular Jewish person on drugs' living in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, while a chemistry student at the University of North Carolina. Though neither he nor his friends would have entered a church, someone reached him with the Christian message and he came to faith in Christ, beginning a Christian journey of over fifty years. He went on to earn an M.S. in Near Eastern studies from Johns Hopkins and a doctorate in theology, and became senior pastor of McLean Bible Church in Virginia, growing it from about 300 members to some 13,000. He later founded Lon Solomon Ministries and its nationally aired 'Not a Sermon, Just a Thought' radio spots, continuing to proclaim the gospel he once resisted.

name: Zvi Kalisher
summary: Born Henryk Weichert in Poland around 1928, Zvi's mother placed him in an orphanage when Germany invaded in 1939, gambling that his blond hair and blue eyes would help him survive; he spent the war hiding his Jewish identity and lost his entire family in the Warsaw Ghetto. At 18, alone in the world, he sailed to British Mandate Palestine and fought in Israel's War of Independence (1948-49). After the war he picked up a Hebrew Bible, intending to improve his Hebrew and find answers about God; puzzling through the Psalms and the Messianic passages, he came to faith in Jesus as the Messiah of Israel. He became one of Israel's most fearless street evangelists, debating Isaiah 53 and Psalm 110 with ultra-Orthodox rabbis in Jerusalem's yeshivas and synagogues, often having rocks thrown at him and being mocked and spat upon. His 'Zvi' column ran for decades in Israel My Glory magazine, and his testimony was published as 'The Best of Zvi' and in Elwood McQuaid's biography 'Zvi: The Miraculous Story of Triumph over the Holocaust'; he died in 2014, and his children and grandchildren continue his witness.
sources: Elwood McQuaid, 'Zvi: The Miraculous Story of Triumph over the Holocaust' (Friends of Israel, 2000)

name: David H. Stern
summary: Born in Los Angeles in 1935, the great-grandson of two of the city's first twenty Jews, Stern earned a Ph.D. in economics from Princeton and became a professor at UCLA. In 1972 he came to faith in Yeshua the Messiah, then earned a Master of Divinity at Fuller Theological Seminary and did graduate work at the University of Judaism. In 1979 he and his family made aliyah and settled in Jerusalem. Stern became one of the founding scholars of modern Messianic Judaism: his 'Jewish New Testament' (1989) and 'Complete Jewish Bible' restored the New Testament's Jewishness for English readers, his 'Jewish New Testament Commentary' addressed Jewish objections verse by verse, and his 'Messianic Jewish Manifesto' gave the movement its ideology, insisting believers could be simultaneously 100% Messianic and 100% Jewish.
sources: David H. Stern, 'Complete Jewish Bible' (Messianic Jewish Publishers)

name: Susan Perlman
summary: Raised in a traditional Jewish home in East New York, Brooklyn, Perlman began searching for deeper answers after her father's death, when her rabbi could only say they could 'hope' there was something beyond this life. During the Jesus movement era she came to faith in Jesus in 1971, convinced she was the only Jew in the world who believed in him. Her family was devastated: her mother told her it would have been better had she come home on drugs or pregnant, and relatives responded with shame, embarrassment, anger, and pity. Three months later a Christian couple mentioned other Jewish believers, and in 1972 Moishe Rosen invited her to California, where she became a co-founder of Jews for Jesus. She served more than forty years as communications director, pioneering the ministry's evangelistic media, and later as Chief Partnership Officer; she has remained, in her words, 'a happily single missionary.'

name: Olivier Melnick
summary: Born and raised in Paris in a secular Jewish family, Melnick is the son of two Holocaust survivors; his maternal grandfather was killed by the Nazis, and his parents, like many survivors, lost any shred of faith in God. He attended synagogue once a year for Yom Kippur only to appease family elders, kept nothing of the tradition, and simply 'knew' that Jesus was not for the Jews. He met his future wife, an American Gentile Christian, who urged him to actually read the Bible; the Messianic prophecies in the Jewish Scriptures convinced him, and he came to faith in the summer of 1983. The couple moved to the United States, where he earned degrees from Moody Bible Institute and Dallas Theological Seminary and joined Chosen People Ministries in 1998 as Northwest regional director. He became an internationally known speaker and author on antisemitism ('They Have Conspired Against You') and now leads Shalom in Messiah Ministries.

name: Kokeb Gedamu
summary: Born into a priestly lineage within the Beta Israel community of Ethiopian Jews, Gedamu is on record as having encountered Yeshua (Jesus) during travels through the Sudan, an event that set the course of his life and calling. He now testifies publicly as 'Rabbi Kokeb,' and his story is also told in his book 'Journey Beyond Imagination.' Public documentation beyond a published video interview is currently thin, so details of the conversion moment and its aftermath await fuller verification.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION: only source located is a published interview ('Ethiopian Jews, an Interview with Rabbi Kokeb Gedamu') referencing his book 'Journey Beyond Imagination'; independent corroboration of the book and conversion details not yet found.

name: Mitsuo Fuchida
summary: Raised in the State Shinto ideology of imperial Japan, Mitsuo Fuchida (1902-1976) led the air attack on Pearl Harbor as a captain in the Imperial Japanese Navy. After the war he returned to farming, haunted by the war's meaninglessness, and began questioning his worldview after encounters with former POWs and the Christian kindness shown to them by Peggy Covell. In 1950 a fellow veteran handed him the testimony tract of Jacob DeShazer, the Doolittle Raider who had become a Christian while imprisoned by the Japanese; struck by DeShazer's account of Bible reading turning hatred into love, Fuchida bought a Bible. He later wrote that he was 'strongly impressed and captivated,' and on April 14, 1950 he accepted Jesus Christ as his personal Savior. For the next 25 years Fuchida served as a traveling evangelist across Japan, the United States and Europe, preaching forgiveness and reconciliation until his death in 1976.

name: Toyohiko Kagawa
summary: Born in Kobe in 1888, Toyohiko Kagawa was the orphaned son of a businessman and a concubine, raised amid Japan's traditional Buddhist-Shinto milieu with little religious conviction. Hoping to learn English, he enrolled in a Bible class taught by American Presbyterian missionaries Drs. Harry Myers and Charles Logan, who took the boy into their homes. He converted to evangelical Protestant Christianity in his teens and was disowned by his extended family for it. After studying theology at Tokyo Presbyterian College, Kobe Seminary and Princeton, he moved in 1909 into a six-foot-square hut in Kobe's Shinkawa slums to live among the poor. Kagawa became Japan's most famous Christian social reformer - organizing labor unions, fighting prostitution and intemperance, campaigning for universal suffrage, and founding cooperatives, schools, hospitals and churches - and was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize and the Nobel Prize in Literature.

name: Uemura Masahisa
summary: Born Michitaro in 1858 into a hatamoto (bannerman) samurai family steeped in Confucian ethics, Uemura Masahisa grew up in the turmoil of the Meiji Restoration, which bankrupted his household. Sent to Tokyo to study, he enrolled in the preparatory school of American missionary James Hamilton Ballagh, encountered Christianity, and was baptized in June 1873 at the Yokohama Public Church; his parents and brothers were later baptized too. Determined to become an evangelist, he trained at the United Seminary and was ordained in 1880. Uemura became one of Japan's leading pastors and theologians, founding Fujimicho Church in Tokyo (which he led for life), pioneering self-supporting Japanese churches free of foreign mission control, and shaping evangelical Protestant thought in the Meiji and Taisho eras.

name: Takashi Nagai
summary: Takashi Nagai (1908-1951) was raised in a Shinto family in Matsue and, as a Nagasaki medical student, became a convinced materialist who dismissed religion as superstition. His mother's death in 1930 unsettled his atheism, and he spent five years wrestling with Blaise Pascal's Pensees and the question 'What is the meaning of our lives?' Boarding with the Moriyama family - descendants of Japan's 'hidden Christians' - and drawn to their devout Catholic daughter Midori, he received baptism as 'Paul' on June 12, 1934, and married Midori that August. He became a pioneer in radiology, served as a military surgeon in China, and survived the Nagasaki atomic bombing of August 9, 1945, in which Midori died at ground zero. From his sickbed he wrote The Bells of Nagasaki and other works preaching radical forgiveness and peace, becoming one of modern Japan's most beloved Catholic voices; his cause for sainthood is under consideration.

name: Tsubasa Yamanaka
summary: Born into a third-generation Soka Gakkai family in Japan, Tsubasa Yamanaka was raised attending the new religion's meetings but treated them as mere family tradition. When his family fell into painful conflict at age 19, he threw himself into Soka Gakkai practice, joining the volunteer Soka Group - but grew troubled seeing members sacrifice jobs and marriages for the organization, and by a senior member's admission that his kindness was done to gain merit (kotoku). Realizing the kindness around him was motivated by self-interest, he cut all ties with Soka Gakkai. He writes that the experience taught him the difference between a merit-based religion and faith based on grace, leading him to recognize the truth of Christianity - salvation freely given through Jesus Christ. He published his testimony in 2025.

name: Yun Chi-ho
summary: Yun Chi-ho (1864-1945) was born into a yangban aristocratic family and educated from childhood in Confucian classics, even attempting the civil-service examinations at age twelve. Exiled to China after his father's political fall, he studied at the Anglo-Chinese College in Shanghai, where Bible reading and religious lectures convinced him that Confucian proverbs could not satisfy the soul's demands. In March 1887 he became a Protestant Christian - the first Korean convert of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South - writing that he had become conscious of his wickedness and his need of a purer soul. Returning to Korea, he became a leader of Korean Methodism: educator, YMCA director, headmaster of Songdo Academy, and president of Yeonhui University. He also kept a famous English-language diary (1883-1943) that remains a key source on Korea's encounter with Christianity and modernity.

name: Yi Sujong
summary: Sujeong Yi (1842-1886) was a Confucian scholar-official of the Joseon dynasty who rescued Queen Min during the 1882 military revolt and was sent to Tokyo to study Western civilization. There, conversations with Japanese Christians and Bible study led him to conclude Protestant Christianity was superior to Confucianism, Buddhism and Catholicism; he was baptized in 1883 by Presbyterian missionary George W. Knox. Yi went on to translate the Gospel of Mark into Korean (6,000 copies printed in 1885), found a Korean church in Tokyo, and write to American Christians urging them to send missionaries to Korea - the first Korean to request foreign missions. Though he died young, before missionaries arrived in Korea, his translation and advocacy laid the foundation for Korean Protestantism.

name: Kim Ku
summary: Kim Ku (1876-1949) grew up in a peasant family in Hwanghae Province educated in the Confucian classics, and as a young man led Tonghak (Eastern Learning) peasant troops against Japanese encroachment; imprisoned and nearly executed in 1897-98, he escaped and wandered Korea, even briefly trying life as a Buddhist monk. Convinced that neither old Confucianism nor Buddhism could awaken the nation, he was urged toward Christianity in 1903 by a former Tonghak comrade turned Presbyterian helper; Kim read Scripture and tracts, attended a Bible class in Haeju, and joined the Presbyterian church. He threw himself into Christian education and evangelism, studying doctrine at Pyongyang and leading Sunday services. Kim Ku went on to become the most revered leader of Korea's independence movement and head of the Korean Provisional Government, his Christian faith shaping his lifelong nationalism. NOTE: he briefly lived as a Buddhist monk, so this entry may overlap the Buddhist-background assignment - included here on the judgment that his formative background was Confucian/Tonghak.

name: Xi Shengmo
summary: Born Xi Zizhi around 1836 near Linfen, Shanxi, he was a Confucian scholar who became enslaved to opium. English Methodist missionary David Hill introduced him to Christianity in the late 1870s; Xi became a Christian in 1879 at age 44 and testified that after native and foreign medicines failed, he prayed for the Holy Spirit while reading the New Testament and was delivered from opium. Baptized in November 1880, he took the name Shengmo - 'Conqueror of Demons' - and opened opium refuges that combined medical treatment with prayer and Bible reading, founding churches and clinics across Shanxi with such energy that missionaries largely stood aside. 'Pastor Hsi' became the most written-about 19th-century Chinese Protestant, subject of Geraldine Taylor's two-volume biography One of China's Scholars: The Culture and Conversion of a Confucianist.

name: Feng Yuxiang
summary: Feng Yuxiang (1882-1948) was born into poverty - his father joined the Qing army to make ends meet - and Feng himself enlisted at age ten, rising through the Beiyang Army with no religious background beyond China's folk traditions. In 1913, while suffering from back sores, a Christian friend introduced him to an American church hospital; impressed that the doctors prayed before and after procedures, and crediting God's grace for his recovery, he was baptized into the Methodist Episcopal Church in 1914 with the encouragement of diplomat Wang Zhengting. Known from 1919 as the 'Christian General,' he governed his territories with paternalistic Christian socialism - banning prostitution, gambling and opium - and zealously evangelized his troops. Though he later moved politically leftward and died in a 1948 ship fire, his conversion remains one of modern China's most famous.

name: Lu Zhengxiang
summary: Lu Zhengxiang (1871-1949), known in the West as Lou Tseng-Tsiang, was raised as a Confucianist and trained as a Qing diplomat, serving as interpreter in St. Petersburg where his mentor Xu Jingcheng urged him to study Christianity, saying 'Europe's strength is found... in her religion.' He was baptized a Catholic (received into the Church and confirmed by the Archbishop of St. Petersburg), and went on to become twice Premier of the Republic of China and head of China's delegation at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference. His devout Belgian Catholic wife deepened his faith; after her death in 1926 he retired from politics and entered the Benedictine abbey of Sint-Andries in Bruges as Dom Pierre-Celestin, ordained a priest in 1935 and named titular abbot by Pius XII in 1946. In his memoir Souvenirs et Pensees (Ways of Confucius and of Christ) he argued that Christianity fulfills rather than destroys Confucianism.

name: Lee Teng-hui
summary: Lee Teng-hui (1923-2020) was born in Japanese-ruled Taiwan into a Hakka family of Sanzhi, raised amid Taiwan's traditional folk religion and ancestor veneration. As a young man he encountered Christianity and was baptized in 1961, joining the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan. Throughout his political career - rising to become Taiwan's president (1988-2000) and the architect of its democratic transition - he regularly preached lay sermons in churches on themes of service and humility. His Christian faith, lived openly in public life, made him one of the most prominent Taiwanese converts from a traditional Chinese religious background. He died in 2020 as an elder of the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan.

name: Paul Wong
summary: Dr. Paul Wong was brought up in Hong Kong in Chinese folk religion - a mix of Buddhist temple visits, Taoist practice and Confucian teachings - and intellectually resisted Christianity through his school years, arguing against the Bible. Seeds were sown at St. Stephen's College and Pui Ching, but the decisive turn came in 1958 when, as a police interpreter, he met missionary Lee Hobel of the Oriental Missionary Society on the Peak Tram; Hobel's intercessory prayers were followed by startling answers - his father's recovery from vomiting blood, his brother's permission to enter Hong Kong, and relief from debt. One night in December 1958 Wong broke down in repentance, and in a small chapel he prayed the sinner's prayer with Hobel kneeling beside him, surrendering his life to Christ. He became a prolific Christian writer, counselor and evangelist in Hong Kong, and led his mother and brothers to faith. His conversion is documented in his published online autobiography.

name: Harbhajan Singh
summary: Harbhajan Singh was a Sikh former landlord in rural Punjab who, by his own account, was a drunkard given to 'all kinds of bad things' before Christ saved him in 1986. After his conversion he began preaching healing and inner peace to fellow Sikhs, many of whom regard Jesus as a figure of mercy. In 1991 he built the Open Door Church in the village of Khojewala despite death threats and a youth-committee ban on construction; by 2003 it had 2,800 baptized members, making it one of the largest buildings in the area with a cross on its gate. His ministry continued amid threats from Hindu-nationalist groups, and he told Christianity Today, 'You can't do God's work if you are afraid. I stood. The Lord saves and protects.'

name: Surinder Kaur
summary: Born in a military hospital in Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, into a devout Sikh family (her father served in the Indian Army), Surinder attended Sikh and sometimes Hindu temples with her family and studied at Catholic schools without ever knowing Jesus as more than one of many gods. In 1991, as a struggling 12th-grade student in Ahmednagar, a senior named Anita shared the gospel with her; after testing God by promising not to cheat in her exams, she borrowed a Bible and studied it daily under a stone shelter for 40 days. One day the verse John 14:6 ('I am the way and the truth and the life') appeared visually magnified on the page, she surrendered to Christ, and she placed third in her college without cheating. Her family tried to stamp out her faith through physical assault, a psychiatric evaluation, Sikh evangelists, and even a witch doctor, but she persevered; she now serves as Christianity Today's South Asia editor and has spent 22 years in full-time ministry across five continents, including advocacy for persecuted Christians.

name: Binder Mahil
summary: Binder Mahil was born into a Jatt-caste Sikh family in Mahilgailan, Punjab, an 'average Sikh' who attended the gurdwara irregularly and spent Sundays drinking with friends. He emigrated to Canada at 19 in 1978; at his non-Christian father's urging he visited a Hindi worship service at South Abbotsford Mennonite Brethren Church, heard the gospel, and was baptized by Pastor David Manuel in 1983. Burdened to reach Punjabi Sikhs in their own language, he started house fellowships and in 1998 co-founded the Punjabi Christian Centre at Bear Creek Community Church in Surrey, B.C., where he was ordained volunteer pastor in 2001. In 2002 he helped plant the Doaba Punjabi Christian Sabha in Banga, Punjab — funded partly by Sikh donors impressed by the converts' changed lives — and he produces the Punjabi radio program 'Mukti da Raah' with Trans World Radio plus evangelistic pamphlets that quote Sikh scriptures to present Christ as the Shabad (Word).

name: Balhar Singh
summary: Balhar Singh was a Sikh who accepted Christ in 1981 while working in West Germany. He returned to India, attended Bible school from 1982 to 1986, and began preaching, starting a church in 1988 with the stated purpose of ministering to the Indian people — a work that bore fruit, including 18 Hindu baptisms over 11 years. He became pastor of the Doaba Punjabi Christian Sabha in Banga, Punjab, the congregation planted with Canadian Sikh-convert partners in 2002 that drew worshippers from Hindu and Sikh backgrounds. Beyond pastoring, he translates Christian literature from English into Punjabi for evangelical organizations and was writing what would be the first-ever Punjabi Bible concordance.

name: Gurmit Singh
summary: Gurmit Singh Virk (born 1965), the Singaporean actor famous as Phua Chu Kang, was born to a Sikh Indian father, Chainchal Singh Virk, and a mixed Chinese-Japanese mother, and was brought up as a Sikh in a poor family. His younger sisters became Christians through a school Bible study class — which angered him, since his father despised Christianity as a 'white man's religion' — and when his mother was diagnosed with stage-four stomach cancer and given six months to live, the sisters invited a pastor to pray for her; she said the sinner's prayer that day. The sisters then invited Gurmit to an evangelistic rally at Singapore's National Stadium, where he heard a voice ask, 'Would you like to be my child?'; he knelt, prayed the sinner's prayer, and became a Christian in 1985. Reading Matthew 7:7, he prayed for his mother's healing, and doctors later declared her cancer inexplicably gone — she lived sixteen more years. He went on to a celebrated acting career and has publicly shared his testimony of coming to know Jesus as Lord and Saviour before audiences of thousands.

name: Gurmukh Singh
summary: Gurmukh Singh was born into a Sikh family in India and married in a Sikh temple; after nine years of long, poorly paid work he suffered constant back pain and found no help at Sikh and Hindu temples or a mosque. His mother took his long-childless sister-in-law — also of Sikh background — to a house-church prayer meeting next door, where she was prayed for and conceived after 18 barren years; his sick brother was likewise healed, and when the pastor prayed for Gurmukh in Jesus' name his own pain left permanently. He began attending the house meetings, decided to follow Jesus, and was baptized in water and the Holy Spirit. His wife, initially unhappy, came to believe after seeing answered prayers and was baptized by their Indian pastor in a river in India; his family in India are now believers, and he worships with a house church in Bristol, England, while praying for his still-Sikh in-laws.

name: Raspal
summary: Pastor Raspal of Gurdaspur district, Punjab, was once a religious Sikh, though his mother was Christian; he became a pastor in 2000 after coming to faith himself. He supports his family by working as a painter while holding evening prayer meetings, and has turned a hall in his house into a church for his village congregation. His conversion testimony is tied to family healings he attributes to church prayer — his father's recovery from a tumour and stroke, and his sister's healing from a throat lump without losing her voice. His son Simon, a graduate, is now training to become a pastor as well.

name: Sangeeta Jain
summary: Sangeeta Jain was born and raised in the United States in a devout Jain family and knew nothing of Christ until her whole family became followers of Jesus in 1990. The turning point came on June 14, 1986, when a devastating car accident left ten-year-old Sangeeta confined to a wheelchair, forcing her to relearn basic daily life while learning to trust God. Undeterred by disability, she earned a bachelor's in electrical engineering and a law degree, worked as an advisor to two high court judges, won Miss Teen of Washington in 1993 as the first wheelchair contestant in the world, and placed third runner-up in the Miss Teen of America pageant. She and her family later settled in India, where they actively share her testimony of God's healing and grace with schoolchildren, churches, hospitals, and civic groups in India and the US, and are associated with the karma2grace.org dialogue ministry.
sources: NEEDS VERIFICATION — sourced from a YouTube testimony description and ministry site only: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dGmOiOsEIBE

name: Ramin Parsa
summary: Raised as a Shiite Muslim in Iran, Ramin Parsa fell into suicidal despair after his father died when Ramin was nineteen. He heard the gospel for the first time through satellite television. Resistant at first, he finally prayed, 'Jesus, if you are God's Son, come into my heart, help me, and save me.' He reported immediately feeling heat, weeping, and receiving peace and joy as his hopelessness, guilt, and shame lifted. (Via Renewal Journal.)

name: John Taimoor
summary: Raised in a Pashtun Muslim setting near the Pakistan-Afghanistan border, John Taimoor first grew curious about Jesus at fourteen when he found the name Isa in the Quran. He searched two years for a 'Book of Isa' until a passing missionary gave him a New Testament. Reading Matthew 5 at home, he experienced what he understood as regeneration by the Holy Spirit, saying he was saved without an altar call or another person's help. Within six months he concluded that Jesus Christ is God in human flesh. (Via Renewal Journal.)

name: The 24-year-old sheikh of Amuria, Uganda
summary: A 24-year-old Muslim sheikh trained in Islamic proselytization traveled to Amuria, Uganda, intending to kill Bishop George Edweu of the Pentecostal Upright Church and destroy the congregation. During the December 4 service, the bishop's message on hearing and understanding the voice of God convicted him of sin. He rushed to the podium, fell at the bishop's feet, confessed, 'I was sent to kill you and destroy the church,' repented in tears, and put his faith in Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. He went into hiding with his wife and two small children under death threats. (Convert unnamed; year of the service unstated in the source. Via Renewal Journal.)

name: Sabina (Central Asian believer)
summary: Sabina, described as a 63-year-old Muslim woman in Central Asia (country unnamed), was declared dead after a coma and spent two days in a morgue. After reviving following a vision, she went directly to a Pentecostal church and surrendered her life to Christ; her family members later became Christians. CAUTION: first name only, country and date unstated, extraordinary claims rest on a thin single-source chain; needs corroboration before citing. (Via Renewal Journal.)

name: Munaf Ali (pseudonym)
summary: Munaf, an imam in an unnamed Middle Eastern country, opposed Christians and reportedly died after collapsing. He claimed Jesus appeared to him, explained the gospel, and returned him to life. Regaining consciousness during burial preparations, he publicly confessed Jesus and became a witness. CAUTION: name changed for security (pseudonym preserved here), country unnamed, extraordinary claims, single source chain (Bibles4Mideast); needs corroboration before citing. (Via Renewal Journal.)

name: Nathan (Iranian believer, name protected)
summary: Nathan grew up in a Muslim family in Tehran; his devout Muslim mother taught him Islamic practices diligently, and he was haunted by fear of losing his parents because of uncertainty about salvation. A Christian relative visited and shared the gospel; though taught the Bible was corrupted, her words about Jesus freeing them from fear resonated. 'Later, I found myself on my knees, asking Jesus to save me.' His mother was undergoing her own transformation at the same time, and Nathan, his mother, father, and brother all embraced Christ, finding refuge in a secret house church. He left Iran as a refugee in 2013 and now plants churches and leads an online fellowship for secret house churches in Iran and Afghanistan from North Carolina. (Name likely protected given the Iranian context; no conversion date stated. Via Renewal Journal.)

name: Omar (Meccan pilgrim)
summary: Omar, a Muslim pilgrim, completed the Hajj to Mecca seeking hope and peace but finished all the rites still feeling empty. At the bus station a driver told him, 'Just go sit on that rock and talk to Isa (Jesus).' Omar did; the moment he said the name 'Isa,' his body shook and he felt power filling his heart and body for two hours. The bus and driver were gone when he returned. Back home he found a man with a JESUS film DVD; watching it, he recognized the actor: 'That's the driver in the bus! He's the One who told me to talk to Isa!' After the full gospel presentation, 'Omar surrendered his life to Jesus as his Savior and Lord,' and a believer in a neighboring country is discipling him. (First name only; date unstated; account rests on the JESUS Film Project report. Via Renewal Journal.)

name: The mosque leader's son (Isfara, Tajikistan)
summary: On January 20, 2004, the son of a local mosque leader shot and killed Pastor Sergei Bessarab in Isfara, Tajikistan, where Bessarab's church was growing as Muslims turned to Christ. Convicted and imprisoned, the killer was eventually celled with a Christian prisoner whom Bessarab himself had led to Christ and discipled. Over time, the mosque leader's son became Bessarab's spiritual grandson, placing his trust in Christ. CAUTION: convert unnamed, no conversion date stated, thirdhand chain (front-line worker to widow to reporter); qualifies in substance but thin. (Via Renewal Journal.)

name: The West African sheikh
summary: In an unnamed West African town, a sheikh's mother began manifesting demonic spirits; witch doctors and Muslim marabouts reading the Qur'an could not help her. In a lucid moment she ran to the home of a Christian woman, collapsed, and lay motionless for eight days while believers prayed; on the eighth day the spirits left and she stood healed. The sheikh came running, saw his mother eating and in her right mind, immediately collapsed to his knees and begged to be taught about their God, and that day both he and his mother became followers of Jesus. Muslim leaders armed themselves over his 'betrayal of Islam'; he forgave them, and he now plants multiplying churches (17 small churches, about 125 new Christians across 70 villages). CAUTION: sheikh unnamed, country and date unstated. (Via Renewal Journal.)

name: Syrian refugee family of eight (Jordan)
summary: A Syrian refugee family of eight lived in a white tent in Jordan. The night before a visit, a glowing man in white opened their tent door and said, 'Hello, my name is Jesus and I am sending a man tomorrow named Daniel to tell you more about me.' The next day a 24-year-old missionary named Daniel walked in and announced, 'Hi, I'm Daniel and I'm here to tell you about Jesus.' He explained the gospel and the whole family converted. The father had served in the Free Syrian Army, had known bloodshed, and was a devout Muslim; the family now plants underground churches in Jordan. CAUTION: group account, every family member unnamed, no date stated; kept with explicit caution. (Via Renewal Journal, January 2017 archive.)
